At Medium effort, Fable 5.2 matches Opus 5.5’s top score for about 40% of the cost per task. BenchCAD 2.1 (with tools) Accuracy vs. cost Fable 5.2 Opus 5.5 Fable 5.1 BenchCAD 2.1 measures hardware engineering, specifically how closely a model’s designs match reference geometry and circuits, and is scored 0–100 with partial credit. At Max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 83.5, ahead of Opus 5.5 (65.3) and Fable 5.1 (44.4). Humanity’s Last Exam (with tools) Accuracy vs. cost Fable 5.2 Opus 5.5 Fable 5.1 Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) is a test of expert-level academic knowledge and reasoning. At Low effort, Fable 5.2 matches Opus 5.5’s top score for less than one-tenth of the cost per task. Chartography (no tools) Accuracy vs. cost Fable 5.2 Opus 5.5 Fable 5.1 Chartography tests how accurately a model can read charts and figures. At Medium effort, Fable 5.2 scores 66.4%, ahead of Opus 5.5 at Max effort (64.4%) for less than one-tenth of the cost per task. Coding Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests. As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below). Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks: Vercel Shopify Datadog Unity Uber Oracle iGent Snowflake Cognition Vercel Shopify Datadog Unity Uber Oracle iGent Snowflake Cognition Quote “The model is in my head. It understands the intent behind every prompt I’ve given it. I haven’t had to say ‘No, I meant…’ a single time. Projects we’ve been pushing along with other models for weeks got finished and approved by our teammates in a few days with Claude Fable 5.2, and the humans reviewing its code had less to say.” Company Vercel Author Joe Haddad, Member of Technical Staff Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 is great for taking a loose idea and refining it. Its answers are really well-considered, and within a few turns I can almost always say ‘ok, go do that,’ and trust that it’ll complete it with little intervention. It feels like working with another staff-level engineer.” Company Shopify Author Tom Pritchard, Staff Engineer Quote “You can just throw Claude Fable 5.2 at new, ambiguous systems it has never seen before, and it will figure out how to actually work within them. It’s almost like an incident commander that can send out faster models to get quick signals and coordinate, which removes that burden from me as an operator.” Company Datadog Author Matt Lee, Senior Staff Engineer Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 can complete tasks that previous models struggled with. The clearest examples so far are building higher-quality 3D scenes from scratch and rebuilding an experience from a visual reference. It’s very strong on the harder game-dev tasks, where it keeps iterating and improving instead of getting stuck.” Company Unity Author Sam Zhang, Creative Technologist Quote “I had Claude Fable 5.2 run a 10–12 hour security audit. It sent out about 170 reviewer agents and came back with a write-up, fix pull requests and a policy proposal. It works until the job is actually complete instead of stopping at a plausible checkpoint. Its self-correction and honesty about gaps impressed me. At High effort, I’d use this over what I run today for long unattended audits and doc-heavy work.” Company Uber Author Andrew Mager, Staff Engineer, Agentic Systems Quote “In one test combining country debt summaries, repayment history, and regional benchmarks, Claude Fable 5.2 generated SQL that returned the expected results. The SQL generated by two other models also ran successfully, but incorrectly summed country-level summary amounts, producing values 5–8x the expected amounts. Getting these business calculations right is why we see value in using Fable 5.2 for enterprise SQL generation.” Company Oracle Author Liyu Gong, Senior Manager of Machine Learning Quote “In a single session, Claude Fable 5.2 built a hypervisor, the software that walls off virtual computers sharing one machine. Its core is mathematically proven to keep them apart. More than 3,500 machine-checked proofs cover every case, not just the ones you test. It’s the first model I’ve seen break a problem this large into pieces it can prove, fit them together, and keep taking on more ambitious work. A very clear upgrade from Fable 5.1.” Company iGent Author Sean Ward, Co-Founder and CEO Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 is the strongest model we have measured on data-eng-bench, our open-source benchmark of 103 data-engineering tasks. It solved tasks consistently across repeated runs and passed every interactive coding task we gave it.” Company Snowflake Author Bala Kasiviswanathan, VP of AI and Developer Experience Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 says it doesn’t know things instead of hallucinating. At one point it told me its last estimate was wrong and that it wouldn’t give a number until it had measured the change. Very impressive!” Company Cognition Author Adhyyan Sekhsaria, Member of Technical Staff Cybersecurity Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.² CVE Rediscovery Accuracy vs. cost Mythos 5.2 Opus 5.5 Mythos 5.1 CVE Rediscovery is an internal cybersecurity evaluation that assesses how many published CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) a model can independently find when given a snapshot of the project before a CVE was fixed. Our October 2026 run against 1,829 CVEs showed Claude Mythos 5.2 outperformed Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 at every effort level. Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program , which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security , which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP. Rubrik Mozilla Rubrik Mozilla Quote “We have worked closely with Anthropic’s new model, Claude Mythos 5.2, to do a next round of high-fidelity threat discovery and elimination within our own systems for potential issues we did not uncover with earlier Mythos models. The output is more readable and empowered our team to spot-check faster and more easily. We built our Code Guardian harness with Mythos 5.1, and we’d switch to Mythos 5.2 to give our customers more powerful cyber capabilities.” Company Rubrik Author Arvind Nithrakashyap, Co-Founder and Chief Technology Officer Quote “Claude Mythos 5.2 is astonishingly good. We’ve worked closely with the Anthropic team all year to harden Firefox with successive generations of Claude models, and each round has left fewer, subtler bugs to find. Even so, Mythos 5.2 roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery metrics of Mythos 5.1 across respective scanning campaigns.” Company Mozilla Author Brian Grinstead, Distinguished Engineer Science and engineering Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas. Theoretical physics Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics. Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here . Protein folding Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid , can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together. Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies: Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Quote “This acceleration could save meaningful time and cost from our capsid folding pipeline, enabling us to deploy compute more efficiently across many capsid properties that are needed for a genetic medicine. We are excited to help Anthropic push the reasoning capabilities further to reduce the cost of designing capsids overall.” Company Dyno Therapeutics Author Sam Sinai, Cofounder and Head of AI Quote “Large protein assemblies, including capsids, remain an open problem for protein modeling, due to the complexity of accurately predicting and positioning the structures of dozens of individual macromolecules, not to mention the inordinately high computational costs involved. Claude’s approach cleverly tackles this problem for symmetric assemblies, making it possible for individual scientists to model systems on personal workstations that would otherwise require dedicated clusters.” Company Columbia University Author Mohammed AlQuraishi, Assistant Professor of Systems Biology and Computer Science Quote “Biohub’s goal in open-sourcing ESMFold2 was to enable the scientific community to build on the biology it has learned. We are excited to see Claude prototype a new sampling procedure that enables predictions of large, symmetric complexes such as AAV capsids—a protein used to deliver gene therapies. We will continue to incorporate such contributions from the community that extend our tools to important application domains.” Company Biohub Author Zeming Lin, Principal Research Scientist Mathematics Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas. Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem , performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30. Read more about the formalization here . Fermat’s Last Theorem proof formalization Completion over time Fable 5.2 Opus 5.5 Formalizing the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in the mathematical programming language Lean. Each line shows the proportion of the full formalization that Fable 5.2 (green line) and Opus 5.5 (orange line) had completed over 30 hours with about 1,000 agents, and a single run per model. At the dashed line (18 hours), both teams resumed from their last save with 12 more hours. Hardware and robotics Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world , showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots. Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode , a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards. Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here . Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots. RoboDojo (average) Max score by model Gemini 4 Argon GPT-6 Astra Fable 5.1 Opus 5.5 Fable 5.2 RoboDojo Sim tests control of a simulated two-arm robot. Scores are based on our internal runs for each model using the highest available effort level. At Max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 64.9%, more than double GPT-6 Astra (29.8%) and Fable 5.1 (27.6%). Research and analysis Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgment on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses. Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2: Jump Trading Balyasny Asset Management Discovered Materials IMC Harvey Fundamental Research Labs XTX Markets Box Jump Trading Balyasny Asset Management Discovered Materials IMC Harvey Fundamental Research Labs XTX Markets Box Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 is incredible at playing every major role within a research system: defining questions, interpreting, coordinating, and of course finding and implementing the key ideas. Definitely one of the strongest on taste and judgment that we’ve seen. In an internal research automation benchmark, it achieved a full 10% lower error than the next best model.” Company Jump Trading Author Lucas Baker, Head of LLM R&D Quote “In a recent evaluation, we asked Claude Fable 5.2 to investigate how one organization tested a new integration in its core technology systems. It traced the answer to the right sources and didn’t overstate what the evidence showed. It also flagged that the question’s framing could be misleading. In investment research, that restraint makes clear what remains unknown and where the market may be mispricing risk or opportunity.” Company Balyasny Asset Management Author Ashish Malik, AI Researcher Quote “Phonon calculations are one of the most expensive routine steps in computational materials science, which is why labs often skip stability checks when screening new materials. Claude Fable 5.2 made Quantum ESPRESSO’s phonon code about 36 times faster on average than stock on the same GPU, taking our 13 benchmark cases from 3.3 hours to under four minutes. That beats Fable 5.1’s speedup by 3–4 times.” Company Discovered Materials Author Akash Ramdas, Co-Founder Quote “With Fable 5.1 we saw the first glimmers of a model coming up with truly innovative research ideas. Claude Fable 5.2 continues that trend. It had the same insight we were impressed with from Fable 5.1 and then came up with a second, entirely new angle. It achieved new best scores on three of the four quant research problems we’ve finished. We’d like to use it for high-impact, long-running research tasks, or for coordinating teams of other models.” Company IMC Author Marquis Wong, Principal AI Engineer Quote “In an I-9 compliance review, Claude Fable 5.2 gave the client clearer direction than Fable 5.1. It identified the employees needing immediate attention and explained how to correct each issue and who should act. It’s an exciting improvement in the model’s ability to give practical legal guidance.” Company Harvey Author Niko Grupen, Head of AI Research Quote “On one task, Claude Fable 5.2 had to pull a company’s financials out of its 10-K into a forecasting model, and the template didn’t say whether a metric should be the reported figure or calculated. It inferred the author’s intent from the cell formatting, caught that the regional numbers didn’t sum to the reported total, and got every cell right. Better judgment calls like that are the main reason it scored 91% on our eval versus 86% for the next best model.” Company Fundamental Research Labs Author Jeffrey Liu, Member of Technical Staff Quote “In our quantitative research work, Claude Fable 5.2 delivered very strong improvements versus Fable 5.1, especially in the setup with multiple coordinating agents. Its maths research capabilities represent another meaningful advance, too.” Company XTX Markets Author Alex Gerko, Founder and CEO Quote “Before putting AI to work across workflows, you need to trust its approach and conclusions. In our testing, Claude Fable 5.2 identified inconsistencies, drew on context across entire document sets, and adjusted recommendations based on relevant evidence. For example, when reviewing files attached to a loan application, it flagged that the salary deposits and the bank statement’s balance didn’t match, so the underwriter could focus on what to check.” Company Box Author Yashodha Bhavnani, VP of AI Products Safety and alignment No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute , Frontier Design , and METR . See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁴ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing. Alignment testing We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models). We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁵ Automated behavioral audit Overall misaligned behavior score Mythos 5.1 Opus 5.5 Sonnet 5.5 Mythos 5.2 Overall score from our automated behavioral audit, a composite of many undesirable behaviors including cooperation with human misuse and autonomous actions across a range of scenarios. Lower scores are better. See Section 6.4.1 of the Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card for full details. We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences). We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1. The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss. Safeguards Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas. AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators. Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report , which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%. We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features). Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards , automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe. Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form . Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring. Availability Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform. This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here . Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program . Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security , powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program . Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs. Footnotes 1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures , a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities. 2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card ). 3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus , EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension , SymProFold , CapBuild , MoLPC , CombFold , Uni-Fold Symmetry , Apodex Discovery , and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 ( PDB:1LP3 ). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2. 4 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication. 5 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards. Meta's Muse Ember is the cheapest model scoring 36 on the Intelligence Index | Artificial Analysis Artificial Analysis K Artificial Analysis Models Coding Agents Image, Speech, Video Inference Leaderboards About AI Trends K All articles November 9, 2026 Meta's newest model Muse Ember scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) at a third of the Cost per Task See model page 
 Muse Ember is Meta's newest efficient-tier model line, with the same input and output token prices as Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna 
 Key Takeaways: 
 ➤  On the Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier at both max and xhigh effort.  Muse Ember (max) is the cheapest model scoring 36 or higher, at $0.14 per task, and Muse Ember (xhigh) scores 34 for $0.12. Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) costs almost 3x more at $0.41 for the same score as Muse Ember (max). Muse Ember (max) is also about 4x cheaper than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max, 33, $0.60) and GLM-5.3-Flash (28, $0.58) 
 ➤  8 points behind Muse Wonder for about 1/50th of the Cost per Task.  Muse Wonder (max) scores 44 at $6.95 per Intelligence Index task 
 ➤  Stands out on AutomationBench-AA.  Muse Ember (max) scores 68.1% on AutomationBench-AA, level with Muse Wonder (max), and beats Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) on GDP.pdf (22.8% vs 20.8%), but trails it on AA-Briefcase (1521 vs 1574 Elo) 
 ➤  Mixed in agentic coding in our Intelligence Index evaluations.  It beats Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (40.9% vs 32.8%) but trails it on FrontierCode 2.0 (27.2% vs 34.9%) 
 ➤  Ahead of similarly priced models when running in its own coding agent.  In Muse Code, Muse Ember (max) scores 46 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, ahead of Claude Haiku 5.5 in Claude Code (max, 37) and GPT-6 Luna in Codex (max, 31) 
 ➤ Knowledge is the main weakness, but it rarely hallucinates. Its AA-Omniscience accuracy of 21.1% is the lowest of the similarly intelligent models we compared, against 34.7% for Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) and 50.5% for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high). This is mostly because it declines to answer 64% of questions, which keeps its hallucination rate at 17.4%, half of Claude Haiku 5.5’s (max) 
 Other details:   
 ➤  Pricing:  $0.10 input / $0.004 cached input / $0.50 output per 1M tokens
➤  Reasoning effort:  results shown at max effort, with xhigh also on the Intelligence vs. Cost chart
➤  Availability:  Meta's first-party API and Muse Code

 Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution 
 
 
 
 
	
 
 
 
 
 Russell Brandom 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 10:00 AM PST · November 9, 2026 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 



 
	
 
 
 
 
 Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.” 

 Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna. 
 
 
 
 Image Credits: Meta Superintelligence Labs 

 At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna. Not only that, it’s cost-competitive with open source competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash.  

 Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness. In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.” 

 With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio. The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.” 

 Ember is the fourth model released under Meta’s Muse brand, following the mid-weight Spark ( released in April ), Spark’s open source twin Glimmer ( released in August ), and the Wonder frontier model ( released in October ). The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.

 Title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs) 
 Authors: Swann Bessa , Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré , Gergely Szilvasy , Hugo Touvron , David Picard , Matthijs Douze , Hervé Jégou View a PDF of the paper titled e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs), by Swann Bessa and 6 other authors 
 View PDF 
 HTML (experimental) 



 
 Abstract: Lloyd's k-means algorithm is a long-running standard for clustering, with applications in data analysis, retrieval, quantization and data curation. In this paper, we introduce an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates, powered by modern deep learning machinery and new insights. We also establish scaling laws on how decay rate and batch size impact final performance. This gives us a formulaic rule to fix them for multiple problem sizes and embedding datasets, without the need for any hyperparameter sweep. The resulting clustering algorithm, coined e-means, is much faster than Lloyd k-means and converges to lower losses, frequently even beating k-means++. On a wide array of embeddings datasets, it beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, which translates to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations. As an example, e-means partitions DINO10B, a dataset of 10 billion DINO embeddings, into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.

 e-means: outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs 
 I’m excited to open-source e-means: a modern, robust k-means algorithm developed at Meta FAIR. A replacement of Lloyd's algorithm, e-means delivers a ~10× speedup in both epochs and wall-clock time while achieving lower loss. 
 Try e-means in your browser

 An order of magnitude less epochs 
 Across a large range of scales and datasets , e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans [2] ), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss [1] . Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss. 

 
 
 

 The k-means problem 
 Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x 1 , ..., x n } ⊂ R d and an integer k , the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c 1 , ..., c k ) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid: 
 \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2, \qquad a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] 
 \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2 \] 
 \[ a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] 
 It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving. 

 The e-means project 
 The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations: 
 
 k-means is one of the rare problems in machine learning where full-batch optimization is still widely used. 
 Mini-batch k-means methods in the literature exist [3] , [4] , [5] , but are mostly based on the MacQueen update rule, released in 1967. 
 Modern deep learning offers optimization tools that can enhance mini-batch methods. 
 
 For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages [6] , which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws ). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups. 

 
 
 
 Moving-average updates 
 Each mini-batch updates every cluster's count and sum. The centroid is their ratio. 
 
 
 
 No hyperparameter tuning 
 Everything is derived from scaling laws. 
 
 
 
 Start and finish 
 Novel initialization and finalization methods. The run ends on each cluster's exact last-epoch mean. 
 
 
 
 Cosine scheduling 
 The step α anneals from α 0 to 0.1 α 0 , as a learning rate does. 
 
 
 
 Dead-cluster revival 
 Clusters with size below a threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. 
 
 
 
 Specialized kernels 
 GPU kernels fuse the nearest-centroid assignment, turning the epoch savings above into matching wall-clock speedups. 
 
 
 
 

 The centroid update rules 
 The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j , a sum S j and a count N j of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio: 
 \[ c_j = S_j / N_j \] 
 They differ only in how S j and N j are updated. Below, s j and n j denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are). 
 Lloyd’s algorithm [7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch: 
 \[ S_j \leftarrow s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow n_j \] 
 so c j is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations). 
 MacQueen’s update [3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them: 
 \[ S_j \leftarrow S_j + s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow N_j + n_j \] 
 so c j is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means [8] , a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters. 
 e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average: 
 \[ S_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,S_j + \alpha\, s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,N_j + \alpha\, n_j \] 
 \[ S_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,S_j + \alpha\, s_j \] 
 \[ N_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,N_j + \alpha\, n_j \] 
 so older assignments are forgotten at rate α , and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs [6] . What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned. 

 
 Why exponential moving average updates and not gradient descent? 
 The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull. 

 
 
 Test error against the effective step a centroid takes, at a large batch, for exponential-moving-average updates (EMA) and plain gradient descent (SGD), each at every step setting tried. DEEP, 1 million vectors, and SIFT, 10 million vectors, 16,384 clusters, 5 epochs, median over 3 seeds. The vertical axis is percent above the best test error in the panel. At its best setting, gradient descent ends 1.6% (DEEP) and 0.4% (SIFT) above the moving average. 
 

 In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method. 
 

 
 Lloyd is a special case of e-means: hyperparameter study 
 If you set the batch to the full dataset, B = n , and α = 1, then N j and S j become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α : Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest. 

 
 
 Validation loss for every batch B and step α , relative to the best cell, after 5 epochs. DEEP, n = 10 6 , k = 1024. The step is constant here (no cosine schedule) so that Lloyd is exactly one of the cells: full batch, α = 1. The lowest losses follow a diagonal band, a larger batch calls for a larger step. 
 

 This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α . 
 

 e-means better escapes local minima 
 To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd.

Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 26% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 3.5% of times.

 Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them. 

 Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws 
 An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α 0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T) , and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales. 
 \[ B = c_B \, k^{b_k} \, n^{b_n} \, T^{b_T} \] 
 \[ \alpha_0 = \min\!\Big(c_\alpha \, k^{a_k} \, B^{a_B} \, n^{a_n} \, T^{a_T},\; 1\Big) \]

 We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α 0 (left) and batch size B (right).

 Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival. 

 The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today. 

 A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec [10] , where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity.

 Extensive experimental validation 
 We validated e-means on 24 different embedding and synthetic datasets and configurations (see paper ). For the video we ran 234 configurations of e-means against k-means (16 datasets, 100k to 100M points): explore every curve in the results map .

Budgets spaced 0.2 epochs apart, median over five seeds. Every dataset needs between 1.6 and 2.4 epochs, against Lloyd’s 25.

# T3 Code

T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app ([iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/t3-code-remote-claude-more/id6787819824), [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.t3tools.t3code)), [web app](https://app.t3.codes) and [Electron-based desktop app](https://t3.codes).

Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

## "Wait, what are you selling me?"

Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

## Installation

> [!WARNING]
> T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:
>
> - Codex: install [Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli) and run `codex login`
> - Claude: install [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) and run `claude auth login`
> - Cursor: install [Cursor CLI](https://cursor.com/cli) and run `agent login`
> - Grok Build: install [Grok Build CLI](https://x.ai/cli) and run `grok login`
> - OpenCode: install [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) and run `opencode auth login`
> - Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use **Install Antigravity** and **Sign in with Google**. No CLI is required.
> - fx: install [fx](https://fx.sh) and run `fx login` on the machine running the T3 Code server ([setup guide](./docs/user/providers-fx.md))

### Command line

```bash
curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex
```

Then run `t3` to start the server and open the local web app. `t3 service install` keeps it running in the background, `t3 update` moves to a newer release, and `t3 --help` has the full reference.

To try it once without installing, run `npx t3@latest`. It offers to install the `t3` command for you.

### Desktop app

Install the latest version of the desktop app from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/releases), or from your favorite package registry:

#### Windows (`winget`)

```bash
winget install T3Tools.T3Code
```

#### Windows (`scoop`)

```bash
scoop install extras/t3code
```

#### macOS (Homebrew)

```bash
brew install --cask t3-code
```

#### Debian, Ubuntu (`.deb`)

Download the `.deb` from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/releases), then:

```bash
sudo apt install ./T3-Code-*.deb
```

#### Arch Linux (AUR)

Stable:

```bash
yay -S t3code-bin
```

Nightly:

```bash
yay -S t3code-nightly-bin
```

The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under [`packaging/aur`](./packaging/aur).

#### Nix (nixpkgs)

```bash
nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code
```

The package is maintained in [nixpkgs](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/tree/nixos-unstable/pkgs/by-name/t3/t3code)
and includes the desktop app (`t3code-desktop`) and the `t3` command.
See [Nix installation](./docs/user/install.md#nix-nixpkgs) for NixOS configuration and updates.

## Some notes

We are very very early in this project. Expect bugs.

We are (mostly) not accepting contributions yet. Small fixes may be considered. Big features will not be.

## Documentation

Full docs live in [docs/](./docs). There's no docs site yet.

- [FAQ](./docs/user/faq.md)
- [Install and first run](./docs/user/install.md)
- [Permission modes](./docs/user/permission-modes.md)
- [Keyboard shortcuts](./docs/user/keybindings.md)
- [Project settings](./docs/user/project-settings.md)
- [Appearance preferences](./docs/user/appearance.md)
- [Remote access from a phone or another machine](./docs/user/remote-access.md)
- [Connect Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT and other agents over MCP](./docs/user/outside-agents.md)
- [Keeping app and server in sync](./docs/user/updating.md)
- [Source control integrations](./docs/user/source-control.md)
- Multiple accounts: [Codex](./docs/user/providers-codex.md) · [Claude](./docs/user/providers-claude.md)
- [Run T3 Code as a background service](./docs/user/background-service.md)

Building from source? Start at [docs/internals/overview.md](./docs/internals/overview.md).

## If you REALLY want to contribute still.... read this first

### Install `vp`

T3 Code uses Vite+ so you'll need to install the global `vp` command-line tool.

#### macOS / Linux

```bash
curl -fsSL https://vite.plus | bash
```

#### Windows

```bash
irm https://vite.plus/ps1 | iex
```

Checkout their getting started guide for more information: https://viteplus.dev/guide/

### Install dependencies

```bash
vp i
```

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) before reporting a bug or opening a PR.

Have a feature request? Start an [Ideas discussion](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/discussions/categories/ideas).

Need support? Join the [Discord](https://discord.gg/jn4EGJjrvv).

readme:signalwire/freeswitch.text: # FreeSWITCH FreeSWITCH is a Software Defined Telecom Stack enabling the digital transformation from proprietary telecom switches to a versatile software implementation that runs on any commodity hardware. From a Raspberry PI to a multi-core server, FreeSWITCH can unlock the telecommunications potential of any device. Combined with our hosted cloud platform, SignalWire, FreeSWITCH can interconnect with the outside world and scale to any size. Visit [https://signalwire.com](https://signalwire.com/) or https://github.com/signalwire for more info. ## Getting Started FreeSWITCH is available on [Github](https://github.com/signalwire/freeswitch) in source code format. You can checkout the development branch and build for many popular platforms including Linux, Windows, MacOSX and BSD. There is an issue tracker and pull request system available as part of the repo online. See https://developer.signalwire.com/freeswitch/FreeSWITCH-Explained/ for more detailed instructions. ## Additional Help If you need assistance or have an interest in using a commercially supported build, you can contact coreteam@freeswitch.com to learn about professional services to support your project. ## Voice-over-IP services - SIP / SMS - App Integrations [SignalWire](https://signalwire.com) is the primary sponsor of the FreeSWITCH project and was founded by the original developers of FreeSWITCH. SignalWire provides scalable services to enhance and scale your project such as SMS, SIP, Serverless Application hosting as well as programmable telecom. mod_signalwire which is distributed in this code base allows you to instantly pair with SignalWire and extend your FreeSWITCH. ## Documentation The main index for documentation is available at: * https://freeswitch.org/confluence/ ### Release notes: * https://freeswitch.org/confluence/display/FREESWITCH/Release+Notes ### Install from packages Step by step tutorials to install FreeSWITCH from packages: * [Using FSGET](/scripts/packaging) [Recommended] * [Debian](https://freeswitch.org/confluence/display/FREESWITCH/Debian) * [Raspberry Pi](https://freeswitch.org/confluence/display/FREESWITCH/Raspberry+Pi) * [CentOS 7](https://freeswitch.org/confluence/display/FREESWITCH/CentOS+7+and+RHEL+7) ### Build from source Example Dockerfiles to build FreeSWITCH and dependencies from source: * https://github.com/signalwire/freeswitch/tree/master/docker/examples Step by step tutorials to build FreeSWITCH with provided dependency packages: * [Debian](https://freeswitch.org/confluence/display/FREESWITCH/Debian#Debian-buildfromsource) [Recommended] * [Raspberry Pi](https://freeswitch.org/confluence/display/FREESWITCH/Raspberry+Pi) * [CentOS 7](https://freeswitch.org/confluence/display/FREESWITCH/CentOS+7+and+RHEL+7) ### How to build Debian packages * [Using FSDEB](/scripts/packaging/build) ## Downloads * [Tarballs](https://files.freeswitch.org/releases/freeswitch/) * [Windows Installer](http://files.freeswitch.org/windows/installer/x64/) * [Windows Sound Packages](https://github.com/freeswitch/freeswitch-sounds/releases) ## Contributions GitHub pull requests are the recommended way to contribute to the FreeSWITCH source code: * https://github.com/signalwire/freeswitch/pulls ## Community Slack is our chat system where the developers, the FreeSWITCH team, and the most active users are present. This is the place to get answers faster and chat with other users in real time. All you need to do is enter your email and verify it on the Slack signup page and you are ready to join in the discussion! Slack Community: * https://signalwire.community/ Mailing list (ARCHIVED): * http://lists.freeswitch.org/pipermail/freeswitch-users/ **Thank you for using FreeSWITCH!**

 Inbound SIP MESSAGE can select the api chat proto and run FreeSWITCH API commands
 

 

 


 
 
 Critical
 
 

 
 andywolk 
 published
 GHSA-mg63-h38w-8p9p 
 Oct 28, 2026 

 
 
 
 


 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Package 

 
 FreeSWITCH 
 (C)
 
 
 

 
 Affected versions 

 <= 1.11.2 
 

 
 Patched versions 

 >= 1.11.3 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 Description 
 

 
 
 Summary 
 sofia_presence_handle_sip_i_message() splits the To user of an inbound SIP MESSAGE on + and treats the left half as a chat proto name, dispatching the message to whichever registered chat interface matches. mod_dptools registers an api chat interface that hands its address to switch_api_execute() . A peer that can deliver a MESSAGE to a profile therefore selects which FreeSWITCH API command the server runs. Nothing restricts the selector, and message-delivery protos are not distinguished from command-execution protos. 
 Impact 
 Command execution with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process: arbitrary OS commands, disclosure of configuration and credentials, and full call control. Where mod_lua is loaded, as stock configuration does, inline Lua with the full standard library is reachable as a second sink. Exploitation of this path has been observed in the wild. 
 Affected configurations 
 Any SIP profile that accepts inbound MESSAGE, which is the default posture: chat handling is on unless a profile sets enable-chat=false , and stock conf/vanilla leaves it on for both the internal and external profiles. No non-default setting is required. The inbound ACL does not cover MESSAGE, so tightening it does not take a profile out of scope. 
 Attack prerequisites 
 Getting a single SIP MESSAGE accepted by a profile. Where MESSAGE authentication is enforced, any one account on that profile is enough: an extension, a handset, or a trunk peer, holding no permission beyond the ability to register. Installations that still carry conf/vanilla/directory/default/default.xml need no account of their own: that file defines <user id="default"> with no password and no a1-hash , and a directory user with neither authenticates successfully unless allow-empty-password is set to false for it. 
 Workarounds 
 
 enable-chat=false on every profile that does not need inbound SIP chat. This stops the message before the proto selector is parsed, and disables all inbound MESSAGE chat delivery on that profile. 
 auth-messages is not sufficient on its own. MESSAGE authentication is enabled by default from version 1.10.7 onward. Combined with removing every directory user that has no password or a1-hash - stock conf/vanilla ships two, default and the Skinny example - it reduces this to authenticated command execution, but does not close the path. 
 disable_system_api_commands=true removes the system API but not the route, which still reaches every other registered API, including module loading and call origination. Worth setting, but it does not close this path. 
 
 Fix 
 A new per-profile enable-chat-api-proto parameter controls whether an inbound MESSAGE may select the api chat proto, and is off unless explicitly set, so the route is closed on every profile by default. A MESSAGE selecting the proto where it is not enabled is answered 403 and logged with the source and the requested command. The comparison is case-insensitive, matching the chat interface registry. Messages carrying no proto selector, or naming another chat proto, route unchanged. The parameter ships commented out in the vanilla profiles and the mod_sofia configuration sample. 
 Credit 
 Örn Arnarson and Gunnlaugur.

 Critical
 

 
 
 
 9.8

# FFmpeg README

FFmpeg is a collection of libraries and tools to process multimedia content
such as audio, video, subtitles and related metadata.

## Libraries

* `libavcodec` provides implementation of a wider range of codecs.
* `libavformat` implements streaming protocols, container formats and basic I/O access.
* `libavutil` includes hashers, decompressors and miscellaneous utility functions.
* `libavfilter` provides means to alter decoded audio and video through a directed graph of connected filters.
* `libavdevice` provides an abstraction to access capture and playback devices.
* `libswresample` implements audio mixing and resampling routines.
* `libswscale` implements color conversion and scaling routines.

## Tools

* [ffmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg.html) is a command line toolbox to
  manipulate, convert and stream multimedia content.
* [ffplay](https://ffmpeg.org/ffplay.html) is a minimalistic multimedia player.
* [ffprobe](https://ffmpeg.org/ffprobe.html) is a simple analysis tool to inspect
  multimedia content.
* Additional small tools such as `aviocat`, `ismindex` and `qt-faststart`.

## Documentation

The offline documentation is available in the **doc/** directory.

The online documentation is available in the main [website](https://ffmpeg.org)
and in the [wiki](https://trac.ffmpeg.org).

### Examples

Coding examples are available in the **doc/examples** directory.

## License

FFmpeg codebase is mainly LGPL-licensed with optional components licensed under
GPL. Please refer to the LICENSE file for detailed information.

## Contributing

Patches should be submitted to [Forgejo](https://code.ffmpeg.org/FFmpeg/FFmpeg/pulls) or the [ffmpeg-devel mailing list](https://lists.ffmpeg.org/mailman3/lists/ffmpeg-devel.ffmpeg.org/) using `git format-patch` or `git send-email`. Github pull requests should be avoided because they are not part of our review process and **will be ignored**.

See [https://ffmpeg.org/developer.html](https://ffmpeg.org/developer.html) for more information.

[![SuperTokens banner](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/supertokens/supertokens-logo/master/images/Artboard%20%E2%80%93%2027%402x.png)](https://supertokens.com/) # Open-Source auth provider Add **secure login and session management** to your apps. [SDKs available](https://supertokens.com/docs/community/sdks) for popular languages and front-end frameworks e.g. Node.js, Go, Python, React.js, React Native, Vanilla JS, etc. ![Architecture Diagram](https://supertokens.com/img/architecture/self_hosted_generic.png) Supertokens architecture is optimized to add secure authentication for your users without compromising on user and developer experience **Three building blocks of SuperTokens architecture** 1. Frontend SDK: Manages session tokens and renders login UI widgets 2. Backend SDK: Provides APIs for sign-up, sign-in, signout, session refreshing, etc. Your Frontend will talk to these APIs 3. SuperTokens Core: The HTTP service for the core auth logic and database operations. This service is used by the Backend SDK ## Features [![Click here to get started](.github/click-here-to-get-started.png)](https://supertokens.com/docs/guides) * Passwordless Login * Social Login * Email Password Login * Phone Password Login * Session Management * Multi-Factor Authentication * Multi Tenancy / Organization Support (Enterprise SSO) * User Roles * Microservice Authentication ## Learn more - [🚀 What is SuperTokens?](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#-what-is-supertokens) - [Philosophy](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#philosophy) - [Features + Demo app](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#features---click-here-to-see-the-demo-app) - [Documentation](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#documentation) - [🏗️ Architecture](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#%EF%B8%8F-architecture) - [☕ Why Java?](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#-why-java) - [⌨️ User Management Dashboard](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#-user-management-dashboard) - [🔥 SuperTokens vs Others](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#-supertokens-vs-others) - [🛠️ Building from source](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#%EF%B8%8F-building-from-source) - [👥 Community](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#-community) - [Contributors](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#contributors-across-all-supertokens-repositories) - [👩‍💻 Contributing](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#-contributing) - [📝 License](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core#-license) ### If you like our project, please :star2: this repository! For feedback, feel free to join our [Discord](https://supertokens.io/discord), or create an issue on this repo ## 🚀 What is SuperTokens? SuperTokens is an open-core alternative to proprietary login providers like Auth0 or AWS Cognito. We are different because we offer: - Open source: SuperTokens can be used for free, forever, with no limits on the number of users. - An on-premises deployment so that you control 100% of your user data, using your own database. - An end-to-end solution with login, sign-ups, user and session management, without all the complexities of OAuth protocols. - Ease of implementation and higher security. - Extensibility: Anyone can contribute and make SuperTokens better! ### Philosophy Authentication directly affects the UX, dev experience, and security of any app. We believe that current solutions cannot optimize for all three "pillars", leading to many applications hand-rolling their own auth. This not only leads to security issues but is also a massive time drain. We want to change that - we believe the only way is to provide a solution that has the right level of abstraction gives you maximum control, is secure, and is simple to use - just like if you build it yourself, from scratch (minus the time to learn, build, and maintain). We also believe in the principle of least vendor lock-in. Your having full control of your user's data means that you can switch away from SuperTokens without forcing your existing users to logout, reset their passwords, or in the worst case, sign up again. ### [Click here](https://thirdpartyemailpassword.demo.supertokens.com/) to see the demo app. - Please visit [our website](https://supertokens.io/pricing) to see the list of features. - We want to make features as decoupled as possible. This means you can use SuperTokens for just login, or just session management, or both. In fact, we also offer session management integrations with other login providers like Auth0. ### Documentation The docs can be seen [on our website](https://supertokens.io/docs/community/introduction). There is more information about SuperTokens on the [GitHub wiki section](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core/wiki). ## 🏗️ Architecture Please find an [architecture diagram here](https://supertokens.io/docs/community/architecture) **For more information, please visit our [GitHub wiki section](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core/wiki/SuperTokens-Architecture).** ## ☕ Why Java? - ✅ Whilst running Java can seem difficult, we provide the JDK along with the binary/docker image when distributing it. This makes running SuperTokens just like running any other HTTP microservice. - ✅ Java has a very mature ecosystem. This implies that third-party libraries have been battle-tested. - ✅ Java's strong type system ensures fewer bugs and easier maintainability. This is especially important when many people are expected to work on the same project. - ✅ Our team is most comfortable with Java and hiring great Java developers is relatively easy as well. - ✅ One of the biggest criticisms of Java is memory usage. We have three solutions to this: - The most frequent auth-related operation is session verification - this happens within the backend SDK (node, python, Go) without contacting the Java core. Therefore, a single instance of the core can handle several 10s of thousands of users fairly easily. - We have carefully chosen our dependencies. For eg: we use an embedded tomcat server instead of a higher-level web framework. - We also plan on using [GraalVM](https://www.graalvm.org/) in the future and this can reduce memory usage by 95%! - ✅ If you require any modifications to the auth APIs, those would need to be done on the backend SDK level (for example Node, Golang, Python..). So you’d rarely need to directly modify/work with the Java code in this repo. ## ⌨️ User Management Dashboard Oversee your users with the [SuperTokens User Management Dashboard](https://supertokens.com/docs/userdashboard/about) ### List users List all the users who have signed up to your application. ![List SuperTokens users](.github/list-user.png) ### Manage users Manage users by modifying or deleting their sessions, metadata, roles and account info. ![Manage users](.github/user-info.png) ## 🔥 SuperTokens vs others Please find a detailed comparison chart [on our website](https://supertokens.io/pricing#comparison-chart) ## 🛠️ Building from source Please see our [wiki](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core/wiki/Building-from-source) for instructions. ## 👥 Community - [Discord](https://supertokens.io/discord) - [Email](mailto:team@supertokens.io) If you think this is a project you could use in the future, please :star2: this repository! ### Contributors (across all SuperTokens repositories)
