Something watched you this week.

Watched shows which satellites passed over any place on Earth in the last 7 days, and the real photos they took. It is free, with no sign-up, and the orbit maths runs in your browser.

www.watched.earth
How it works  ·  Run locally  ·  Self‑hosting


Palm Jumeirah, Dubai, on 9 November 2026. Open the same place live.

## What it does 1. **Pick a place.** Search a city, a landmark or coordinates, use your location, or start from an example: Area 51, Central Park, Giza, Uluru, Palm Jumeirah. 2. **It finds the passes.** While the globe flies there, your browser replays the past week of orbits for nearly 400 imaging, weather, radar and crewed satellites, and notes every time one's field of view crossed your spot. 3. **It finds the photos.** At the same time it searches the Sentinel-2 and Landsat archives and NASA's weather imagery, matches each photo to the pass that took it, and checks whether your spot was under cloud. The results open with a summary (*In the last 7 days, 260 satellites watched Palm Jumeirah. 28 photos were made public.*), then the photos, a timeline of the week and every pass. 4. **Replay a pass.** The satellite flies its real track while the strip of ground its camera sees (its swath) sweeps across the place. The photo then develops line by line in the direction of flight, the way the satellite's camera recorded it. 5. **Share it.** Post the link anywhere and it shows a preview card made from the real photo, or from the pass's geometry when there is no photo.


Left: a pass replay, the photo developing line by line as the satellite recorded it. Right: the landing page, with every active satellite in the catalog around the globe.


The same lookup on a phone, and the preview card for a shared pass.

## What *watched* means Every pass gets one of four labels, and only the first means a photo exists. The line in italics is the rule behind each one. | Label | What it means | |:--|:--| | ◆ **Watched** | A real photo of this place exists in a public archive.
*A Sentinel-2, Landsat or weather photo was matched to the pass. A VIIRS daily mosaic still unchecked after 3.5 s also counts, if the same satellite has a verified mosaic on a later day.* | | ◇ **Likely watched** | A fixed camera's swath covered this place. No photo of it is published.
*Sentinel-2 or Landsat in daylight, or a polar weather satellite, with no photo found.* | | □ **Could have pointed here** | A steerable or private camera was in range. Its operator doesn't say whether it looked.
*A commercial camera in daylight, or a radar satellite at any hour.* | | + **Passed overhead** | Crossed your sky, with no camera known to be recording this place.
*The ISS or Tiangong at least 10° above the horizon, or a Sentinel-2 or Landsat pass over open ocean (outside Sentinel-2's acquisition plan).* | The results headline (*260 satellites watched Palm Jumeirah*) counts every satellite with at least one pass, whatever its label, so *watched* there is meant broadly; only ◆ passes come with a photo. The second line counts the photos that were made public, and starts with "At least" while archives are still answering. Geostationary weather satellites never pass; they sit over the equator all week, so they are listed separately and not counted. The app says *watched*, never *photographed*. ## Accuracy and limits - Passes are searched for satellites whose cameras, radars or crews Watched knows about, and the geostationary weather satellites that can see the place are listed as watching all week. The rest of the catalog is drawn on the globe but not searched. Military and intelligence satellites mostly aren't in public catalogs. - In the photos Watched shows, a pixel is 10 m across at best, bigger than a car, so you can't be seen in them. Commercial cameras in the *could have pointed here* group see down to about 30 cm, but their operators don't publish where they pointed or what they saw. - The public orbit data (element sets) is accurate to about a kilometre when it is issued and drifts after that, so pass times can be off by a few seconds. - Archives publish a few hours to a couple of days after capture, so the newest passes may not have a photo yet. - Sentinel-2 and Landsat photos are toned the same way across the whole frame: a black point, a white point and a brightness curve, a little extra saturation, smoothed compression blocks and light sharpening. Nothing is added or removed. Everything uncertain is labelled as such in the app. ## How it works

Built with TypeScript, React 19, three.js through React Three Fiber, zustand and Vite. The pass search (SGP4, the standard model for public orbit data) and photo toning run in your browser, in Web Workers; the backend is three Vercel functions and an optional Supabase database. Four parts are worth a closer look. [`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) covers the rest, including photo toning, the cloud check at your spot and the share cards, and [`docs/DESIGN.md`](docs/DESIGN.md) covers the visual system. ### A pass search with no gaps Call *θ* the angle, at Earth's centre, between the satellite and the place, and *θ*field the largest *θ* at which the place can be in the camera's view. That angle can change no faster than *ω*max, the orbit's peak angular rate with a 10% margin for perturbations, plus Earth's rotation. So the coarse search steps by |*θ* − *θ*field| / *ω*max, clamped between 5 s and 30 min. Between any two samples the same rate limit gives a lower bound on *θ*, so every interval where *θ* could reach *θ*field is flagged, and no pass falls between samples. Golden-section search then finds closest approach to ±0.1 s, and bisection finds entry and exit to ±0.5 s. Against a one-second brute force, 22 adversarial cases (both poles, the antimeridian, Null Island, swaths down to 32 km) show no missed passes; where timing is measured, the worst difference is 0.65 s. A week for all 394 satellites (1,860 passes in the test case) takes 1.3 s on one thread in Node; the browser splits it across up to four Web Workers, two on phones. See [`src/engine/passes.ts`](src/engine/passes.ts). ### About 17,000 satellites on the GPU The globe draws every active satellite in the catalog (16,894 on 9 November 2026). Their element sets become mean Keplerian elements with SGP4's own J2 and J4 secular rates, and a vertex shader solves Kepler's equation for every object, every frame. Against full SGP4 over ±24 h, the median error in low orbit is about 17 km, one or two pixels at globe scale, though one object in twenty is off by more than 100 km. The pass search always uses full SGP4. The globe itself is Earth-fixed and lit by the sun's true direction, computed to about 0.01°, so the terminator, the ocean glint and the city lights are where they really are. See [`src/engine/elements.ts`](src/engine/elements.ts). ### Archive time is not overpass time A Sentinel-2 scene's archive timestamp (the `datetime` in its STAC record, the catalog format these archives share) marks the start of the strip the satellite was recording, which can begin minutes before it reaches a given spot (6 min 53 s in one measured case). A photo matches the pass of the same satellite (same NORAD catalog number) whose closest approach falls between 10 minutes before and 60 minutes after that time, and the app always shows the predicted pass time. See [`src/engine/match.ts`](src/engine/match.ts). ### A locked-down backend Vercel serves the static app and three functions: share cards (`/api/og`), share pages (`/s/:id`) and the usage-event relay (`/api/e`). Supabase holds lookups, shares and usage counts. Row-level security is on, every table privilege is revoked, clients can only call a handful of Postgres functions, and an hourly pg_cron job rolls up and prunes the events. ## Privacy The orbit maths runs in your browser. The site counts how it is used; it does not track people. | Record | What Watched keeps | |:--|:--| | Lookup | A cell about 10 km across (0.1°), and that place's country and town. | | Share | The town-level place name, a point rounded to about 1 km (0.01°), the pass and its photos, and a view count. | | Visit | What happened (searches, results, passes and photos opened, shares, errors, page speed), tied to a random ID that lives only as long as the browser tab, with the device class, your country (from Vercel's edge), the referring site, any UTM tags and the app version. | Raw events and visits are deleted after 90 days. Daily usage totals, lookups and shares are kept. Watched's database never stores exact coordinates, IP addresses, cookies or full referrer URLs, and the event relay never reads the IP. The app never sends street-level place names. Vercel and Supabase see IP addresses in transit and in their own request logs, like any host. Other services see the place too. [Photon](https://photon.komoot.io) sees what you type, or your coordinates if you use your location. Planetary Computer and NASA GIBS see the point and the area around it, to send the photos. Element 84 sees it only when Planetary Computer is down. Vercel Web Analytics receives the page address, which for a place link includes its coordinates and name. Usage events are sent only from watched.earth, and never from a development build, an automated browser or a tab opened with `?noanalytics=1` (for as long as that tab stays open). The flag doesn't stop lookups and shares being counted: any build with Supabase configured counts them, development included. Vercel Web Analytics is cookieless and ignores the flag. ## Run it locally You need Node 22.12+, 24 or 26+, the versions Vitest supports. ```bash git clone https://github.com/dev-Armaan/satellites.git cd satellites npm install npm run dev ``` The app runs at `http://localhost:5173` with no configuration. Without a backend nothing is recorded, the places-checked counter on the landing page is hidden, and share links carry the pass in the URL instead of a short `/s/` link. To turn on lookups and shares: 1. Create a Supabase project and apply the migrations, as [`docs/SELF-HOSTING.md`](docs/SELF-HOSTING.md) shows. 2. Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` and set `VITE_SUPABASE_URL` and `VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`. Use the publishable key, never a secret key: `VITE_` variables are bundled into the JavaScript that every visitor downloads. 3. Run `npm run dev` as before, or `npx vercel dev` to serve the share pages and cards in `api/` as well. Vercel asks to link a project the first time. The places-checked counter appears once a project has 1,000 lookups, 50 of them in the last 24 hours. ### Tests and scripts ```bash npm test # engine, imagery and UI tests (Vitest) npm run test:backend # tests for the api/ functions npm run typecheck # tsc -b npm run build # the app and the /admin page, into dist/ npm run data:celestrak # refresh the orbit catalog (CelesTrak asks for 2 hours between downloads) npm run textures -- ./maps # rebuild public/textures from the source maps in ./maps # render share cards for sample passes to image files (needs no server or database) npx tsx scripts/backend-render-og.ts ``` The built textures are committed, so you rarely need `npm run textures`. It needs Python 3 and Pillow, and reads the source maps listed at the top of `scripts/build-textures.py`. ### Useful URLs | URL | What it does | |:--|:--| | `/?q=lat,lon&n=name` | Opens a place directly. Add `&p=` to open a pass. | | `/?debug=gl` | WebGL diagnostics. | | `/?sandbox=` | Development pages (dev server only): `engine`, `backend`, `globe`, `imagery`, `results`, `shell`. | | `/admin.html?mock=1` | The stats page with fixture data (dev server only). | ## Self-hosting Watched is a static Vite build, three Vercel functions, an optional Supabase project and a GitHub Action that keeps the orbit catalog fresh. To run your own copy: 1. Fork the repository and import it into Vercel. It works as is, with no backend. 2. Enable GitHub Actions on your fork so the catalog refresh runs. Forks start with scheduled workflows off. 3. For lookups, shares and stats, apply `supabase/migrations` to your own Supabase project (they need pg_cron), set `VITE_SUPABASE_URL` and `VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` in Vercel, and make yourself admin with `scripts/backend-set-admin.sh`. Every database script needs `SUPABASE_PROJECT_REF` and has no default, so none of them can touch someone else's project by accident. 4. For usage events, add your domain to `PRODUCTION_HOSTS` in `src/lib/telemetry.ts`. A fork sends none until you do. The full guide is [`docs/SELF-HOSTING.md`](docs/SELF-HOSTING.md). ## Project layout
Show the directory tree ``` index.html app shell and static boot screen admin.html /admin stats page (separate build: vite.admin.config.ts) vercel.json functions, headers, /s/:id and bot-unfurl routes, SPA fallback src/ main.tsx entry; analytics and in-app events after first paint (production only) types.ts shared contracts app/ phase controller, boot curtain, error notice, telemetry wiring engine/ catalog, satellite profiles, SGP4, pass search and worker pool, matching, weather and geostationary legs, GPU elements, the report imagery/ STAC and GIBS, crop and mask URLs, pixels worker, cloud at your spot, Photon, time zones globe/ three.js / React Three Fiber scene: Earth, atmosphere, clouds, stars, GPU satellites, pass sequence, swath, camera ui/ system primitives, HUD, landing, results, share, About lib/ geo maths, backend client, telemetry, layout state/ zustand store and scene clock styles/ tokens, fonts, base admin/ /admin page (Supabase Auth) sandbox/ development-only ?sandbox= pages api/ og.tsx (share card), s.ts (share page), e.ts (events relay), _lib, _fonts, _assets public/ data/ (orbit catalog), textures/, brand/, og-default.png supabase/ migrations 0001 to 0007, SQL tests scripts/ catalog fetch, textures, fonts, card render, migrate, admin, verify, SQL test, purge docs/ DESIGN.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, SELF-HOSTING.md .github/workflows/ catalog.yml (orbit catalog refresh) ```
## Data and credits | Source | Credit | |:--|:--| | Orbits | Element sets from [CelesTrak](https://celestrak.org), based on US Space Force tracking data, refreshed every 6 hours. SGP4 by [satellite.js](https://github.com/shashwatak/satellite-js). | | Sentinel‑2 | Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data, followed by the year each photo was taken. | | Landsat | Landsat imagery courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey and NASA. | | NASA GIBS | Imagery from NASA's GIBS, part of EOSDIS.  Something watched you this week. 
 
 Watched shows which satellites passed over any place on Earth in the last 7 days, and the real photos they took. It is free, with no sign-up, and the orbit maths runs in your browser.
 
 
 www.watched.earth 
 
 How it works  ·  Run locally  ·  Self‑hosting 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Palm Jumeirah, Dubai, on 9 November 2026. Open the same place live . 
 
 What it does 
 
 Pick a place. Search a city, a landmark or coordinates, use your location, or start from an example: Area 51,
Central Park, Giza, Uluru, Palm Jumeirah. 
 It finds the passes. While the globe flies there, your browser replays the past week of orbits for nearly 400
imaging, weather, radar and crewed satellites, and notes every time one's field of view crossed your spot. 
 It finds the photos. At the same time it searches the Sentinel-2 and Landsat archives and NASA's weather
imagery, matches each photo to the pass that took it, and checks whether your spot was under cloud. The results
open with a summary ( In the last 7 days, 260 satellites watched Palm Jumeirah. 28 photos were made public. ),
then the photos, a timeline of the week and every pass. 
 Replay a pass. The satellite flies its real track while the strip of ground its camera sees (its swath)
sweeps across the place. The photo then develops line by line in the direction of flight, the way the
satellite's camera recorded it. 
 Share it. Post the link anywhere and it shows a preview card made from the real photo, or from the pass's
geometry when there is no photo. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Left: a pass replay, the photo developing line by line as the satellite recorded it. Right: the landing page, with every active satellite in the catalog around the globe. 
 
 
 
 
 
 The same lookup on a phone, and the preview card for a shared pass. 
 
 What watched means 
 Every pass gets one of four labels, and only the first means a photo exists. The line in italics is the rule behind
each one. 
 
 
 
 Label 
 What it means 
 
 
 
 
 ◆  Watched 
 A real photo of this place exists in a public archive. A Sentinel-2, Landsat or weather photo was matched to the pass. A VIIRS daily mosaic still unchecked after 3.5 s also counts, if the same satellite has a verified mosaic on a later day. 
 
 
 ◇  Likely watched 
 A fixed camera's swath covered this place. No photo of it is published. Sentinel-2 or Landsat in daylight, or a polar weather satellite, with no photo found. 
 
 
 □  Could have pointed here 
 A steerable or private camera was in range. Its operator doesn't say whether it looked. A commercial camera in daylight, or a radar satellite at any hour. 
 
 
 +  Passed overhead 
 Crossed your sky, with no camera known to be recording this place. The ISS or Tiangong at least 10° above the horizon, or a Sentinel-2 or Landsat pass over open ocean (outside Sentinel-2's acquisition plan). 
 
 
 
 The results headline ( 260 satellites watched Palm Jumeirah ) counts every satellite with at least one pass,
whatever its label, so watched there is meant broadly; only ◆ passes come with a photo. The second line counts the
photos that were made public, and starts with "At least" while archives are still answering. Geostationary weather
satellites never pass; they sit over the equator all week, so they are listed separately and not counted. The app
says watched , never photographed . 
 Accuracy and limits 
 
 Passes are searched for satellites whose cameras, radars or crews Watched knows about, and the geostationary
weather satellites that can see the place are listed as watching all week. The rest of the catalog is drawn on the
globe but not searched. Military and intelligence satellites mostly aren't in public catalogs. 
 In the photos Watched shows, a pixel is 10 m across at best, bigger than a car, so you can't be seen in them.
Commercial cameras in the could have pointed here group see down to about 30 cm, but their operators don't
publish where they pointed or what they saw. 
 The public orbit data (element sets) is accurate to about a kilometre when it is issued and drifts after that, so
pass times can be off by a few seconds. 
 Archives publish a few hours to a couple of days after capture, so the newest passes may not have a photo yet. 
 Sentinel-2 and Landsat photos are toned the same way across the whole frame: a black point, a white point and a
brightness curve, a little extra saturation, smoothed compression blocks and light sharpening. Nothing is added or
removed. 
 
 Everything uncertain is labelled as such in the app. 
 How it works 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Built with TypeScript, React 19, three.js through React Three Fiber, zustand and Vite. The pass search (SGP4, the
standard model for public orbit data) and photo toning run in your browser, in Web Workers; the backend is three
Vercel functions and an optional Supabase database. 
 Four parts are worth a closer look. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md covers the rest, including photo
toning, the cloud check at your spot and the share cards, and docs/DESIGN.md covers the visual
system. 
 A pass search with no gaps 
 Call θ the angle, at Earth's centre, between the satellite and the place, and θ field the largest θ 
at which the place can be in the camera's view. That angle can change no faster than ω max , the orbit's
peak angular rate with a 10% margin for perturbations, plus Earth's rotation. So the coarse search steps
by | θ − θ field | / ω max , clamped between 5 s and 30 min. Between any two samples the
same rate limit gives a lower bound on θ , so every interval where θ could reach θ field is flagged,
and no pass falls between samples. Golden-section search then finds closest approach to ±0.1 s, and bisection
finds entry and exit to ±0.5 s. 
 Against a one-second brute force, 22 adversarial cases (both poles, the antimeridian, Null Island, swaths down to
32 km) show no missed passes; where timing is measured, the worst difference is 0.65 s. A week for all 394 satellites
(1,860 passes in the test case) takes 1.3 s on one thread in Node; the browser splits it across up to four Web
Workers, two on phones. See src/engine/passes.ts . 
 About 17,000 satellites on the GPU 
 The globe draws every active satellite in the catalog (16,894 on 9 November 2026). Their element sets become mean
Keplerian elements with SGP4's own J2 and J4 secular rates, and a vertex shader solves Kepler's equation for every
object, every frame. Against full SGP4 over ±24 h, the median error in low orbit is about 17 km, one or two pixels at
globe scale, though one object in twenty is off by more than 100 km. The pass search always uses full SGP4. The globe
itself is Earth-fixed and lit by the sun's true direction, computed to about 0.01°, so the terminator, the ocean
glint and the city lights are where they really are. See src/engine/elements.ts . 
 Archive time is not overpass time 
 A Sentinel-2 scene's archive timestamp (the datetime in its STAC record, the catalog format these archives share)
marks the start of the strip the satellite was recording, which can begin minutes before it reaches a given spot
(6 min 53 s in one measured case). A photo matches the pass of the same satellite (same NORAD catalog number) whose
closest approach falls between 10 minutes before and 60 minutes after that time, and the app always shows the
predicted pass time. See src/engine/match.ts . 
 A locked-down backend 
 Vercel serves the static app and three functions: share cards ( /api/og ), share pages ( /s/:id ) and the
usage-event relay ( /api/e ). Supabase holds lookups, shares and usage counts. Row-level security is on, every table
privilege is revoked, clients can only call a handful of Postgres functions, and an hourly pg_cron job rolls up and
prunes the events. 
 Privacy 
 The orbit maths runs in your browser. The site counts how it is used; it does not track people. 
 
 
 
 Record 
 What Watched keeps 
 
 
 
 
 Lookup 
 A cell about 10 km across (0.1°), and that place's country and town. 
 
 
 Share 
 The town-level place name, a point rounded to about 1 km (0.01°), the pass and its photos, and a view count. 
 
 
 Visit 
 What happened (searches, results, passes and photos opened, shares, errors, page speed), tied to a random ID that lives only as long as the browser tab, with the device class, your country (from Vercel's edge), the referring site, any UTM tags and the app version. 
 
 
 
 Raw events and visits are deleted after 90 days. Daily usage totals, lookups and shares are kept. 
 Watched's database never stores exact coordinates, IP addresses, cookies or full referrer URLs, and the event relay
never reads the IP. The app never sends street-level place names. Vercel and Supabase see IP addresses in transit and
in their own request logs, like any host. 
 Other services see the place too. Photon sees what you type, or your coordinates if you
use your location. Planetary Computer and NASA GIBS see the point and the area around it, to send the photos.
Element 84 sees it only when Planetary Computer is down. Vercel Web Analytics receives the page address, which for a
place link includes its coordinates and name. 
 Usage events are sent only from watched.earth, and never from a development build, an automated browser or a tab
opened with ?noanalytics=1 (for as long as that tab stays open). The flag doesn't stop lookups and shares being
counted: any build with Supabase configured counts them, development included. Vercel Web Analytics is cookieless
and ignores the flag. 
 Run it locally 
 You need Node 22.12+, 24 or 26+, the versions Vitest supports. 
 git clone https://github.com/dev-Armaan/satellites.git
 cd satellites
npm install
npm run dev 
 The app runs at http://localhost:5173 with no configuration. Without a backend nothing is recorded, the
places-checked counter on the landing page is hidden, and share links carry the pass in the URL instead of a short
 /s/ link. 
 To turn on lookups and shares: 
 
 Create a Supabase project and apply the migrations, as docs/SELF-HOSTING.md shows. 
 Copy .env.example to .env.local and set VITE_SUPABASE_URL and VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY . Use the
publishable key, never a secret key: VITE_ variables are bundled into the JavaScript that every visitor
downloads. 
 Run npm run dev as before, or npx vercel dev to serve the share pages and cards in api/ as well. Vercel asks
to link a project the first time. 
 
 The places-checked counter appears once a project has 1,000 lookups, 50 of them in the last 24 hours. 
 Tests and scripts 
 npm test # engine, imagery and UI tests (Vitest) 
npm run test:backend # tests for the api/ functions 
npm run typecheck # tsc -b 
npm run build # the app and the /admin page, into dist/ 

npm run data:celestrak # refresh the orbit catalog (CelesTrak asks for 2 hours between downloads) 
npm run textures -- ./maps # rebuild public/textures from the source maps in ./maps 

 # render share cards for sample passes to image files (needs no server or database) 
npx tsx scripts/backend-render-og.ts 
 The built textures are committed, so you rarely need npm run textures . It needs Python 3 and Pillow, and reads the
source maps listed at the top of scripts/build-textures.py . 
 Useful URLs 
 
 
 
 URL 
 What it does 
 
 
 
 
 /?q=lat,lon&n=name 
 Opens a place directly. Add &p=<pass id> to open a pass. 
 
 
 /?debug=gl 
 WebGL diagnostics. 
 
 
 /?sandbox=<name> 
 Development pages (dev server only): engine , backend , globe , imagery , results , shell . 
 
 
 /admin.html?mock=1 
 The stats page with fixture data (dev server only). 
 
 
 
 Self-hosting 
 Watched is a static Vite build, three Vercel functions, an optional Supabase project and a GitHub Action that keeps
the orbit catalog fresh. To run your own copy: 
 
 Fork the repository and import it into Vercel. It works as is, with no backend. 
 Enable GitHub Actions on your fork so the catalog refresh runs. Forks start with scheduled workflows off. 
 For lookups, shares and stats, apply supabase/migrations to your own Supabase project (they need pg_cron), set
 VITE_SUPABASE_URL and VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY in Vercel, and make yourself admin with
 scripts/backend-set-admin.sh . Every database script needs SUPABASE_PROJECT_REF and has no default, so none of
them can touch someone else's project by accident. 
 For usage events, add your domain to PRODUCTION_HOSTS in src/lib/telemetry.ts . A fork sends none until you do. 
 
 The full guide is docs/SELF-HOSTING.md . 
 Project layout 
 
 Show the directory tree 
 index.html app shell and static boot screen
admin.html /admin stats page (separate build: vite.admin.config.ts)
vercel.json functions, headers, /s/:id and bot-unfurl routes, SPA fallback
src/
 main.tsx entry; analytics and in-app events after first paint (production only)
 types.ts shared contracts
 app/ phase controller, boot curtain, error notice, telemetry wiring
 engine/ catalog, satellite profiles, SGP4, pass search and worker pool, matching,
 weather and geostationary legs, GPU elements, the report
 imagery/ STAC and GIBS, crop and mask URLs, pixels worker, cloud at your spot, Photon, time zones
 globe/ three.js / React Three Fiber scene: Earth, atmosphere, clouds, stars,
 GPU satellites, pass sequence, swath, camera
 ui/ system primitives, HUD, landing, results, share, About
 lib/ geo maths, backend client, telemetry, layout
 state/ zustand store and scene clock
 styles/ tokens, fonts, base
 admin/ /admin page (Supabase Auth)
 sandbox/ development-only ?sandbox= pages
api/ og.tsx (share card), s.ts (share page), e.ts (events relay), _lib, _fonts, _assets
public/ data/ (orbit catalog), textures/, brand/, og-default.png
supabase/ migrations 0001 to 0007, SQL tests
scripts/ catalog fetch, textures, fonts, card render, migrate, admin, verify, SQL test, purge
docs/ DESIGN.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, SELF-HOSTING.md
.github/workflows/ catalog.yml (orbit catalog refresh)
 
 
 Data and credits 
 
 
 
 Source 
 Credit 
 
 
 
 
 Orbits 
 Element sets from CelesTrak , based on US Space Force tracking data, refreshed every 6 hours. SGP4 by satellite.js . 
 
 
 Sentinel‑2 
 Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data, followed by the year each photo was taken. 
 
 
 Landsat 
 Landsat imagery courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey and NASA. 
 
 
 NASA GIBS 
 Imagery from NASA's GIBS, part of EOSDIS. GOES via NOAA and CIRA, Himawari via JMA. 
 
 
 Archives 
 Microsoft Planetary Computer and Element 84 Earth Search . 
 
 
 Places 
 Photon by komoot. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). 
 
 
 Textures 
 Solar System Scope ( CC BY 4.0 ), from NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble, partly by way of the three.js examples. Resized, re-encoded and repacked for this project. 
 
 
 Fonts 
 Instrument Sans and Serif by Instrument, Martian Mono by Evil Martians (SIL OFL 1.1). 
 
 
 
 The screenshots in this README and the default share image contain modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2026. Licenses
and attribution for every bundled asset are in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md .

# CUI **A UI library for C that draws its own components.** [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/yappologistic/CUI/ci.yml?branch=master&label=CI&style=flat-square&labelColor=24292f)](https://github.com/yappologistic/CUI/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/yappologistic/CUI?style=flat-square&labelColor=24292f&color=57606a)](https://github.com/yappologistic/CUI/releases) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-57606a.svg?style=flat-square&labelColor=24292f&color=57606a)](LICENSE) [Live site](https://yappologistic.github.io/CUI/) · [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) · [Tutorial](docs/tutorial.md) · [Components](docs/components.md) · [Downloads](https://github.com/yappologistic/CUI/releases)
Every image on this page is drawn by CUI, from plain C.
CUI is an immediate-mode UI library written in C99. You describe the screen with function calls every frame. CUI lays it out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws it with OpenGL or its own software renderer, in a window on Windows, macOS or Linux, or in a browser through WebAssembly. - **About 190 components**, from buttons and text fields to a data grid, charts, a code editor and docking panels. - **No dependencies.** One CMake target, or two files (`cui.h` and `cui.c`) dropped into your project. - **Small.** A complete app, window, fonts and all, is about 250 KB. There is no browser or runtime inside. - **MIT licensed.** ## Try it first - **In your browser:** the [live site](https://yappologistic.github.io/CUI/) runs every component and the example apps. It is the same C code, compiled to WebAssembly. - **On your computer, without a compiler:** each [release](https://github.com/yappologistic/CUI/releases) has the example apps built for Windows, macOS and Linux. - **In code:** the [tutorial](docs/tutorial.md) builds a to-do app in about 130 lines. ## A small program ```c #include #include int main(void) { cui_app *app = cui_app_create(&(cui_app_desc){ .title = "Hello", .width = 420, .height = 300 }); if (!app) return 1; bool notifications = true; int clicks = 0; while (cui_app_frame(app)) { cui_ctx *ui = cui_app_ui(app); cui_column(ui, .pad = 32, .gap = 16) { cui_heading(ui, "Hello, CUI", 2); cui_secondary(ui, "A native window, a few components " "and no dependencies."); cui_switch(ui, "Notifications", ¬ifications); cui_row(ui, .gap = 8) { if (cui_button(ui, "Click me", .variant = CUI_BUTTON_PRIMARY)) clicks++; cui_textf(ui, "Clicked %d times", clicks); } } } cui_app_destroy(app); return 0; } ```
**A component is a function call.** It draws itself, handles input and returns what happened: `cui_button` returns true on the frame it is clicked. **Options are named arguments.** Leave one out and it takes its default. **Your variables are the state.** The screen is described again every frame, so there are no widgets to create, keep or update.
## What it is, and what it is not CUI draws every component itself. It does not wrap the system's buttons and menus, so an app looks the same on every system and does not look like the system's own apps. "Native" here means compiled code in a real window, with nothing interpreted and no web view. How it sits beside the libraries you may know: - **Dear ImGui and Nuklear** are also immediate-mode. They are aimed mostly at tools and debug panels inside a program that already has a renderer. CUI uses the same model for the app itself: it opens the window, and its components come with the things end users expect, such as full text editing, animation, light and dark themes and right-to-left layouts. - **Qt, GTK and wxWidgets** keep a tree of widgets for you and are far more mature. They have screen reader support, complete input-method support and years of use behind them. If you need those today, use one of them. - **Electron and web views** ship a browser with your app. CUI ships about 250 KB. CUI is a good fit for a desktop tool, an editor, a dashboard or a game's interface written in C or C++, where you want it small and want it to look finished without designing every control. Read [Limitations](#limitations) before you decide. ## Install With CMake (GCC, Clang, MSVC and MinGW are tested): ```cmake include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare(cui GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/yappologistic/CUI.git GIT_TAG v1.3.1) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(cui) target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE cui::cui) cui_app_target(my_app) # no console window on Windows, and only the code your app uses ``` Without CMake, take `cui.h` and `cui.c` from a [release](https://github.com/yappologistic/CUI/releases) and compile them with your program. [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) has the exact commands for both, and CI runs those commands on every push. To build the library and run an example: ```sh git clone https://github.com/yappologistic/CUI.git cmake -S CUI -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --build build ./build/examples/tracker ``` Linux needs the X11 development headers (`libx11-dev`). Windows and macOS need nothing beyond the system SDK. ## What is in it | Group | Components | |---|---| | **Basics and actions** | text, buttons, icon buttons, split and toggle buttons, menus, command palette | | **Inputs** | text field, text area, number, money, tags, one time code, select, combobox, multi-select, shortcut recorder, dropzone | | **Selection and pickers** | checkbox, switch, radio, slider, chips, date and date range, time, color, emoji, knob and fader | | **Navigation and windows** | tabs, sidebar, breadcrumb, menu bar, toolbar, status bar, document tabs, docking panels | | **Overlays and feedback** | dialog, sheet, popover, tooltip, toast, alert, progress, skeleton, empty state, guided tour | | **Data** | table, data grid for very large data, tree, tree table, list, file browser with open and save dialogs | | **Code and text** | code block, code editor, diff viewer, markdown view, JSON viewer, terminal, log console, hex viewer | | **Charts** | line, bar, donut, sparkline, gauge, candlestick, heatmap, treemap, radar, funnel, sankey, scatter | | **Planning** | kanban board, week and month calendars, gantt chart, node editor | | **Developer tools** | trace viewer, network waterfall, flame graph, dependency and commit graphs, CI pipeline, test explorer, regex tester, query builder | | **Instruments** | dot-matrix chart, chart annotations, event track on a time axis, readout, dot-matrix display | | **Conversation and AI** | chat, comments, composer, reasoning and tool calls, agent plan, sources and citations | | **Your own** | a canvas with a 2D drawing API, per-component state and spring animation | Every component has a page with a live example, its options, its data structures and what it does with the keyboard: on the [site](https://yappologistic.github.io/CUI/#/components), or in [Components](docs/components.md) and [More components](docs/components-more.md).
Pictures of the larger components
Docking: drag a tab to stack it or split any side; the layout saves as a short string · docs
Data grid: 2,000 virtualized rows, filters, sorting, resizable columns and spreadsheet style selection
Kanban: the lifted card follows the pointer and the column opens a slot for it Command palette: fuzzy search, groups and shortcuts
Pickers: a date range with presets over two months, and wheels that spin with momentum
More: charts, planning, conversation, effects
Charts: calendar heatmap, sankey and radar, with a live task plan Dock, tiles and player: icons grow under the pointer, the waveform seeks on click
Conversation: grouped bubbles, threads, a rolling counter, presence Spotlight cards: the surface and edge nearest the pointer light up
Gantt: drag to reschedule, pull the ends to resize, arrows follow dependencies
## Example apps Complete apps in [`examples/`](examples), each a single C file. They run in the browser on the [site](https://yappologistic.github.io/CUI/#/apps).
Muse: reasoning, tool calls, sources, a plan and a composer with a model picker · assistant.c
Orbit: grouped issues, custom glyphs, an activity pane · tracker.c Larkspur: figures, charts and a sortable table · dashboard.c

## Themes ```c cui_set_theme(ui, CUI_THEME_DARK); /* animates */ cui_set_accent(ui, CUI_ACCENT_BLUE); /* neutral, violet, blue, green, amber, orange, coral, rose */ ``` Colors are named tokens (`CUI_COLOR_SURFACE`, `CUI_COLOR_ACCENT` and so on), so your own drawing follows the theme too. See [Theming](docs/theming.md). ## Size and speed | Measure | Result | |---|---| | `hello` on Linux, the whole executable, stripped | about 250 KB | | `assistant` (the AI app above), the whole executable | about 350 KB | | The whole library: every component, both renderers, the X11 backend, fonts and icons | about 1,050 KB | | Build, lay out and paint one frame (gallery pages, 1240 × 820 points at 2×) | 0.09 to 0.75 ms, most under 0.25 | | A real app in use (Notes, Mail, an IDE; software renderer, 1280 × 800) | 2 to 3% of one core, 11 to 13 MB of memory | | Library memory over an hour of use | 2 to 9 MB, flat, with nothing left after `cui_destroy` | | CPU while nothing happens | 0%: the app waits for events | An app carries only the components it calls, which is why `hello` is a quarter of the library. The times are wall clock on a 4 core cloud VM. `cui_bench` in [`tests/`](tests) reproduces them, and [Performance](docs/performance.md) describes the hour-long runs behind the memory and CPU rows. ## Platforms | Platform | Backend | Renderer | Tested in CI | |---|---|---|---| | Windows 7+ | Win32 (per monitor DPI, dark title bar) | OpenGL 3.3, GDI software fallback | MSVC, MinGW | | macOS 10.13+ | Cocoa (Retina, native menus, text input) | OpenGL 3.3+, layer software fallback | Apple clang | | Linux, BSD | X11 (XIM text input, HiDPI) | OpenGL 3.3 (GLX), XPutImage fallback | GCC, Clang | | Wayland and others | SDL2 or GLFW | OpenGL 3.3 | GCC | | Browser | WebAssembly, plain clang ([how](docs/getting-started.md#run-in-the-browser)) | WebGL2, or software | Docs site, every push | | Anything | Your own | Your own (one shader) | | To use CUI inside an engine with your own window and renderer, see [Integration](docs/integration.md) and [Rendering](docs/rendering.md). The core only emits triangles. ## Limitations - **No screen reader support.** There is no accessibility tree yet. This rules CUI out for apps that must be accessible to blind users. - **The keyboard does not reach everything.** Most components work from the keyboard and each one's page lists its keys. Some parts still need a pointer: the rating, the histogram slider's handles, swipe actions, the reorderable list, the JSON viewer, the agent plan's steps, blame, the time histogram, and the choices inside the open time picker and color picker. - **Complex scripts are partial.** Text is UTF-8 with kerning and font fallback, and layouts mirror for right-to-left languages. Arabic-script shaping and bidirectional text are an optional, experimental build option for static text ([details](docs/integration.md#optional-arabic-script-text-shaping)). CJK works once you add a fallback font. - **Input methods compose in the system's window.** Committed text arrives; the text being composed is not drawn inline. - **No native Wayland backend.** Use the SDL2 or GLFW backend, or XWayland. - **No Android or iOS.** Layouts adapt to phone widths and touch, and apps run in mobile browsers, but there is no platform layer for phones. - **It is new.** Version 1.0 was released in November 2026, so it has little real-world use behind it yet. The [changelog](CHANGELOG.md) lists what each release changed. ## How it is built and tested Most of CUI's code is written by AI models under the maintainer's direction. Every commit names the model that wrote it in a `Co-Authored-By` trailer, and the [contribution rules](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md) ask the same of everyone who sends a change. Because of that, the tests are what the project stands on. Every push runs 19 CI jobs: - unit, interaction and render tests on Windows (MSVC and MinGW), macOS and Linux (GCC and Clang, with the X11, SDL2 and GLFW backends); - a fuzzer that drives the gallery and the example apps with random input under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer; - real windows opened on all three systems; - the single-file build with GCC and Clang; - the commands of the getting-started guide, taken from the guide and run as written. The images in [`docs/images`](docs/images) are rendered by the tests, so a visual change and its documentation move together. ```sh cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug cmake --build build ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure ``` ## Documentation | Guide | What it covers | |---|---| | [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) | Install, build, the frame loop, your first screens | | [Tutorial](docs/tutorial.md) | Build a small, complete app step by step | | [Building an app](docs/apps.md) | The window, when frames happen, what components return, threads, shipping | | [Recipes](docs/recipes.md) | Complete programs: a form, a sorted table, a background task, saved settings | | [Layout](docs/layout.md) | Rows, columns, sizes, alignment, grids, scrolling, split views | | [Components](docs/components.md) and [more](docs/components-more.md) | Every component: what it is, usage, options, keyboard | | [Theming](docs/theming.md) | Tokens, light and dark, accents, fonts, motion | | [Icons](docs/icons.md) | The built-in Lucide icons, and how to use another icon font | | [Custom components](docs/custom-components.md) | The canvas, the drawing API, state and animation | | [Integration](docs/integration.md) | Your own window, input and renderer; C++; binary size | | [Rendering](docs/rendering.md) | The vertex format and the reference shader | | [Performance](docs/performance.md) | How memory and speed are tested, and the results | | [Function reference](https://yappologistic.github.io/CUI/#/reference) | Every public function with its signature, on the site | | [Questions](docs/faq.md) | What CUI is and is not, how it compares, what it cannot do | | [How CUI is built](docs/architecture.md) | The code map and the outline every component follows | | [Design principles](docs/design.md) | The visual rules every component follows | The [live site](https://yappologistic.github.io/CUI/) has the same guides with every component running beside its page. It is rebuilt from `master` on every push; to run it locally, use `web/tools/serve.sh` (needs clang with the `wasm32` target). ## Contributing Bug reports and pull requests are welcome, from people and from AI agents. Every report needs an honest account of who wrote it (and which model, if an AI did) and evidence you produced yourself: the commands you ran and their output. [Contributing](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md) explains what that means. ## Credits Type: [Inter](https://rsms.me/inter/) and [Geist](https://vercel.com/font) (SIL Open Font License).  CUI 
 A UI library for C that draws its own components. 
 
 
 
 Live site ·
 Getting started ·
 Tutorial ·
 Components ·
 Downloads 
 
 
 
 
 
 Every image on this page is drawn by CUI, from plain C. 
 
 CUI is an immediate-mode UI library written in C99. You describe the screen with function calls every frame. CUI lays it out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws it with OpenGL or its own software renderer, in a window on Windows, macOS or Linux, or in a browser through WebAssembly. 
 
 About 190 components , from buttons and text fields to a data grid, charts, a code editor and docking panels. 
 No dependencies. One CMake target, or two files ( cui.h and cui.c ) dropped into your project. 
 Small. A complete app, window, fonts and all, is about 250 KB. There is no browser or runtime inside. 
 MIT licensed. 
 
 Try it first 
 
 In your browser: the live site runs every component and the example apps. It is the same C code, compiled to WebAssembly. 
 On your computer, without a compiler: each release has the example apps built for Windows, macOS and Linux. 
 In code: the tutorial builds a to-do app in about 130 lines. 
 
 A small program 
 #include <cui/cui.h> 
 #include <cui/cui_app.h> 

 int main ( void ) {
 cui_app * app = cui_app_create ( & ( cui_app_desc ){
 . title = "Hello" , . width = 420 , . height = 300 });
 if (! app ) return 1 ;
 bool notifications = true;
 int clicks = 0 ;

 while ( cui_app_frame ( app )) {
 cui_ctx * ui = cui_app_ui ( app );
 cui_column ( ui , . pad = 32 , . gap = 16 ) {
 cui_heading ( ui , "Hello, CUI" , 2 );
 cui_secondary ( ui , "A native window, a few components " 
 "and no dependencies." );
 cui_switch ( ui , "Notifications" , & notifications );
 cui_row ( ui , . gap = 8 ) {
 if ( cui_button ( ui , "Click me" , . variant = CUI_BUTTON_PRIMARY ))
 clicks ++ ;
 cui_textf ( ui , "Clicked %d times" , clicks );
 }
 }
 }
 cui_app_destroy ( app );
 return 0 ;
} 
 
 
 
 
 A component is a function call. It draws itself, handles input and returns what happened: cui_button returns true on the frame it is clicked. 
 Options are named arguments. Leave one out and it takes its default. 
 Your variables are the state. The screen is described again every frame, so there are no widgets to create, keep or update. 
 
 
 
 What it is, and what it is not 
 CUI draws every component itself. It does not wrap the system's buttons and menus, so an app looks the same on every system and does not look like the system's own apps. "Native" here means compiled code in a real window, with nothing interpreted and no web view. 
 How it sits beside the libraries you may know: 
 
 Dear ImGui and Nuklear are also immediate-mode. They are aimed mostly at tools and debug panels inside a program that already has a renderer. CUI uses the same model for the app itself: it opens the window, and its components come with the things end users expect, such as full text editing, animation, light and dark themes and right-to-left layouts. 
 Qt, GTK and wxWidgets keep a tree of widgets for you and are far more mature. They have screen reader support, complete input-method support and years of use behind them. If you need those today, use one of them. 
 Electron and web views ship a browser with your app. CUI ships about 250 KB. 
 
 CUI is a good fit for a desktop tool, an editor, a dashboard or a game's interface written in C or C++, where you want it small and want it to look finished without designing every control. Read Limitations before you decide. 
 Install 
 With CMake (GCC, Clang, MSVC and MinGW are tested): 
 include ( FetchContent )
 FetchContent_Declare (cui
 GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/yappologistic/CUI.git
 GIT_TAG v1.3.1)
 FetchContent_MakeAvailable (cui)
 target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE cui::cui )
 cui_app_target ( my_app ) # no console window on Windows, and only the code your app uses 
 Without CMake, take cui.h and cui.c from a release and compile them with your program. Getting started has the exact commands for both, and CI runs those commands on every push. 
 To build the library and run an example: 
 git clone https://github.com/yappologistic/CUI.git
cmake -S CUI -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
./build/examples/tracker 
 Linux needs the X11 development headers ( libx11-dev ). Windows and macOS need nothing beyond the system SDK.

# Exact **Write an app once. It runs natively on the web, macOS, iOS, and Linux, and an AI agent can build it, run it, see it, and test it on every one of them.** > [!TIP] > **Try it with a coding agent.** On a Mac with Xcode, Rust, Bun, and Chrome installed, > give Claude Code this prompt: > > ```text > Clone https://github.com/expo/exact and follow its README to make a new Exact > app with `exact new`. Run `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` once first. Make a todo > list where I can add items, check them off, delete them, > and see how many are left. Put the view in Contract and keep the list in `app.ts`. > Write an `app.test.contract`, pass it on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator with > `scripts/agent.mjs`, then open the app for me on all three. > ``` > > A fresh agent given the earlier version of this prompt on a clean clone (2026-10-04, Hermes already in the > machine cache, Cargo's cache warm) finished in about 57 minutes, and its tests passed > on all three platforms. About 25 of those minutes were the first macOS and iOS builds, > roughly 13 minutes each; later builds take a minute or two. On a machine that has > lacked Hermes, its source build came first and added time. Current setup downloads and > verifies the pinned host/iOS bundles once instead; ordinary builds stay offline.
Web iOS macOS
The browser's own DOM and CSS UIKit views, native controls and the system's tab bar AppKit views and native controls
One app.contract, the same screen on three hosts, captured by the agent driver. Softwear is a demonstration store you can generate from exact-templates: it shows Alternative Apparel's catalog, is not affiliated with that brand, and takes no real orders or payments. Exact is a cross-platform application runtime. You describe your interface in **Contract**, a small declarative language, and you write your data logic in **TypeScript or Rust**. The Contract compiler turns the interface into a compact *plan*. On the web, that plan becomes one ES module over a ~20 KB runtime that drives the real DOM. On macOS, iOS, and Linux, a Rust runner executes the same plan, a Rust layout kernel computes every box with CSS rules, and each platform draws with its own tools: AppKit, UIKit, or a GPU painter. There is no webview and no JavaScript bridge in the UI, and no app JavaScript runs before the first pixel. > [!NOTE] > Exact is pre-1.0 and changes daily. There is no API stability, no backwards > compatibility, and no migration guide, by design (`rules/DEFERRED.md`). This > repository, `exact2`, is a rebuild of an earlier one ("exact1"). Its design documents > are imported under `llp/research/` as research, never as authority. Upgrade note (2026-10-16): Snapback mutation replies with `ok: false` now throw `refused(why)` and expose `failure(slot)`; see the [before/after and inherited-app commands](snapback4/README.md#updating-an-inherited-app). ## Contents - [Three principles](#three-principles) - [How it works](#how-it-works) - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [Contract](#contract) - [Example apps](#example-apps) - [What works today, and what doesn't yet](#what-works-today-and-what-doesnt-yet) - [Repository map](#repository-map) - [Working on Exact](#working-on-exact) ## Three principles ### 1. Agent native Exact assumes much of the code will be written by AI agents. An agent can make an app, run it, look at it, operate it, and prove it works without a person in the loop. - **Ten operations, the same on every host.** `tree · screenshot · tap · type · state · layout · logs · clock · prefer · perf` drive the web, macOS, iOS (Simulator or a real iPhone), and Linux through one script, `scripts/agent.mjs`. There are ten on purpose: the predecessor's agent API grew to eighty wire names, one reasonable addition at a time. - **The clock belongs to the agent.** Between two operations nothing moves. Instead of sleeping until an animation finishes, the agent says `clock +60000` or `clock settle` and reads the result. No timing flakes, no waits. - **Tests are scripts of those operations.** An `app.test.contract` file runs unchanged on any host, with no second evaluator. - **Every tool speaks to machines.** `contract build --json` gives diagnostics with stable ids and source ranges. `contract symbols` gives navigation. A development source map leads from any node on screen back to the line that declared it. The driver refuses to drive a build older than its sources and names the rebuild. - **Contract is small on purpose.** A whole app fits in a context window. Every write is declared, every list is keyed, every value is typed. Mistakes are refusals that say what to do, not quiet misbehavior. ```sh bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" \ "clock +60000" state "screenshot out.png" ``` ### 2. Speed is king Speed of the app and speed of the loop. Each budget in `rules/RULES.md` is tracked on every commit, and a regression is a P0 with a name on it. | Budget | Target | |---|---| | Cold start to interactive first frame | 100 ms p50 | | Dev restart, edit to present | 100 ms p50 | | App JavaScript executed before first pixel | none | | Touch one line, rebuild that crate | 30 s | | The whole blocking check suite | 65 s | How the design keeps those numbers: - **The boot path executes and compiles nothing.** TypeScript is compiled to Hermes bytecode at build time and loads after the first pixel. The first frame comes from data baked into the plan. - **Pay only for what you use.** GPU rendering, the Markdown editor, text flow, and browser SQLite are separate artifacts, loaded on demand. Nothing is a feature flag on a core crate. - **The web gets its own small runtime.** On the RealWorld ("Conduit") benchmark, Exact's runtime was up about 300 ms before the React SSR build had hydrated. It used 26 KB of code against React's 81 KB ([LLP 1071](llp/1071-exact2-web-target.rfc.md)). - **Edits land in about a tenth of a second.** On a fresh app made by `exact new`, a saved Contract or TypeScript edit was rebuilt and in the page in 99 ms. ### 3. Write the web, ship the platform What you write is CSS: the vocabulary, the layout model, the development loop. What you leave unsaid is the platform's: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, the keyboard and accessibility come out as an app built by hand with UIKit or AppKit would have them, and on the web as a carefully built web app would. What you write wins. The order is author, then platform, then CSS's default, and one test settles a dispute: would someone who knows the platform notice? ([LLP 1115](llp/1115-write-the-web-ship-the-platform.principle.md)) - Layout is CSS's, because a person can't see a layout default, only its result. A bare node is `display: block`, `box-sizing: content-box`, `flex-direction: row`, `flex-shrink: 1`, the same as a bare `
`. - Names are CSS's, because names are what you write: `font-size`, `object-fit`, `text-overflow`, `line-clamp`, `light-dark()`, `env(safe-area-inset-top)`. The compiler refuses an alias and names the web's spelling. - Unsaid presentation is the platform's. Text is the system's label colour and size (17 points on an iPhone, 13 on a Mac, the reader's setting in a browser), a `button` is the system's button, a pushed screen has the system's Back. An app that says less looks more at home. - The browser is the parity oracle for layout and for what you wrote. Native layout given the same inputs, Canvas 2D, SVG, gradients, and authored motion are checked against what Chrome draws. - The web is also the development loop. You work on the seconds-long web loop, and the native hosts are swept behind you. - Any unavoidable deviation in layout is declared, with its reason, in [`llp/1001-kernel-v1.spec.md`](llp/1001-kernel-v1.spec.md). For example, Taffy has no `position: static`. Writing the web doesn't mean the lowest common denominator. Where a platform can do more (real HTML in an SVG `foreignObject` on the web, MapKit through a native module on Apple), Exact lets it. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph author["You write"] C["app.contract
view · state · actions"] D["app.ts or a Rust crate
data sources"] end C --> K["Contract compiler"] --> P["plan
tables + bytecode"] P --> W["Web
one ES module, ~20 KB runtime,
the browser's DOM and CSS"] P --> R["Rust runner
+ layout kernel (Taffy)"] R --> M["macOS
AppKit + CoreText"] R --> I["iOS
UIKit + CoreText"] R --> L["Linux
vello GPU / tiny-skia CPU"] D -.->|answers, checked against declared shapes| W D -.-> R ``` - **Contract** (`contract/`) is compiled in four passes: syntax, types, analysis, and lowering. At build time the plan is *baked*: constant data is evaluated into it, so the first frame needs nothing else. - **The runner** (`runner/`) is the plan's virtual machine. It handles keyed component instances, events, timers on a seekable clock, and the data seam. - **The kernel** (`kernel/`) is a columnar node arena with CSS layout through a patched [Taffy](vendor/taffy/EXACT-PATCHES.md). The host measures text: CoreText on Apple, cosmic-text on Linux. On the web, the browser lays out the same CSS itself, so the web build carries no layout engine. - **Hosts** (`host/`) present the tree. The web host writes DOM nodes, and the browser runs CSS transitions. The Apple host is a static library with a C ABI under AppKit and UIKit presenters. The Linux host paints the tree itself, onto DRM/KMS with evdev input, or into an offscreen buffer. - **Data sources** sit below one seam. TypeScript runs on Hermes on native hosts and in the browser's own engine on the web. Rust runs natively, and can be replaced live (as a shared library, or as Wasm on iOS and the web). Every answer is checked against the shape Contract declared. Grants control network, files, SQLite, and secrets. - **Optional pieces** are separate artifacts: a wgpu GPU module (Metal on Apple, WebGPU in the browser), native modules (a hyphenated tag backed by a platform widget, like MapKit), and a [game engine](game/README.md) add-on. ## Quick start These steps were run on macOS on Apple Silicon. Linux works for the web loop and the Linux host. ### 1. Install the tools - **Rust** through [rustup](https://rustup.rs). The pinned stable toolchain in `rust-toolchain.toml` installs itself the first time Cargo runs. - **[Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.4.2**, the version `package.json` pins. Node and npm are not needed. - **Google Chrome.** The agent drives the web through headless Chrome. Set `CHROME` to use another Chromium. - **Xcode**, for the macOS and iOS hosts. - **Hermes**, only for TypeScript apps on native hosts. Exact consumes Ibex's pinned, attested `260318099.0.4` release bundle; ordinary Cargo builds are offline and never download or compile an engine. Install it once for each target before building (for this Mac, use `aarch64-apple-darwin`): ```sh cargo run --manifest-path vendor/ibex/crates/hermes-lean-sys-installer/Cargo.toml -- --target ``` The installer verifies the bundle and publishes it under `~/.cargo/hermes-lean-sys/`. The v4 set supports macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS devices and the universal iOS Simulator, plus tvOS devices and arm64 tvOS Simulators. Linux and Windows select Ibex's English `intl` tier; Apple keeps Hermes's OS-backed Intl. `HERMES_LEAN_SYS_DIR` is only an explicit development override, not normal setup. To install the pinned Bun beside any existing installation: `curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | BUN_INSTALL=~/.bun-1.4.2 bash -s bun-v1.4.2`. Use `~/.bun-1.4.2/bin/bun` for the commands below if it is not on your PATH. `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` installs the declared stable and web nightly Rust toolchains, their components/targets (the nightly's clippy lints a game's web bake), matching wasm-bindgen, pinned Binaryen and Bun dependencies, installs the pinned Hermes host bundle and the iOS/tvOS bundles this Mac builds, and fetches the crates of exact2's lock and the game SDK's (`game/app/shells.lock`), since every bake resolves offline. It keeps Binaryen in `~/.cache/exact/binaryen`; builds find it automatically. `setup --check` invokes Ibex's installer in its offline check mode for that same target set. The resolver authenticates the canonical receipts, archives, compiler and host/target HBC pairing without installing anything; its exit status and diagnostic are the check's result. ### 2. Run Caltrain in the browser ```sh git clone https://github.com/expo/exact.git cd exact bun scripts/exact.mjs setup bun host/web/dev.mjs # Caltrain, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ ``` The first run compiles the toolchain, which takes a few minutes. After that, open [`apps/caltrain/app.contract`](apps/caltrain/app.contract), change some text, and save. The page rebuilds and reloads in about a tenth of a second. Add `--lan` to open the same page from a phone on your network. The server answers only to the names it prints (a DNS-rebinding guard; any other `Host` gets 421); to share it through a tunnel such as `tuft host`, name the tunnel's host with `--allow-host ` (repeatable; `name:port` pins a port). An allowed name reaches the page and its reload stream, never the local installer's token. ### 3. Run it natively ```sh bun host/apple/build.mjs --run # macOS bun host/apple/build.mjs --ios --run # an iOS Simulator (--device --run for a connected iPhone) cargo build --profile host-dev -p caltrain-linux # Linux: a DRM/KMS console, or headless anywhere (--release to ship) ``` A first native build takes ten to fifteen minutes on a laptop; later builds reuse it and take a minute or two. Watch its output rather than waiting blind. iOS commands use an iPhone simulator that's already booted, or boot the newest iPhone Pro. To choose one, set `EXACT_SIM` to its name or UDID (or pass `--sim` to `build.mjs`), and keep the same setting for `agent.mjs ios`. On Linux, a development build can serve its screen with `EXACT_VNC=1` and `EXACT_VNC_PASSWORD` set to 1–8 bytes. It listens on `127.0.0.1:5900`; an explicit `EXACT_VNC=host:port` selects another address. Production bakes ignore both variables. ### 4. Drive it the way an agent does ```sh bun host/web/build.mjs caltrain-web # the build the agent's web host serves bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" state "screenshot out.png" bun scripts/agent.mjs web --test apps/caltrain/app.test.contract ``` Swap `web` for `macos`, `ios`, or `linux` once that host is built. Caltrain's three tests take about two seconds on the web host. Each operation is one shell argument, so quote it: `"type new-todo Buy milk"` types `Buy milk` (everything after the target is the text). `"screenshot film.png over 600 every 50"` films motion as a contact sheet; use an `.apng` name to get an animation. ### 5. Make your own app ```sh bun scripts/exact.mjs new ../hello # or run `bun link` once, then `exact new ../hello` cd ../hello bun exact.mjs contract types app.contract -o app.contract.d.ts # first run builds the compiler bun exact.mjs web # the dev loop, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ bun exact.mjs test web tests/*.test.contract # the app's *.test.contract, or the files named bun exact.mjs mac --run # this Mac bun exact.mjs ios --run # an iOS Simulator ``` `exact new` creates a standalone app: `app.contract` (the view), `app.ts` (its data), `app.json` (the manifest: name, bundle id, hosts, deploy policy), and small `web/` and `apple/` host crates. Its `AGENTS.md` (and `CLAUDE.md`) points a coding agent at [`docs/start-here.md`](docs/start-here.md), the one guide it must read, and at `bun exact.mjs help` for the commands, including `bun exact.mjs contract …` for the compiler and `contract vocab` for the card of what an app writes (`--all`: every tag and property Contract accepts). Before any of it, run `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` once; `setup --check` names everything this machine is missing without changing it. It has its own Cargo workspace, which uses your exact2 checkout by path. To drive it from exact2, point `EXACT_APP_DIR` at it: ```sh EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun host/web/build.mjs hello-web EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun scripts/agent.mjs web --app hello tree "screenshot hello.png" ``` Look at every screenshot, not just the test result: a test passes on a layout that spills off the screen. `bun exact.mjs agent "screenshot out.png"` shows the app on each host in its own session; for a copy you launched yourself, use `xcrun simctl io screenshot out.png` on iOS. `bun scripts/exact.mjs` also runs apps from this repository as real Mac apps: `exact run markdown README.md`, or `exact install markdown` to put `mdview` on your `PATH`. `exact list` shows what's here. ### Feedback An app's `AGENTS.md` asks its agent to record friction in one line, `bun exact.mjs feedback note ""`. A failed or slow drive, build or verify, and a passing `test` or `verify`, end with one line naming it, at most once a day per project. A note stays in the app's `.exact/` with exact2's commit, the last command's verb, exit code and duration, and the OS; never any command output, or the app's code or files. It goes to Expo (`https://exact-diaries.ccheever-0f6.workers.dev`) only when the project's answer allows: `always`, or a yes to `ask`, the default, after `bun exact.mjs feedback` shows exactly what would go. `bun exact.mjs feedback never` stops it for a project; `EXACT_FEEDBACK=0` silences the nudges and refuses every send on the machine. [docs/diary.md](docs/diary.md) has the details. ## Contract An agent building an app starts at [start-here.md](docs/start-here.md), the only required reading, then looks up the [recipe](docs/recipes/) for each question. For more, read the complete [guide for humans](docs/contract-for-humans.md), or look things up in the [guide for agents](docs/contract-for-agents.md) or the [grammar and vocabulary reference](docs/contract-grammar.md). Contract describes what an app shows and how its state changes. It doesn't fetch, read files, or run arbitrary code. That's what data sources are for. Here is a complete todo app: a Contract file, a TypeScript file, and a test. This exact app was built for web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator, and its test passed on all three. To try it in an app created with `exact new`, replace `app.contract` and `app.test.contract` with the examples below. In `app.ts`, keep the generated `export const appId = …` line and replace the rest with the TypeScript below. ```contract // app.contract: the view, its state, and what each action changes. It names no colour, // font or control size: each host draws its own heading, field, button, checkbox and list. shape Todo id: string title: string done: bool shape Change count: number component Todos state draft = "" mutation changed as shape Change refreshes todos resource todos = todos() as shape Todo[] derive left = todos.filter(t => not t.done).length action edit(value: string) draft = value action add if draft.trim() != "" send changed = addTodo(draft.trim()) draft = "" action toggle(id: string, done: bool) send changed = setDone(id, done) action remove(id: string) send changed = removeTodo(id) view list appearance="auto" height="100%" section header text `${left} left` role="heading" testId="count" row input value=draft input=edit submit=add placeholder="What needs doing?" aria-label="New todo" testId="new-todo" flex=1 min-width=0 button press=add buttonStyle="filled" testId="add" text "Add" section for t in todos key=t.id row testId=`todo-${t.id}` input type="checkbox" checked=t.done change=toggle(t.id) aria-label=t.title testId=`toggle-${t.id}` text t.title flex=1 button press=remove(t.id) destructive=true testId=`remove-${t.id}` text "Delete" ``` ```ts // app.ts: keeps the list, and answers what app.contract asks for import type { Answer, Sources } from './app.contract.d.ts'; export const grants = ''; // e.g. 'net.fetch https://api.example.com' type Todo = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean }; let todos: Todo[] = []; let next = 1; const sources: Sources = { todos: () => todos, addTodo: ([title]) => { todos = [...todos, { id: String(next++), title, done: false }]; return { count: todos.length }; }, setDone: ([id, done]) => { todos = todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done } : t)); return { count: todos.length }; }, removeTodo: ([id]) => { todos = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id); return { count: todos.length }; }, }; export const answer: Answer = (source, args, store, storage, native) => sources[source](args, store, storage, native); ``` ```contract-test // app.test.contract: runs on any host with `scripts/agent.mjs --test` test "add, finish and delete" expect text "count" == "0 left" type "new-todo" "Buy milk" tap "add" type "new-todo" "Walk the dog" type "new-todo" key "Enter" expect text "count" == "2 left" tap "toggle-1" expect text "count" == "1 left" tap "remove-1" expect tree missing "todo-1" expect tree has "todo-2" ```

The view never edits the list itself. An action `send`s a *mutation* to a source, `app.ts` changes its data and answers, and `refreshes todos` asks for the list again. Data lives in one place, and every change to it is a named, typed call an agent can see. This list lives in memory. To keep it across launches, give `app.ts` a grant like `sqlite.open app:/data/todos.db` and use `storage.sqlite`, as [Fieldnotes](apps/fieldnotes) does. ### The pieces | Concept | What it is | |---|---| | `shape` | A closed record type. Fields are `number`, `string`, `bool`, another shape, `option`, or `T[]`. | | `component` | A unit of UI. The first one in a file is the root. Components take `props`, can `inject` what an ancestor `provide`s, and can fill a `slot` with `children`. | | `state` | A value the component owns, its type inferred or declared (`state picked: option = none`). Under a `for`, child state belongs to that keyed row. | | `derive` | A value computed from others, recomputed when they change. | | `resource` | Data from a source: `resource x = source(args) as shape T`. When the arguments change, the source is asked again. | | `mutation` / `send` | A change made through a source: `send x = source(args)`. `refreshes r` asks resource `r` again afterward, `pending(x)` and `failed(x)` show progress, and `failure(x)` says why a resource failed. | | `action` | The only place state changes. What it writes is inferred from its body, and `let` binds a local inside it. | | `task` | Work on a schedule: `every(1000, tick)`, `after(ms, a)`, `every(frame, a)`. | | `view` | Indented elements, `if … else`, `for … key=…` (a key is required), `match` over options, and calls to other components. | | `style` / `class=` | A named set of CSS properties. The node's own attributes win, and there is no cascade. | | `fn`, `xs.map` / `xs.filter` / `xs.join` | Pure, single-expression helpers. Recursion is refused. | | Built-in functions | The web's string and array methods by their names, called on the value (`xs.length`, `s.trim()`, `s.includes(t)`, `xs.at(-1)`), and functions (`first(xs)`, `formatDate`, `formatNumber`); all are listed with their types under `stdlib` in [`plan/tables/format.json`](plan/tables/format.json). | | `routes` | A router: a location and a retained stack per tab, moved with `open`, `push`, `replace`, and `back`, and read with `top`. | | `font` | Declares a font family and binds it to files at build time. | | `use … from "./x.contract"` | Imports components, shapes, styles, and `fn`s from another Contract file. | | `testId` | A stable name for the agent, tests, and accessibility tools. | ### What Contract leaves out, and why - **No JavaScript in the view, and no I/O.** Expressions have no effects. Effects happen only in actions, as assignments, `send`, `refresh`, or commands like `focus(…)` and `share(…)`. Data crosses one seam: a source answers, and the runner checks the answer. - **No loops in actions, no `await`.** A list is a view's keyed `for`, a computation is a `derive` or a `fn` (an action may name a value with `let`), and anything slower lives in a source. A list that changes changes where its data lives, through a mutation, as in the example above. That's what lets the plan be baked, diffed, inspected, and executed the same way on four hosts. - **No escape hatch; access hatches.** Nothing steps outside the plan. Where an app needs a platform widget, it uses a *native module*: a hyphenated tag like `exact-map`, backed by Swift, Kotlin or Rust, laid out by the kernel like any other box. Where it needs the platform object Exact itself built (a `UIView`, a navigation controller, a DOM element), it marks the node `hatch="word"` and its native code is handed that object: an *access hatch*, the panel a machine is built with so its insides can be reached. It configures what Exact made and changes Contract state only by acting on authored nodes, as a person would. These limits serve the principles. An agent can't wire up a data race it can't write. A plan with no JavaScript in it starts fast. A view written in CSS's own words lays out the same on every host and looks at home on each. ### The compiler talks back ```sh $ cargo run -q -p contract -- build app.contract app.contract:4:5 [type-assign] `count` is `number`, cannot assign `string` app.contract:7:23 [lower-unknown-attr] `text` has no attribute `size`; `size` is spelled `font-size` here, the web's name (LLP 1017 §8.1) ``` One run reports up to twenty independent errors, not just the first. Other subcommands: `--json` for tools, `symbols` (definitions and references as JSON), `fmt` (source-preserving), `types` (generates `app.contract.d.ts` for TypeScript sources), and `rust` (shapes for a Rust data crate). The full language is specified in [LLP 1006](llp/1006-contract-compiler-v1.spec.md), [LLP 1017.000](llp/1017.000-contract-v1-1.spec.md) (v1.1), and [LLP 1017.003](llp/1017.003-map-filter-join.spec.md). Data sources are covered in [LLP 1027](llp/1027-typescript-data-sources.rfc.md). ## Example apps Each app lives in [`apps//`](apps). Run one on the web with `bun host/web/dev.mjs --app `, on macOS with `bun host/apple/build.mjs -apple --run`, and on iOS by adding `--ios`.
