Try Nexus Products Models Research Customers Resources Docs Log in Nexus Platform Get started Nexus For work and co-work Platform For systems and apps All security bulletins Security bulletin Update on October 2026 security incident Last updated November 9, 2026 Active monitoring On this page The update Further activity Data involved What we have done Contact The update This is an update to our previous security bulletin published on October 9, 2026. In response to the incident, we notified law enforcement and obtained assistance from a leading cybersecurity firm, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, to help conduct forensic analysis. At the time of publishing the bulletin, only Fireworks stored secrets (e.g. used in evaluation jobs) were known to have been accessed. Since then, we discovered impacts to account and billing information. For a limited set of accounts, we also discovered impact to secrets, datasets, and incomplete models. The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to Large Language Models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways, known as "LLMJacking". On November 2, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant published a blog post about the rise of LLMJacking, their motives, techniques used, and mitigation. Further activity A third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks R&D machines experienced a security incident on October 23. On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact. We detected this activity on the same day, and followed our incident response processes to take immediate remediation measures and close known critical vulnerabilities. As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use. Data involved The affected internal application provided access to the following categories of information: Resource metadata , such as Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation time, etc. Billing information , such as billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage. Payment card numbers are not stored by Fireworks and were not impacted. Model weights and datasets , for certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed. We are notifying customers whose data was impacted, and providing details about the impact and recommended response actions. We have not detected any impact to Inference , Training SDK and Nexus , which are all zero data retention (ZDR) by default. These findings are based on our investigation to date. Our investigation is ongoing and may reveal additional information. What we have done Working with Unit 42, Fireworks identified and implemented security hardening procedures, including: Access and credential lockdown . Fireworks revoked and replaced credentials and service accounts, removed unnecessary elevated privileges, and tightened controls designed to prevent new unauthorized credentials from being created. Network isolation . Fireworks restricted unauthorized network pathways and isolated affected systems designed to prevent further unauthorized activity and movement between systems. Data protection . Fireworks reviewed and tightened access to data storage and analytics systems and enforced controls designed to prevent public or unauthorized access to stored data. Forensic and audit integrity . Fireworks secured and enhanced our logging and monitoring systems. As part of our response, we’ve disabled self-serve dataset uploads and downloads used by Batch Inference and dataset-based training while we investigate this incident. Training SDK remains available with ZDR, i.e. no training data stored at rest, and Fireworks Lab-based training operates in an isolated environment with additional network and storage protection. We continue to work with Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 on our investigation and security hardening. We will continue to monitor our systems 24/7 and will provide further updates on our investigation as appropriate. Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude

 Newsletter 
 
 


 
 
 Sponsored by: doubleAI — doubleAI’s Maxwell makes software faster as it runs, no code changes needed. Now in early access 
 
 


 
 

 


 
 Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude 
 9th November 2026 



 Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. 
 Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: 
 
 You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. 
 The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. 
 Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep! 
 I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. 
 Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such. 
 Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. 
 The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. 
 How it works 
 When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract: 
 
 We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. 
 
 That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! 
 Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. 
 When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. 
 How I built it 
 I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: 
 
 Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve 
 There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it 
 I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from 
 There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app 
 Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? 
 
 That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. 
 The research looked good, so I told it: 
 
 Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else 
 
 That got me to this point —most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. 
 I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. 
 I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. 
 This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. 
 On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn. 
 From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran: 
 
 I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate 
 
 This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map. 
 
 what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...] 
 Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps 
 
 That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps. 
 
 each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp 
 
 That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound. 
 
 The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays 
 
 Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for. 
 
 There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for 
 Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is 
 
 At this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location? 
 
 I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app. 
 
 And since I had one spare device, I then said: 
 
 add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far 
 
 Giving Claude Code ears 
 I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears . 
 Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone. 
 I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket. 
 Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem. 
 I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not. 
 Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun. 


 
 Posted 9th November 2026 at 11:57 pm · Follow me on Mastodon , Bluesky , Twitter or subscribe to my newsletter

 Around '05 or so, the house we were staying in started beeping. Smoke alarm sounds, as usual. For almost a day we couldn't find the source. Contacted the owners -- they didn't know it either. They bought the house few years prior, so not much of a help. Standing in the hallways listening at different angles, as the article says, didn't help. No Fable in '05 either. So I had to improvise. Got a ~1 meter stick and two headphones (every headphone is a microphone, even if it sucks as a microphone). Plugged them into the stereo mic port, and started recording in Audacity. The phase shift between L and R pointed directly to the source. Took about 4 or 5 beeps to get the sucker. Turns out, it was hiding above the ceiling tiles in the garage. My wife still tells this story to all her friends as one of my biggest life achievements. Everything I shipped, the companies I founded -- pales in comparison to finding a dead smoke alarm reply rkagerer 10 minutes ago | parent | next [–]

 it didn't have to be sensitive or even high quality. The beep was loud enough to register on these improvised "mics" and the phase shift of up to 3ms (~50 samples at 16 kHz) was clearly visible reply brookst 42 minutes ago | parent | prev | next [–]

 It’s because it doesn’t have enough overtones, or a notable attack. You might have noticed that some trucks these days make a weird noise when they back up instead of a beep. They’re using white noise because it’s easier to locate; it has many overtones that allow your brain to pick the sound out of the background more easily, and thus more easily correlate the signals from both ears. You get a much more accurate location just from hearing that sound than you ever could with a pure tone. reply HPsquared 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Consider a pure sine wave, it's harder (in theory anyway) to match the signals from the left and right ears, and identify the time delay between the two signals: each cycle of the wave is just like the others, so there's no distinct signature to match and say "the sound reached the left ear 0.5 ms before it reached the right ear". This is especially the case for higher frequencies where there can be something like aliasing. Animal species sometimes use this in different sounds they make. An alarm call has that kind of "smooth tone" characteristic, so a predator can't locate the source of the sound but it still works to raise the alarm. Meanwhile more social sounds are more "chirpy" and sharp, so they can locate each other. reply thenthenthen 4 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–]

 Yes, but that's also O(log n) physical effort. This one's O(1) sitting on your butt.  Good point about the moving effort required. But if moving an object takes constant time, then it's O(n) overall -- since <incorrect argument deleted>. So O(n) moves are done, and this dominates the log n term for the number of steps. reply peri-cl 7 hours ago | root | parent | next [–]

O(log n) is if you can split the collection in half in an O(1) step, like, *shoving* the whole pile together as a unit O(n) if you're moving items one at a time.  Horrible public key tricks: 
 2026-11-08 — 2026-11-09 
 
 

So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS.
It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website.
Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing:
even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.
 
... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections,
and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4" 
 
 
 
 There is prior art of protest SSL implementations ,
but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic.
Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing:
therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.
 
The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key.
Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes).
However, while the resulting public key would be weak, no one would know unless they try to break it.
 
A good protest should be obvious:

 First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA.
To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n).
Pick a small number, e as public exponent.
 
The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent:
 
 
 # Encryption requires knowing e (public) 
cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n
 
 
The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n.
Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q.
 
 
 # Decryption requires knowing d (pivate) 
= cyphertext^d mod n

= plaintext^e^d mod n
= plaintext^(e*d) mod n
= plaintext^1 mod n
= plaintext
 
 
 
-->
 Ok, back to vanity keys. 
The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001),
because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster.
In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there.
 
The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message.
However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus.
 
My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value.
Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding.
Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p.
 
The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q:
which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred.
Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product:
 
 
58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176
 (incrementing until the next prime...) 
58174124 * 9184918 43 = 5343245836 7670532 
 
 
As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged.
The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner. 
 
From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key:
 
 
 # Single domain 
 openssl req -new -key priv.pem -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request 
 certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request 

 # Wildcard 
 cat > config <<EOF 
 [ req ]
req_extensions = req_ext

[ req_ext ]
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[ alt_names ]
DNS.1 = *.example.com
DNS.2 = example.com 
 EOF 
 openssl req -new -key priv.pem -config config -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request 
 certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request 
 
... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte,
it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable.
However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works:
this should take less than four attempts. 
 
The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key.
Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated.
 
Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet,
and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) avalable charaters provides plenty of space for jokes.
Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer:
this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice. 
 
 As for security , this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key.
However, it should still be secure:
nearly identical methods have been considered as a form of compression.
If the top-half of the modulus is fixed to a well known value, it doesn't have to be sent or stored as part of the key.
 
A reduction of around 1/2 can be achieved through division, but the state of the art can
fix 2/3 of the key, reducing the size to 1/3 of standard RSA while retaining a similar level of security...
although I should note that such tricks have largly been abandoned in favor of other crytosystems which can directly use small keys.
 
The manipulation of q may produce primes that are very close together, which makes it possible to factor n and recover the private key.
A very small d value can also be a problem.
Both of these are unlikely, but my script doesn't check for insecure values 
 
However, regardless of the key's security, it should be perfectly fine for a public website:
modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires a man-in-the-middle attack even if the private key is compromised.

Your TV can see through walls:

 Your TV can see through walls: 
 2025-08-02 — 2026-02-23 
 
 

This is a spectogram of the signal from a local TV station:
 
 
 ATSC digital TV signal. (Recorded using an Ettus USRP B200) 
 
 
 
Walking between the receiver and TV station causes a slight disturbance to the signal, but it's nothing to write home about:
 
 
 Walking through the signal path 
 
For this capture, I moved the antenna a few centimeters:
 
 
 Where'd my signal go? 
 
 This is selective fading : The direct signal is being canceled out by a strong reflection. 
Because the phase of the reflection depends on frequency, this effect is not uniform over the whole signal. 
Apart from being annoying if you're trying to watch TV, this state is extremely sensitive to any nearby movement.
 
Here's what happened to the signal when I got up from my chair:
 
 
 
... and here's me walking around in a neighboring room:
 
 
 Stripes! 
 
 The gaps between the stripes happen when my reflection perfectly cancels out the residual signal, which happens each time the path length changes by one wavelength.
Let's use this to figure out how fast I was walking:
 
The gap between each stripe is around 70 pixels, and the waterfall has an update rate of 150 Hz...
 
 
70 pixels * 1 second/150 pixels = 0.47 seconds = 2.1 Hz
speed of light / 490 MHz * 2.1 Hz = 1.3 m/s = 4.6 km/h
 
 
I was walking perpendicular to the direct signal path, so the speed can be used as is, without any adjustments for geometry. 
 
 So, a simple radio reciever is able to detect motion and provide an estimated speed 
— and it's not just TV that works for this: any wideband radio signal like WiFi or LTE can be used in much the same way. 
Those make worse demonstrations because they have a messy waterfall, but it's possible extract the same data with a bit of work.
 
Happy paranoia!

# python-formalization

A Lean 4 model of CPython 3.15.2, written by AI agents, tested against the real interpreter, and reviewed function by function. Along the way it found hundreds of bugs in CPython.

**Write-up:** [broyojo.com/python-formalization](https://broyojo.com/python-formalization/)

<!-- stats:start -->
| | |
|---|---|
| Lean code | 613,318 lines in 1,539 files |
| Theorems and lemmas | 18,898, all checked on every build |
| Top-level properties | 3,834 proven, 588 refuted, 94 open |
| Functions reviewed faithful | 4,071 of 26,004 in scope (15.7%) |
| Bug records | 418 that reproduce on 3.15.2, each with a reproducer |
<!-- stats:end -->

## How it works

Every function, bytecode instruction and grammar rule in the CPython 3.15.2 source tree is a row in an inventory (`coverage/methods/`). Each row goes through four steps:

1. **Mirror.** An agent writes a Lean model that follows the C or Python source line by line: same branch order, same error messages, same integer overflow. Each step cites the 3.15.2 source. Python callbacks are modelled as code that can raise, change state and re-enter.
2. **Differential test.** The model and the real `python3` run side by side on generated inputs (`difftest/`) until they agree on at least 50,000 cases across several seeds.
3. **Prove or refute.** Properties are stated over all inputs and proved in Lean. A false statement is refuted with a counterexample, never weakened. The build rejects `sorry`, `native_decide` and new axioms.
4. **Review.** A separate agent that did not write the model checks it against the source, runs each property on the real interpreter, and asks whether a broken implementation would also satisfy the theorem. Only rows marked `FAITHFUL` in `coverage/review/` count as covered.

When a refuted property turns out to be CPython's fault, it becomes a bug record in `bugs/`: a reproducer that prints `REPRODUCED` on 3.15.2, the cause with line numbers, a duplicate search of the CPython tracker, and a priority.

## Layout

```
lean/PyLean/<Area>/        models and proofs, one directory per area of CPython
lean/PyLean/Registry.lean  one entry per property: source citation, status, theorem
lean/Audit.lean            checks every registry theorem and the axioms it uses
lean/DiffMain.lean         `pydiff`, the Lean side of the differential tests
difftest/                  case generators and the harness that compares Lean with CPython
coverage/methods/          the inventory: one row per function with its status
coverage/review/           independent review verdicts (FAITHFUL / HOLLOW) per row
bugs/                      one YAML record per finding; FINDINGS.md lists them
reports/                   triage of bug records and draft upstream issues
site/                      generator for the write-up (docs/index.html)
AGENTS.md                  instructions the modelling agents follow
coverage/REVIEW_PROMPT.md  instructions the reviewing agents follow
```

## Running it

You need the Lean toolchain pinned in `lean/lean-toolchain` (Lean 4.35.0, installed by `elan`) and a CPython 3.15.2 build on `PATH` as `python3`. A full build is large: plan for a machine with 64 GB of RAM or more.

```sh
cd lean && lake build && lake env lean Audit.lean      # build every model and proof, then audit
python3 difftest/rangeslice_diff.py --cases 50000       # one area's model against CPython
python3 scripts/check_bugs.py                           # every bug record still reproduces
python3 scripts/check_coverage.py                       # coverage totals from the inventory
```

We ran heavy jobs on a build machine on our own Kubernetes cluster. `sky/builder.yaml` sets it up with SkyPilot, and `scripts/r <command>` syncs the checkout and runs the command there.

## Doing this for another project

Nothing here is specific to Python. To apply the method to another language, library or format:

- Start from `AGENTS.md` and `coverage/REVIEW_PROMPT.md`, and replace the CPython specifics.
- Build an inventory of every function in one pinned version (`scripts/list_python_functions.py` is ours).
- Keep coverage counted only through independent review (`scripts/check_coverage.py`).

The write-up's last sections list the practices that mattered most.

## Contributing

Help is welcome. Most of CPython is still unmodelled, and the method needs more reviewers as much as more models. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Citation

```bibtex
@misc{andrews2026formalizing,
  author       = {Andrews, David and Zhang, Chao},
  title        = {Formalizing {CPython}: A Lean Model of {CPython} 3.15.2},
  year         = {2026},
  howpublished = {\url{https://broyojo.com/python-formalization/}},
  note         = {Code: \url{https://github.com/Broyojo/python-formalization}}
}
```

Apache License 2.0 (see `LICENSE`). Excerpts of CPython quoted in the models remain under the PSF License; see `NOTICE`.

## Credits

**Authors:** [David Andrews](https://broyojo.com/) and [Chao Zhang](https://chaozhang.org/).

Built by David Andrews using Opus 5.5. Inspired by Miles Cranmer's [julia-in-lean](https://github.com/MilesCranmer/julia-in-lean).

Formalizing CPython 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 David Andrews 

 
 
 Formalizing CPython 
 AI agents wrote 613,318 lines of Lean that copy Python's internals line by line, tested every piece against the real Python, had a computer check every proof, and turned up 418 bug reports in Python along the way. 
 David Andrews and Chao Zhang 9 November 2026 Code and data 
 

 
 
 CPython · Objects/rangeobject.c 
 static unsigned long get_len_of_range ( long lo, long hi, long step) { assert(step != 0 ); if (step > 0 && lo < hi) return 1UL + (hi - 1UL - lo) / step; else if (step < 0 && lo > hi) return 1UL + (lo - 1UL - hi) / ( 0UL - step); else return 0UL ; } 
 Lean copy · RangeSlice/Model.lean 
 def getLenOfRange (lo hi step : Int ) : Int := if step > 0 ∧ lo < hi then uadd 1 ( usub ( usub ( toU hi) 1 ) ( toU lo) / toU step) else if step < 0 ∧ lo > hi then uadd 1 ( usub ( usub ( toU lo) 1 ) ( toU hi) / usub 0 ( toU step)) else 0 -- step ≠ 0 is assumed by every proof -- uadd, usub: C's unsigned arithmetic, -- which wraps around past 2^64 
 
 A function from CPython's C source (left) and the Lean copy an agent wrote of it (right). Hover over a line to see its counterpart. 
 

 

 
 TL;DR 
 
 We pointed Opus 5.5 at CPython, the program that runs almost all Python code, and had it rewrite its functions in Lean , a language for writing machine-checked proofs. 
 Each rewrite copies the original line by line and is tested against real Python on tens of thousands of inputs before anyone tries to prove anything about it. 
 A function only counts once a second agent, which didn't write it, checks the work and agrees it holds up. 4,071 functions have passed that check so far. 
 The result is 613,318 lines of Lean across 1,539 files, with 18,898 theorems and lemmas, all checked by Lean's proof checker on every build. 
 Along the way the proofs turned up 418 bug reports. Most are small, but about 55 can crash the interpreter or corrupt memory from ordinary Python code. 
 
 
 


 
 Checked and accepted Written, not yet accepted Not started 
 All of CPython 16% Interpreter core 10% Built-in types 35% C modules 19% Parser 31% Grammar rules 100% Standard library 9% 
 How much of each part of CPython 3.15.2 has been copied, tested, proved and accepted by review. Code with nothing to check, such as memory bookkeeping, is left out. 
 

 
 Why bother 
 Python doesn't have a precise written definition. There is a reference manual, but in practice "Python" means whatever CPython does, and CPython is hundreds of thousands of lines of C plus a large standard library. The manual covers normal use. It says little about the odd cases, and that's where bugs hide: an object that changes a dictionary while that dictionary is searching for it, an error thrown halfway through an update, a number one past the largest the C code was written for. 
 Writing a proof about a function forces you to say exactly what it does in all of those cases. You can't leave anything vague, because the proof checker won't accept it. That makes proofs a good way to find the places where the code doesn't do what everyone assumes. 
 We wanted to see how far this goes on a code base as large and old as CPython, and whether the results stay trustworthy when most of the work is done by AI. 

 How it works 
 Every function goes through the same four steps. 
 

 
 
 Copy Rewrite the function in Lean, following the original code line by line, including its error messages and its odd corners. 
 Test Run the copy and the real Python side by side on at least 50,000 tricky inputs. Any disagreement means the copy is wrong. 
 Prove State something that should always be true and have the computer check the proof. If it's actually false, prove that instead. 
 Check A second agent that didn't do the work reviews it against the original and tries to break it. Only what survives counts. 
 
 

 
 The code at the top of this page is step one for a small piece of CPython: the C function that works out how many numbers are in a range , next to its Lean copy. The copy keeps the C code's exact arithmetic, including how its numbers wrap around when they get too big. The proof about it shows that this function, the slower version CPython uses for very large numbers, and the code that chooses between them always give the same, correct count. 
 

 
 Proofs that prove nothing 
 The hardest part wasn't getting AI agents to write proofs. It was getting proofs that actually mean something. 
 Our first attempt asked the agents for breadth: copy every function and prove at least one thing about each. They did. Then a separate review found that fewer than half of the functions it checked held up, and in one file only 21%. The proofs were all correct. They just didn't say anything useful. For example, "if this function returns a number, the number is at least zero" is true, but a function that always crashes also satisfies it. 
 So the reviewer now asks one question about every proof: could a broken version of the function pass it too? 
 

 
 
 
 Version of the function "If it returns, the answer is ≥ 0" "It always returns the right count" 
 
 The real one passes passes 
 Always crashes passes caught 
 Returns 0 for very large numbers passes caught 
 Off by one when counting down passes caught 
 
 
 
 Two true statements about the same function. The first one lets every broken version through, so a function whose only proof looks like it doesn't count. 
 

 
 Fixing a weak proof usually means going back and making the copy more realistic, for example letting a user's code throw an error in the middle of a function. The charts below show how that went for ten files. Each point is one round of review. The lines sometimes go down: when a reviewer finds that an accepted proof is wrong about real Python, everything that relied on it is taken back out. 
 

 
 Functions accepted Objects/typeobject.c 135 of 142 accepted · 5 reviews Objects/genobject.c 56 of 56 accepted · 5 reviews Objects/setobject.c 46 of 46 accepted · 7 reviews Modules/_json.c 45 of 48 accepted · 5 reviews Lib/enum.py 37 of 39 accepted · 9 reviews Lib/random.py 37 of 38 accepted · 3 reviews Objects/abstract.c 41 of 43 accepted · 2 reviews Objects/rangeobject.c 33 of 33 accepted · 2 reviews Lib/pickletools.py 31 of 33 accepted · 2 reviews Modules/binascii.c 35 of 40 accepted · 2 reviews Rounds of review → 
 Share of each file's reviewed functions accepted after each round of review, taken from the project's history. Each point is one review; the scale is the same in every chart, from 0% to all of the functions reviewed in that file. Accepted functions include ones the reviewer confirmed have nothing to check, such as memory bookkeeping. 
 

 
 When a correct proof is wrong anyway 
 A checked proof guarantees that a statement follows from the copy. It doesn't guarantee the copy matches real Python, and testing only covers the inputs you thought to try. So every accepted statement is also run against real Python. That caught several proofs that were valid and still wrong. 

 The 16-terabyte string 
 The copy of Python's fast JSON encoder assumed memory requests always succeed. So it "proved" the encoder could build its indentation strings for any nesting depth, including one that needs 16 terabytes of memory. Real Python runs out of memory. The fixed copy now treats every memory request as something that can fail. 

 Nine extra steps, just once 
 A proof said Python's pickle module never goes deeper than a certain number of nested calls. That turned out true except in a brand-new Python process. There, the first time it encodes a string, it quietly loads a text codec, and that load uses nine more nested calls. Our tests never saw it, because the test harness had already loaded the codec. 

 Error types have families 
 In Python, catching a TypeError also catches any more specific error built on top of it. Three separate copies checked an error's exact name instead. All three had proofs that a custom error type could break. 

 Memory that comes back 
 The copy of Python's set assumed that once memory is freed, the same address never comes back. Real memory allocators reuse addresses all the time. CPython uses a "did the address change?" check to notice when user code has swapped out the set's internals. With reuse, that check can be fooled. Fixing the copy turned an accepted proof into a real memory bug, now one of our bug reports. 

 What we found 
 When a proof fails because Python itself is wrong, and not the copy, we write it up as a bug report. Each report includes a short script that shows the bug on Python 3.15.2 (for most, also on the development version), a search for duplicates already reported, and an honest rating of how much it matters. 
 

 
 C and Python versions disagree 129 Other 122 Wrong result 56 Crash 28 Memory corruption 27 Doesn't match the docs 26 Wrong error or message 18 Missing input check 12 
 418 bug reports by type. "C and Python versions disagree" means a module has two implementations, a fast one in C and a backup in Python, and they give different answers to the same call. 
 

 
 Most are small: an error message that's wrong, an edge case that behaves differently from the documentation, two versions of a function that disagree. About 55 are more serious and can crash Python or corrupt its memory using nothing but normal Python code, usually by having user code change a container while C code is in the middle of using it. Python doesn't treat running hostile Python code as a security boundary, so these are ordinary bugs. The ones not already on CPython's tracker are being reported to the project, starting with this post. Six small examples of different kinds: 
 

 
 
 Crash 
 A dictionary call that crashes Python 
 Calling setdefault on an object's attribute dictionary with a StrEnum key crashes the interpreter, if another object of the same class has that attribute and this one doesn't. 
 class Key(StrEnum):
 NAME = "name" 
 class User: pass 
a = User(); a.name = "ada" 
b = User(); b.age = 36 
vars(b).setdefault(Key.NAME, "anon" )
 # Segmentation fault 
 
 
 Memory corruption 
 An XML edit that corrupts memory 
 Assigning to a backwards slice of an ElementTree element should insert, as it does for a list. Instead it duplicates one child without taking a reference and loses another. 
 e = ET.Element( "root" )
e[:] = [ET.Element(f "a{i}" ) for i in range ( 7 )]
e[ 5 : 2 ] = [ET.Element( "X" )]
[c.tag for c in e]
 # 'a2' appears twice, 'a4' is gone 
 
 
 Wrong error 
 An email header that breaks the parser 
 A Message-ID with a space inside square brackets makes Python's email parser fail with an internal error. The header comes from whoever sent the email. 
 msg = email.message_from_string(
 "Message-ID: <a@[ x]>\n\nhi\n" ,
 policy=policy.default)
msg[ "Message-ID" ]
 # UnboundLocalError 
 
 
 Silently wrong result 
 Base32 padding that depends on position 
 New in Python 3.15, the base32 decoder can ignore chosen characters. If = is one of them, where it appears still changes the result. 
 a2b_base32 ( b"AAAAAAA" , ignorechars= b"=" )
 # Error: Incorrect padding 
 a2b_base32 ( b"AAAA=AAA" , ignorechars= b"=" )
 # b'\x00\x00\x00\x00' 
 
 
 Missing error 
 An enum error that disappears 
 Giving an enum value to a second member should raise an error. If the class's __repr__ is broken, the error is swallowed and the call quietly does nothing. 
 class W( Enum ):
 A = 1 ; B = 2 
 def __repr__ (self): return 5 
W.B. _add_value_alias_ ( 3 )
W.A. _add_value_alias_ ( 3 ) # returns None 
 
 
 C and Python disagree 
 Two picklers, two limits 
 Python has a C pickler and a pure-Python one. They give up at different nesting depths. This difference was first reported in 2008 and is still open. 
 v = []
 for _ in range ( 400 ): v = [v]
 pickle . dumps (v, 5 ) # works 
 pickle . _dumps (v, 5 ) # RecursionError 
 
 

 
 Every report, with its script, is in the repository . 

 Do this for your own project 
 None of this is specific to Python. It works for anything with source code you can read and a working version you can run: another language, a library, a file format, a compiler. What made the difference for us: 
 
 Pick one exact version and stick to it. Every copy points at specific lines in that version. 
 List everything first. Count progress against the full list, so nothing gets skipped quietly. 
 Copy the code, not the documentation. A copy written from the docs agrees with the docs, and the bugs are where the code and the docs disagree. 
 Let user code misbehave. Model callbacks that throw errors or change things mid-operation. That's where the worst bugs were. 
 Test before you prove. Proving things about a wrong copy wastes time. 
 When something is false, keep the counterexample. Don't water the statement down until it becomes provable. 
 Check proved statements against the real thing. A valid proof about a wrong copy is the most misleading result you can get. 
 Count only what an independent reviewer accepts, and have that reviewer ask whether a broken version would pass. 
 
 The instructions our agents worked from are in the repository and meant to be reused: AGENTS.md for the agents doing the work, REVIEW_PROMPT.md for the reviewers, and the full list of functions with their status in coverage/methods . 

 Related work 
 The closest project is julia-in-lean , which did this for the Julia language and directly inspired this one 1 . It modelled Julia's standard library in Lean, tested the models against Julia, recorded about 400 bugs and filed 75. Its finding that 128 of 130 quick proofs had quietly assumed away the hard case shaped our review rules. A recent paper models NVIDIA's PTX GPU instruction set in Lean to prove GPU kernels correct 2 , building on earlier formal work on PTX's memory model 3 . 
 For Python specifically, λπ 4 and a K framework semantics of Python 3.3 5 described the language mathematically; this project copies CPython's actual code instead. Similar efforts exist for JavaScript 6 , 7 and WebAssembly 8 , and CompCert 9 and seL4 10 remain the high bar for fully verified software. Comparing two implementations on the same inputs, the testing half of this project, goes back decades 11 , 12 . 

 Where it stands 
 The project started on 29 October 2026. 4,071 of the 26,004 functions worth checking (15.7%) have been copied, tested, proved and accepted by review. The Lean code is 613,318 lines in 1,539 files, containing 18,898 theorems and lemmas; 3,834 of the top-level properties are proved and 588 are proved false with a counterexample. Most of Python is still ahead, especially the large part of the standard library written in Python itself. Multithreading is out of scope for now. In these 57 files, every function copied so far has passed review. The 30 with the most accepted functions: 
 Python/bytecodes.c 310 Grammar/python.gram 278 Lib/collections/__init__.py 184 Lib/_pydecimal.py 160 Lib/_pydatetime.py 150 Modules/_struct.c 122 Objects/longobject.c 119 Objects/listobject.c 114 Objects/memoryobject.c 107 Objects/dictobject.c 104 Objects/bytesobject.c 100 Objects/exceptions.c 97 Objects/unicodeobject.c 94 Objects/bytearrayobject.c 93 Modules/arraymodule.c 84 Lib/_collections_abc.py 81 Modules/_operator.c 73 Modules/itertoolsmodule.c 72 Modules/_collectionsmodule.c 64 Python/codecs.c 61 Lib/operator.py 59 Lib/_pyio.py 58 Objects/typeobject.c 57 Lib/weakref.py 54 Objects/genobject.c 46 Lib/urllib/parse.py 46 Parser/action_helpers.c 43 Modules/_zoneinfo.c 43 Objects/floatobject.c 38 Objects/tupleobject.c 37 
 The project is open, and help is welcome. Most of CPython is still unmodelled: pick a file whose functions are still marked todo in coverage/methods , follow AGENTS.md , and send a pull request. Independent reviews of existing work count as much as new models. See CONTRIBUTING.md . 

 Cite

 title = {Formalizing {CPython}: A Lean Model of {CPython} 3.15.2},

 note = {Code: \url{https://github.com/Broyojo/python-formalization}}
}

The full full-stack framework for Rust

[![Crates.io][crates-badge]][crates-url] [![Docs.rs][docs-badge]][docs-url] [![MIT licensed][mit-badge]][mit-url] [![Build Status][actions-badge]][actions-url] [![Discord chat][discord-badge]][discord-url]
[crates-badge]: https://img.shields.io/crates/v/topcoat.svg?style=flat-square [crates-url]: https://crates.io/crates/topcoat [docs-badge]: https://img.shields.io/docsrs/topcoat?style=flat-square [docs-url]: https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat [mit-badge]: https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg?style=flat-square [mit-url]: https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat/blob/main/LICENSE [actions-badge]: https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/tokio-rs/topcoat/ci.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square [actions-url]: https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat/actions?query=workflow%3ACI+branch%3Amain [discord-badge]: https://img.shields.io/discord/500028886025895936.svg?logo=discord&style=flat-square [discord-url]: https://discord.gg/tokio Topcoat is a modular, batteries-included Rust framework for building full-stack apps. It prioritizes simplicity and productivity. See [Learn Topcoat](#learn-topcoat) to get started, or the [Roadmap](#roadmap) for what's coming next. **Early-stage and experimental. Expect breaking changes.** ```rust,ignore use topcoat::{ Result, context::Cx, router::{module_router, page}, view::{View, component, view}, }; #[tokio::main] async fn main() { topcoat::start(module_router!().build()).await.unwrap(); } #[page] async fn home(cx: &Cx) -> Result { Ok(view! { hello(name: "World") }) } #[component] async fn hello(cx: &Cx, name: &str) -> Result { Ok(view! {

"Hello, " (name) "!"

}) } ``` ## What makes Topcoat different ### Client reactivity without the boilerplate Topcoat renders all markup on the server: components can be async and query the database directly, eliminating all the traditional boilerplate needed for a separate API layer. Interactivity does not have to cost a round-trip, though. A `$(...)` expression is ordinary type-checked Rust that Topcoat evaluates on the server for the initial render and also translates to JavaScript, so it re-runs instantly in the browser. No wasm bundle, no client build step: ```rust,ignore #[component] async fn faq(cx: &Cx) -> Result { let open = signal(cx, || false); Ok(view! { // Runs entirely in the browser; no server round-trip.

"A full-stack Rust framework."

}) } ``` When an update does need the server, like fresh search results, mark the component as a `#[shard]`. Topcoat re-renders it on the server whenever one of its `$(...)` arguments changes and swaps the new HTML in place: ```rust,ignore #[component] async fn search(cx: &Cx) -> Result { let query = signal(cx, String::new); Ok(view! { // Updates as the user types. search_results(query: $(query.get())) }) } #[shard] async fn search_results(cx: &Cx, query: String) -> Result { Ok(view! {
    // Your own server-side code, like a database query: for product in search_products(cx, &query).await? {
  • (product.name)
    • }
}) } ``` ### Powerful, unsurprising HTML templates The `view!` macro stays true to HTML and Rust. Use familiar Rust control flow as part of your templates: ```rust,ignore view! {
for item in nav_items { (item.label) }
} ``` Use the `topcoat fmt` CLI command to automatically format `view!` snippets (and other macros) across your codebase. ### Module-based routing Topcoat can optionally infer your route tree from your app's module structure (without a build step): ```text src/ |-- app.rs -> / (and the root layout) `-- app/ |-- about.rs -> /about |-- _marketing.rs (layout, no URL segment) |-- _marketing/ | `-- pricing.rs -> /pricing |-- posts.rs -> /posts |-- posts/ | `-- id.rs -> /posts/{post_id} `-- api/ `-- health.rs -> GET /api/health ``` ### Premade components you can edit Topcoat UI is a component library based on [Tailwind](https://tailwindcss.com/) inspired by [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/). Components are copied into your project via the `topcoat ui` CLI command, meaning you can freely change their design and functionality to fit your use case: ```rust,ignore #[component] async fn delete_card(cx: &Cx) -> Result { Ok(view! { card( card_header( card_title("Delete workspace") card_description( "This permanently removes the workspace and all of its data." ) ) card_footer( attrs: attributes! { class="justify-end" }, button(variant: ButtonVariant::Ghost, "Cancel") button(variant: ButtonVariant::Destructive, "Delete workspace") ) ) }) } ``` ### Asset bundling The bundler scans your compiled binary for `asset!` calls, copies (or even downloads) every file into a local asset directory, and allows Topcoat to serve them efficiently with aggressive browser caching. ```rust,ignore const FERRIS: Asset = asset!("./ferris.png"); view! { } ``` Topcoat also ships with utilities for web fonts and icons, as well as easy integrations for [Fontsource](https://fontsource.org/) (Google Fonts) and [Iconify](https://icon-sets.iconify.design/). ### Built-in Tailwind support Enable the `tailwind` feature to integrate [Tailwind](https://tailwindcss.com/) into your project: ```rust,ignore view! { } ``` ## Learn Topcoat **Start here** - [Getting started](https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat/blob/main/docs/getting_started.md): create an app with `topcoat new` and run the dev server. - [Manual setup](https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat/blob/main/docs/manual_setup.md): add dependencies and wire up a minimal app yourself. - [Source code formatting](https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat/blob/main/docs/cli/fmt.md): `topcoat fmt` for macro bodies. **Rendering** - [`view!`](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/view/macro.view.html) mixes HTML, Rust expressions, control flow, and component calls. - [`#[component]`](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/view/attr.component.html) makes async functions callable from markup with named arguments and child content. - [`attributes!`](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/view/macro.attributes.html) collects attributes to pass through components and spread onto elements. - [`class!`](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/view/macro.class.html) joins base, optional, and conditional CSS classes. - [`suspense`](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/view/struct.suspense.html) shows a fallback while content loads. [`error_boundary`](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/view/struct.error_boundary.html) shows one if rendering fails. - [`live!` and `emit!`](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/view/macro.live.html) replace part of a page as async work produces new HTML. **Routing** - [Router](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/router/index.html): pages, layouts, and API routes; manual and auto-discovered. - [Module-based routing](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/router/macro.module_router.html): derive the route table from your module tree. - [Linking to handlers](https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat/blob/main/docs/router/href.md): use `href!` for navigation links, form actions, and redirects. **Working with requests** - [Context (`Cx`)](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/context/index.html): read request data and values stored by type. Add shared values with the router builder's `.with`, or use `cx.with` to add a value for part of a request. - [Memoization](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/context/attr.memoize.html): `#[memoize]` for per-request caching and fan-out dedup. - [Cookies](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/cookie/index.html): read and write the request cookie jar, with signed, encrypted, and prefixed cookies. - [Sessions](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/session/index.html): bring-your-own-storage session authentication: login/logout lifecycle, sliding expiration, and token rotation. **Asset system** - [Assets](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/asset/index.html): declare assets in Rust, serve them with content-hashed URLs. - [Fonts](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/font/index.html): bundle and serve web fonts. - [Icons](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/icon/index.html): download Iconify icon sets or declare your own. **Client reactivity** - [The runtime](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/runtime/index.html): signals, `$(...)` expressions, `@` event handlers, and `:` bind attributes. - [Expressions](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/runtime/macro.expr.html): the dual Rust/JavaScript expression language and its vocabulary. - [Procedures](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/runtime/attr.procedure.html): async server functions callable from the browser. - [Shards](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/runtime/attr.shard.html): components that re-render on the server when their arguments change. - [Client-side navigation](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/runtime/struct.link.html): links, prefetching, and navigation without a full document reload. **Miscellaneous** - [Topcoat UI](https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat/blob/main/docs/ui.md): premade components vendored into your project for you to edit. - [Metadata](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/metadata/index.html): titles, descriptions, and link previews for search engines and social networks, set per layout and page. - [Localization](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/l10n/index.html): choose the language for each request and display translations from Fluent files. - [Mail](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/mail/index.html): build mail with `Mail::builder`, deliver through SMTP, file, or in-memory transports. **Third-party integrations** - [Tailwind](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/tailwind/index.html): Tailwind CSS without Node, wired into the asset pipeline. - [htmx](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/htmx/index.html): drive partial HTML swaps from the server with request/response header helpers. - [Alpine AJAX](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/alpine_ajax/index.html): drive partial HTML swaps from the server with Alpine AJAX's request-header conventions. - [Datastar](https://docs.rs/topcoat/latest/topcoat/datastar/index.html): patch elements and signals into the page over server-sent events. ## Roadmap Planned features we'd like to bring to Topcoat. Have an idea? [Open an issue](https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat/issues). - [ ] Static export - [ ] (More) reactivity (`topcoat-runtime`) - [ ] More Topcoat UI components, full "blocks" e.g. sign-in form - [ ] Better [Toasty](https://github.com/tokio-rs/toasty) integration (safely create/update records from forms without listing out all the fields) - [ ] Validations - [ ] `OpenAPI` endpoints - [ ] Docs for how to deploy Topcoat - [ ] Pre-rendering for static pages - [ ] `WebTransport` - [ ] Image optimization / resizing - [ ] Markdown support - [ ] Easier-to-use middlewares like rate-limiting - [ ] Authentication - [ ] Background jobs - [ ] Islands

No results found View all tags pikaju released this 09 Nov 18:45 v0.12.0 c249820 This commit was created on GitHub.com and signed with GitHub’s verified signature . GPG key ID: B5690EEEBB952194 Verified Learn about vigilant mode . This release reworks some foundations of Topcoat. Most apps will need many small edits. We are sorry for the churn, but we believe these changes make Topcoat simpler and more extensible. The upgrade guide at the end lists the required changes. Context One context Route context Router settings Page metadata Macros Context comes first One argument style Completions while typing Formatting Removed cookie! and mail! Path parameter accessors Mail Fixes Upgrade guide Checklist Renamed and removed APIs Behavior changes Context One context Topcoat used to keep app context and request context apart, each with its own functions. They are now one context, read with context , try_context and the new iter_context . Adding a value with cx.with(value) shadows older values of the same type instead of replacing them. The router can now provide a default that a layer, layout or page changes for its own part of the app. use topcoat :: context :: { Cx , context } ; struct Greeting ( & ' static str ) ; let router = module_router ! ( ) . with ( Greeting ( "Hi" ) ) . build ( ) ; # [ layer ( "/formal" ) ] async fn formal ( cx : & Cx , body : Body , next : Next < ' _ > ) -> Result < Response > { next . run ( & cx . with ( Greeting ( "Good day" ) ) , body ) . await } # [ page ] async fn home ( cx : & Cx ) -> Result < impl View > { let Greeting ( greeting ) = context :: < Greeting > ( cx ) ; Ok ( view ! {

( greeting )

} ) } Shadowed values stay available. iter_context::(cx) visits every value of a type, closest first, which is useful for values that several scopes add to, such as breadcrumbs. #[memoize] now also tracks values set on the router, so a function that reads a shadowed value runs again for the child context only. Migrating is mostly a rename: - module_router!().app_context(PageViews::default()) + module_router!().with(PageViews::default()) - let views = app_context::(cx); - let user = try_request_context::(cx); + let views = context::(cx); + let user = try_context::(cx); See context . Route context Routes, pages, layouts and layers can now attach values with with(...) . When a request matches, the router adds the values of every layer, layout and the route itself to the context before any of them run. For example, a page could use this to tell its outer layout which to show: struct Title ( & ' static str ) ; # [ layout ( "/" , with ( Title ( "My shop" ) ) ) ] async fn shell ( cx : & Cx , slot : Slot < ' _ > ) -> Result < impl View > { let Title ( title ) = context :: < Title > ( cx ) ; Ok ( view ! { <! DOCTYPE html> <html> <head><title> ( title ) ( slot ) } ) } # [ page ( "/products" , with ( Title ( "Products" ) ) ) ] async fn products ( cx : & Cx ) -> Result < impl View > { Ok ( view ! {

"Products"

} ) } Any type can be route context, so apps and libraries can define their own per-route settings without new router APIs. Here, a layer enforces a role that a page declares: struct RequireRole ( Role ) ; # [ layer ] async fn roles ( cx : & Cx , body : Body , next : Next < ' _ > ) -> Result < Response > { if let Some ( RequireRole ( role ) ) = try_context :: < RequireRole > ( cx ) { if ! current_user ( cx ) . await ? . has_role ( * role ) { return Err ( forbidden ( ) . into ( ) ) ; } } next . run ( cx , body ) . await } # [ page ( with ( RequireRole ( Role :: Admin ) ) ) ] async fn settings ( cx : & Cx ) -> Result < impl View > { .. . } Values follow the module tree. A layout's values apply to every page below it, and a layer's values apply to every route and page under its path. Inner values shadow outer ones. The values are built once with the router, so they cannot read the request. For values that depend on it, store a BoxCxFn , an async function of cx that you call when you need the value. The admin demo uses this for breadcrumbs, where each page adds a Crumb and the outer layout collects them with iter_context . See route context . Router settings Some router settings that had their own builder methods are now context values. You set them for the whole app with .with(...) on the router builder, and for part of the app with with(...) on a route, page, layout or layer. Features that wrap requests, such as cookies and the browser runtime, are added as layers. module_router!() - .compression(Compression::new().brotli(false)) - .origin_policy(OriginPolicy::new().trust_origins(["https://accounts.example.com"])) - .base_url("https://example.com") - .prefetch(PrefetchMode::Viewport) - .suspense(SuspenseMode::Wait) - .cookies() - .sessions(SessionConfig::default()) - .runtime() + .with(Compression::default().brotli(false)) + .with(OriginPolicy::trust_origins(["https://accounts.example.com"])) + .with(BaseUrl::new("https://example.com")?) + .with(PrefetchMode::Viewport) + .with(SuspenseMode::Wait) + .layer(CookieLayer::new()) + .layer(RuntimeLayer::new()) .build() Per-route settings replace BodyLimit::at and OriginPolicy::exempt_paths : # [ route ( POST "/upload" , with ( BodyLimit :: max ( 32 * 1024 * 1024 ) ) ) ] async fn upload ( cx : & Cx , bytes : Bytes ) -> Result < ( ) > { .. . } # [ route ( POST "/webhook" , with ( OriginPolicy :: dangerous_disable ( ) ) ) ] async fn webhook ( cx : & Cx ) -> Result < ( ) > { .. . } # [ route ( GET "/export.zip" , with ( Compression :: disable ( ) ) ) ] async fn export ( cx : & Cx ) -> Result < Response > { .. . } Sessions only need the CookieLayer now. Change their defaults with .with(SessionLifetime(duration)) and .with(SessionTokenStore::new(store)) . RuntimeLayer::new().max_runs_per_connection(n) replaces the builder method of the same name. Page metadata The new metadata module renders the page title, description, canonical URL, robots, theme color, Open Graph and X tags. It is built on route context. Layouts set defaults, pages override single fields, and topcoat::metadata::tags() renders the result at the top of . use topcoat :: metadata :: { Metadata , OpenGraph } ; # [ layout ( "/" , with ( Metadata :: new ( ) . title ( "Acme" ) . description ( "Everything you need for tea." ) . open_graph ( OpenGraph :: new ( ) . site_name ( "Acme" ) . image ( asset! ( "./preview.png" ) ) ) ) ) ] async fn shell ( cx : & Cx , slot : Slot < ' _ > ) -> Result < impl View > { Ok ( view ! { topcoat :: metadata :: tags ( ) ( slot ) } ) } # [ page ( "/products" , with ( Metadata :: new ( ) . title ( "Products" ) ) ) ] async fn products ( cx : & Cx ) -> Result < impl View > { .. . } t! and asset! values can be passed directly. For values that need a database lookup, use Metadata::from_fn : # [ page ( "/product" , with ( Metadata :: from_fn ( async |cx| { let product = find_product ( cx ) . await ? ; Ok ( Metadata :: new ( ) . title ( product . name . clone ( ) ) ) } ) ) ) ] Canonical and Open Graph URLs must be absolute, so add .with(BaseUrl::new(...)?) to the router when you use relative paths. The metadata feature is enabled by default. See page metadata and examples/metadata . Macros Topcoat's macros were added one at a time and drifted apart. Some took context and some did not, and options used = in some places and : in others. A macro is only worth having when it does something plain Rust cannot, like checking HTML at compile time or bundling an asset. So we gave the remaining macros the same rules and removed macros that added little value over a plain builder. Almost all of the resulting changes are caught by the compiler, and we think a smaller set of consistent macros is worth it. Context comes first Functions with #[component] , #[page] , #[route] , #[layout] , #[layer] , #[shard] , #[procedure] and #[memoize] must now take cx: &Cx as their first parameter, even when they do not use it. #[page] - async fn home() -> Result { + async fn home(cx: &Cx) -> Result { #[layout] - async fn shell(slot: Slot<'_>) -> Result { + async fn shell(cx: &Cx, slot: Slot<'_>) -> Result { #[route(POST)] - async fn save(Form(input): Form, cx: &Cx) -> Result { + async fn save(cx: &Cx, Form(input): Form) -> Result { view! , live! , emit! and attributes! no longer support the cx => prefix. Instead, they use the cx variable in scope, so to change the context of a view, shadow cx first. let cx = cx.with(PrefetchMode::Never); - view! { cx => + view! { link(href: href!(reports), "Reports") } view! moves cx into the view like any other captured variable and does not clone it. If a view must outlive the current function, for example in a stream, add let cx = cx.clone(); before it. One argument style Attribute macros take options as key = value , like #[serde(rename = "...")] . Function-like macros take key: value , like component props in view! . - t!(greeting, name = user.name) + t!(greeting, name: user.name) - segment!(kind = CatchAll, rename = "path"); + segment!(kind: CatchAll, rename: "path"); path_param! and module_param! already use : for the parameter type, so their error handler moves to an else clause. - module_param!(pub post_id: u64, error = bad_request); + module_param!(pub post_id: u64 else bad_request); href! took path parameters as wrapper types in path order. It now takes them as name: value pairs, in any order. - href!(post, PostId(42)) + href!(post, post_id: 42) The name refers to the parameter like a normal Rust path. When post_id is in scope, write post_id: 42 . Otherwise, import it or write its path, such as posts::post_id: 42 . See links . Component calls used to accept a missing comma between the last prop and the first child, as in card(title: name "child") . This was a bug, and the comma is now required. Completions while typing Topcoat macros now handle incomplete code much better, which makes rust-analyzer work more reliably inside them. For example, a half-typed user. in a component body or a prop no longer breaks the rest of the macro, so rust-analyzer can still complete it. Option names in function-like macros also complete, and a misspelled option is reported on the option itself. Formatting topcoat fmt now formats every Topcoat macro, including attributes such as #[page(...)] and macros such as href! , asset! and path_param! . Run it once after upgrading. See topcoat fmt . To support this, asset! is now a procedural macro. Its path must be a string literal, and a missing local file is a compile error. Two new prefixes are available. {mod}/ points at the module's own directory, so src/about.rs can use asset!("{mod}/hero.png") for src/about/hero.png . {out_dir}/ points at the build script output. Removed cookie! and mail! cookie! and mail! turned into the same builder calls you can write yourself. Plain builders give you completions, normal type errors and rustfmt, and they work with if and loops. - cookies(cx).add(cookie!("theme" = theme)); - cookies(cx).add(cookie! { "session" = token; Path = "/"; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite = Lax }); + cookies(cx).add(("theme", theme)); + cookies(cx).add( + Cookie::build(("session", token)) + .path("/") + .secure(true) + .http_only(true) + .same_site(SameSite::Lax), + ); - let mail = mail! { - from: "welcome@example.com", - to: "ada@example.com", - subject: "Welcome!", - html: {

"Welcome!"

}, - }?; + let mail = Mail::builder() + .from(Mailbox::new("welcome@example.com")?) + .to([Mailbox::new("ada@example.com")?]) + .subject("Welcome!") + .html(cx, view! {

"Welcome!"

}) + .await? + .build()?; send(cx, mail).await?; Path parameter accessors path_param! and module_param! now generate an accessor function named after the parameter. It returns the parsed value, which is still parsed only once per request. The accessor has the visibility you give the macro, so other modules can import it like any other function. The generic path_param::(cx) function and the generated wrapper types such as PostId are removed. module_param!(pub post_id: u64 else bad_request); #[page] async fn post(cx: &Cx) -> Result { - let id = path_param::(cx)?; + let id = post_id(cx)?; See path parameters . Mail Mail is configured with a Mailer in the context, which also makes it easy to swap the transport in tests. - module_router!().mail(MailConfig::builder().transport(transport).build()) + module_router!().with(Mailer::new(transport)) MailBuilder::build() now returns a Result and checks the sender, recipients, body, attachments and headers. A built Mail always has these, so its accessors no longer return Option . The Message-ID and date are set when the mail is built and the Message-ID no longer contains the machine's hostname. Mailboxes are created with Mailbox::new , Mailbox::named or by parsing a string. See mail . Fixes Props and local variables can have the same name as a component. topcoat l10n check , topcoat asset list and the other commands that build now respect default-run in packages with several binaries. The Tailwind CLI download is verified against checksums shipped with Topcoat. accept_language no longer requires the l10n-fluent feature. FileTransport no longer writes the Bcc header, matching delivered mail. Upgrade guide The compiler reports most of these changes. Each item links to the section with a full example. Checklist Add cx: &Cx as the first parameter of every #[component] , #[page] , #[route] , #[layout] , #[layer] , #[shard] , #[procedure] and #[memoize] function. It must be named exactly cx . ( details ) Remove cx => from view! , live! , emit! and attributes! . Where you passed a different context, shadow cx before the macro. ( details ) Replace app_context , request_context and their try_ versions with context and try_context , and .app_context(value) with .with(value) . ( details ) Set compression, origin policy, base URL, prefetch mode and suspense mode with .with(...) on the router. ( details ) Replace .cookies() with .layer(CookieLayer::new()) and .runtime() with .layer(RuntimeLayer::new()) , and remove .sessions(...) . ( details ) Replace BodyLimit::at and OriginPolicy::exempt_paths with with(...) on the routes they covered. ( details ) Change the options of t! and segment! from = to : . ( details ) Change error = ... in path_param! and module_param! to else ... . ( details ) Change href! parameters such as PostId(42) to post_id: 42 . ( details ) Add a comma between the last prop and the first child in component calls. ( details ) Use a string literal path in asset! . ( details ) Replace cookie! with Cookie::build and mail! with Mail::builder() . ( details ) Replace path_param::(cx) with post_id(cx) . ( details ) Replace .mail(...) with .with(Mailer::new(transport)) , and handle the Result from MailBuilder::build() . ( details ) Run topcoat fmt . ( details ) Renamed and removed APIs Before After CxTestBuilder::new().app_context(a).request_context(b).build() Cx::new().with_many((a, b)) Cx::new(app_context) Cx::new().with_shared(map) RouterBuilder::get_app_context::() RouterBuilder::try_context::() .layer(BodyLimit::max(n)) .with(BodyLimit::max(n)) Compression::new() Compression::default() Compression::off() Compression::disable() OriginPolicy::new() OriginPolicy::default() SessionConfig::builder().token_store(s).lifetime(d) .with(SessionTokenStore::new(s)).with(SessionLifetime(d)) RuntimeLayer RuntimeLayer::new() href!(POSTS) for a Path constant href!((POSTS)) asset!(path, rename) asset!(path, rename: rename) topcoat_asset::asset! , asset_options! topcoat::asset::asset! SendError::delivery(err) SendError::new(err) Behavior changes These still compile, so check them by hand: Adding the same type to the router twice no longer panics. The later value wins. A type that was in both app context and request context now has one lookup, and the request value wins. MailBuilder::html renders the view right away and panics on live views, since mail cannot stream. Assets 2 Loading Uh oh! There was an error while loading.
