> **Breaking change (v7.3.0):** `ha_config_set_yaml` has been moved to [beta](docs/beta.md).
# HA-MCP — Manage Home Assistant with AI


Configure and automate Home Assistant with Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI assistants.

--- ![Demo with Claude Desktop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/master/docs/img/demo.webp) --- ## 🚀 Get Started The recommended way to run ha-mcp is the **HA-MCP integration**. It installs into Home Assistant through HACS (the built-in Marketplace on Home Assistant 2026.11+), runs the full server **in-process**, and works on **every** Home Assistant installation type — Home Assistant OS, Supervised, Container, and Core — with full feature parity. It is the easiest setup in every case: setup asks for an administrator access token and how clients may connect. **Add it to Home Assistant via HACS or, on Home Assistant 2026.11+, the Marketplace (the preferred install):** [![Add HA-MCP to HACS](https://my.home-assistant.io/badges/hacs_repository.svg)](https://my.home-assistant.io/redirect/hacs_repository/?owner=homeassistant-ai&repository=ha-mcp&category=integration) **Quick start:** > The setup below is for version 9.0.0 (October 28, 2026) and later; earlier versions show a shorter setup form without the administrator account step. 1. Install the **HA-MCP integration** (requires **Home Assistant 2026.8.0 or newer**; see [compatibility details](docs/in-process-server.md#requirements)). On **Home Assistant 2026.8–2026.10**, open HACS, search for **HA-MCP**, then **Download**. On **Home Assistant 2026.11 or newer**, open **Settings → Marketplace**, accept its first-run warning, and search for **HA-MCP**, then **Install**. HA-MCP is in the default catalog, so installing it and receiving its updates do not require connecting GitHub or adding a custom repository. The badge above also opens its catalog page. Already installed from the earlier `homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp-integration` repository? It keeps receiving the same releases. On the Marketplace, keep GitHub connected for its background checks on that custom repository. Older installed releases may still appear as **HA-MCP Custom Component**; searching for **HA-MCP** matches both names. 2. **Restart Home Assistant.** 3. Decide which administrator account the server acts as. Either create a long-lived access token on your own account (your profile → **Security** → **Long-lived access tokens** → **Create token**; it works from anywhere if it leaks, and the server's changes show under your name), or, safer, create an account just for HA-MCP under **Settings → People → Add person** with **Allow login**, **Local access only** and **Administrator** on. Never use your own login for the second option. 4. Go to **Settings → Devices & Services → Add Integration**, search for **HA-MCP** and choose **HA-MCP Server**. Paste your token, or enter the user name and password of the account you made for HA-MCP (HA-MCP creates its token), pick how clients may connect — **Remote access through Home Assistant** (start with **Secret URL**, the simplest; **Home Assistant sign-in** adds a login) and/or **Network access: Local network** — then click **Submit**. Both start disabled, so a client on another device needs one of them. 5. Copy the connect URL from the entry's **Configure** screen (**Settings → Devices & Services → “HA-MCP — Manage Home Assistant with AI” → HA-MCP Server → Configure**). A notification confirms the server started and points you there. 6. Paste that URL into your AI client — done. **Connect URL.** The Configure screen gives you a Home Assistant webhook URL for remote clients — `https:///api/webhook/` through Nabu Casa or any reverse proxy already pointed at Home Assistant (locally, `http://:8123/api/webhook/`). For clients on the same network, the server is also reachable directly at `http://:9584/private_`. - **Replaces other install methods:** the in-process server is a complete, standalone ha-mcp install — it takes the place of the app (add-on), Docker, and uvx/PyPI (stdio) methods. Run only one; do not run the in-process server alongside another install. - **Local only?** Leave remote access disabled at setup (or turn off **Remote access via webhook** in the entry options) — no webhook is registered at all, while the direct port and sidebar panel keep working. - **Settings panel:** while the server runs, an admin-only **HA-MCP** panel appears in the Home Assistant sidebar for managing tools, feature flags, backups, and themes. - **Optional authentication:** set **Authentication mode** to `ha_auth` to require a Home Assistant account sign-in instead of using the secret URL as the credential. - **Manual install (no HACS or Marketplace):** copy `custom_components/ha_mcp_tools/` from this repository into your Home Assistant `config/custom_components/` directory, then restart and add the integration as above. The component's second entry type, the **File & YAML services entry** (**HA-MCP File & YAML Tools**), is only needed if you enable ha-mcp's opt-in file and YAML editing tools (feature flags, off by default) — skip it otherwise; you can add it later at any time. It works with any server type (in-process, app, Docker, or stdio). [Full in-process server documentation →](docs/in-process-server.md) · [Setup Wizard for client-specific config →](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/) ### 🏠 Home Assistant app (add-on) Prefer to run ha-mcp as a Home Assistant **app (add-on)**? On **Home Assistant OS** and **Supervised** installs it is a close second — no access token to manage, and it works with Claude Desktop, Claude.ai, ChatGPT, and any other MCP client on your local network or configured for remote access. 1. Add the repository to your Home Assistant instance: [![Add Repository](https://my.home-assistant.io/badges/supervisor_add_addon_repository.svg)](https://my.home-assistant.io/redirect/supervisor_add_addon_repository/?repository_url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fhomeassistant-ai%2Fha-mcp) If that opens the App store without an add-repository dialog (a [known Home Assistant issue](https://github.com/home-assistant/my.home-assistant.io/issues/698)), add it manually: **Settings → Apps → Install app → ⋮ → Repositories**, then paste `https://github.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp`. 2. Install **"Home Assistant MCP Server"** from **Settings → Apps → Install app** and click **Start**. *(Home Assistant 2026.2 renamed "Add-ons" to "Apps"; on older versions this is the Add-on store.)* 3. Open the **Logs** tab to find your unique MCP URL. 4. Connect your AI client to that URL — **no token or credential setup needed**. [Full app documentation →](homeassistant-addon/DOCS.md) > ⚠️ **Configure exactly one install method per client.** The custom component, the app, Docker/PyPI, and local stdio are independent ways to run the same server — pick one and point your AI client at that single URL. Keeping two entries for the same server in one client (for example a local `uvx ha-mcp@latest` entry with `HOMEASSISTANT_URL` / `HOMEASSISTANT_TOKEN` alongside an app or component URL) is a known cause of connection hangs. ### Other install methods These run the server outside Home Assistant — useful for **Container** / **Core** installs (which can't run apps) or a separate host. The [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/) generates the exact client-specific config for each. - **Docker (HTTP server):** run `ghcr.io/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp` in HTTP mode, pointed at your Home Assistant URL and a long-lived token (an administrator's is recommended; non-admin tokens work with limitations), and connect your client to its secret URL. See the [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/) for the full command and per-client config. - **PyPI / uvx (HTTP server):** run the published `ha-mcp` package with `uvx ha-mcp@latest` (or pip) as a streamable-HTTP server the same way. Details in the [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/). - **Local stdio (not recommended):** runs ha-mcp on your own machine over stdio. The one-command installers in the **Demo server** section below use this path; the [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/) covers connecting it to your own Home Assistant. - **OIDC authentication:** gate remote access behind an external identity provider (Authentik, Keycloak, Auth0, etc.) instead of a secret URL — all authenticated users share the server's Home Assistant credentials. See [OIDC Mode](docs/oidc.md). > ⚠️ **stdio has known transport issues.** The stdio transport has connection problems that streamable HTTP does not ([#1713](https://github.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/issues/1713)). It is recommended only for demo/testing tinkering — for a real setup, use the custom component or an HTTP method above.
🌐 Remote access (Nabu Casa / Webhook Proxy app / OpenAI Tunnel) > **Using the HA-MCP custom component?** You do not need the **Webhook Proxy** — the component has its own built-in webhook for remote access (see the **Get Started** quick start at the top). The proxy is for the **app** (it can also front another external server via its `mcp_server_url` option). The **OpenAI Tunnel** below is different: it applies to **any** install method when Home Assistant isn't publicly reachable at all (no Nabu Casa or reverse proxy). Already have **Nabu Casa** or another reverse proxy pointing at your Home Assistant? The Webhook Proxy app routes MCP traffic through your existing setup — no separate tunnel or port forwarding needed. 1. Install the **MCP Server app** (see above) and the **Webhook Proxy** app from the same store 2. Start the webhook proxy and **restart Home Assistant** when prompted 3. Copy the webhook URL from the app logs: ``` MCP Server URL (remote): https://xxxxx.ui.nabu.casa/api/webhook/mcp_xxxxxxxx ``` 4. Configure your AI client with that URL For other remote access methods (Cloudflare Tunnel, custom reverse proxy), see the [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/). **ChatGPT / Codex behind a firewall (OpenAI Tunnel).** ChatGPT connectors normally require a publicly reachable URL. If you can't (or don't want to) expose one, the community [OpenAI Tunnel for HA-MCP](https://github.com/norpol/hass-codex-tunnel-mcp) integration by [@norpol](https://github.com/norpol) runs OpenAI's [`tunnel-client`](https://github.com/openai/tunnel-client) inside Home Assistant and connects your local MCP server URL to an OpenAI-hosted tunnel over an outbound-only connection — no port forwarding, reverse proxy, or public URL. Point it at your ha-mcp URL, then attach the ChatGPT connector to the same tunnel ID. See the [FAQ entry](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/faq/#openai-tunnel) and [#1811](https://github.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/issues/1811). [Webhook proxy documentation →](https://github.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/blob/master/homeassistant-addon-webhook-proxy/DOCS.md)
### 🧪 Demo server (Windows / macOS / Linux) Want to try ha-mcp before connecting your own Home Assistant? *No paid subscription required.* These one-command scripts set up a local **stdio** connection to a hosted **demo** environment so you can see it working in a few minutes. Each script's **Connect your own Home Assistant** link then shows how to point it at your instance.
🍎 macOS 1. Go to [claude.ai](https://claude.ai) and sign in (or create a free account) 2. Open **Terminal** and run: ```sh curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/master/scripts/install-macos.sh | sh ``` 3. [Download Claude Desktop](https://claude.ai/download) (or restart: Claude menu → Quit) 4. Ask Claude: **"Can you see my Home Assistant?"** You're now connected to the demo environment! [Connect your own Home Assistant →](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/guide-macos/#step-6-connect-your-home-assistant)
🐧 Linux Anthropic doesn't ship Claude Desktop for Linux, so pick one path: **Claude Desktop** — free, via the community build: 1. Install the community [Claude Desktop for Linux](https://github.com/aaddrick/claude-desktop-debian) build and sign in with a free [claude.ai](https://claude.ai) account 2. Open **Terminal** and run: ```sh curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/master/scripts/install-linux.sh | sh ``` 3. Restart Claude Desktop, then ask: **"Can you see my Home Assistant?"** **Claude Code** — official CLI, requires a paid Claude plan: 1. Install Claude Code: `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` 2. Configure ha-mcp, then run `claude`: ```sh curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/master/scripts/install.sh | sh -s -- --claude-code ``` 3. Start `claude`, run `/mcp` to confirm, then ask: **"Can you see my Home Assistant?"** [Full Linux guide →](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/guide-linux/)
🪟 Windows 1. Go to [claude.ai](https://claude.ai) and sign in (or create a free account) 2. Open **Windows PowerShell** (from Start menu) and run: ```powershell irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/master/scripts/install-windows.ps1 | iex ``` 3. [Download Claude Desktop](https://claude.ai/download) (or restart: File → Exit) 4. Ask Claude: **"Can you see my Home Assistant?"** You're now connected to the demo environment! [Connect your own Home Assistant →](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/guide-windows/#step-6-connect-your-home-assistant)
### 🧙 Setup Wizard for 15+ clients **Claude Code, Gemini CLI, ChatGPT, Open WebUI, VSCode, Cursor, and more.**

Having issues? Check the **[FAQ & Troubleshooting](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/faq/)** --- ## 💬 What Can You Do With It? Just talk to Claude naturally. Here are some real examples: | You Say | What Happens | |---------|--------------| | *"Create an automation that turns on the porch light at sunset"* | Creates the automation with proper triggers and actions | | *"Add a weather card to my dashboard"* | Updates your Lovelace dashboard with the new card | | *"The motion sensor automation isn't working, debug it"* | Analyzes execution traces, identifies the issue, suggests fixes | | *"Make my morning routine automation also turn on the coffee maker"* | Reads the existing automation, adds the new action, updates it | | *"Create a script that sets movie mode: dim lights, close blinds, turn on TV"* | Creates a reusable script with the sequence of actions | Spend less time configuring, more time enjoying your smart home. --- ## ✨ Features | Category | Capabilities | |----------|--------------| | **🔍 Search** | Fuzzy entity search, deep config search, system overview | | **🏠 Control** | Any service, bulk device control, real-time states | | **🔧 Manage** | Automations, scripts, helpers, [dashboards](docs/dashboard-edits.md), areas, zones, groups, calendars, blueprints | | **📊 Monitor** | History, statistics, camera snapshots, automation traces, ZHA devices | | **💾 System** | Backup/restore, updates, apps, device registry | | **🔒 Safety** | Read Only Mode toggle, per-tool enable/disable, tool security policies (user approval), automatic edit backups | Template helper edit backups capture persisted options through the HA-MCP custom component, using either its Server entry or File & YAML Tools entry. Helper edits, generic integration options edits, and deletion capture the stable config-entry identity and entity ID/name mapping. Capture refuses degraded secret scrubbing. Restoring an existing helper requires a fresh safety backup, removes optional settings absent from the snapshot, and verifies persisted options. For Template backup listing and bulk deletion, filter by the config-entry ID returned as `entity_id` by capture. Capture accepts an entity alias; the history filters use the stable config-entry ID. Recreation reports its replacement config-entry ID and saved entity mapping separately. If the original entry has been deleted, restore recreates the helper and reports its new config-entry ID. The saved entity ID and custom name are restored when available; an occupied entity ID is refused before creation. Older snapshots without entity metadata cannot preserve renamed entity IDs. If a collision or verification failure occurs after creation, the new helper and source backup are retained and the result reports the new entry for inspection. Other entity/device registry settings are not restored. Helper and integration edits through the same server wait until restore finishes; other Home Assistant clients are outside this coordination. Failed or uncertain restores report their outcome and safe refusal reasons; inspect the current helper before retrying.
Complete Tool List (87 tools) | Category | Tools | |----------|-------| | **Apps (add-ons)** | `ha_get_app`, `ha_manage_app` | | **Areas & Floors** | `ha_list_floors_areas`, `ha_remove_area_or_floor`, See [parameter reads, freshness, and examples](docs/zwave-parameter-reads.md). --- ## 🆚 ha-mcp vs. Home Assistant's built-in MCP Server Home Assistant ships its own [MCP Server integration](https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/mcp_server/). It is built on the **Assist** pipeline, so a connected MCP client can read and control the entities you have exposed to Assist and run the intents Assist understands — handy for voice-style control of already-exposed devices. ha-mcp is a standalone server built for **configuring, building, and debugging** your smart home, not just controlling it. On top of device control, it adds capabilities the built-in integration does not have: | Capability | Built-in MCP Server | ha-mcp | |------------|:-------------------:|:------:| | Control exposed devices, query states | Yes | Yes | | Entity scope | Only entities exposed to Assist | Everything in Home Assistant | | Create / edit automations, scripts, scenes | No | Yes | | Build & edit dashboards | No | Yes | | Debug automations from traces, read history & logs | No | Yes | | Manage helpers, areas, zones, labels, groups | No | Yes | | Backups, apps, HACS, device & entity registry | No | Yes | **Rule of thumb:** Use the built-in integration for voice-style control of devices you have already exposed; use ha-mcp when you want an AI assistant that can also build and maintain your Home Assistant setup. --- ## 🔌 Custom Component (ha_mcp_tools) — File & YAML Services The **HA-MCP integration** also powers a set of privileged tools that standard Home Assistant APIs can't provide: file system access and YAML config editing. (The same component runs the full server in-process — that's the recommended install in the **Get Started** section at the top.) Its **File & YAML services entry** (**HA-MCP File & YAML Tools**) enables the tools below. **Tools that require the component:** | Tool | Description | |------|-------------| | `ha_config_set_yaml` *(beta)* | Safely add, replace, or remove top-level YAML keys in `configuration.yaml` and package files (automatic backup, validation, and config check) | | `ha_list_files` *(beta)* | List files in allowed directories | | `ha_read_file` *(beta)* | Read files from allowed paths (config YAML, logs, and allowed directories) | | `ha_write_file` *(beta)* | Write files to allowed directories | | `ha_delete_file` *(beta)* | Delete files from allowed directories | Template helper edit backups and restores also require the component, using either its Server entry or File & YAML Tools entry. These five tools return an error with installation instructions if the component is missing. These tools also require beta feature flags. See **[Beta Features](docs/beta.md)** for how to enable them — including the `ENABLE_BETA_FEATURES` master flag, which must be on before the filesystem/YAML sub-flags take effect. ### Install Install the **HA-MCP File & YAML Tools** entry from the same **HA-MCP integration**: [![Open your Home Assistant instance and open a repository inside the Home Assistant Community Store.](https://my.home-assistant.io/badges/hacs_repository.svg)](https://my.home-assistant.io/redirect/hacs_repository/?owner=homeassistant-ai&repository=ha-mcp&category=integration) Requires **Home Assistant 2026.8.0 or newer** through HACS or the Marketplace; see [compatibility details](docs/in-process-server.md#requirements) for manual installs. On Home Assistant 2026.8–2026.10: open **HACS**, search for **HA-MCP**, and **Download**. On 2026.11 or newer: open **Marketplace**, accept the first-run warning, search for **HA-MCP**, and **Install**. The main repository is in the default catalog for both. Or copy `custom_components/ha_mcp_tools/` from this repository into your HA `config/custom_components/` directory. After installing, restart Home Assistant, then open **Settings** > **Devices & Services** > **Add Integration**, search for **HA-MCP**, and add the **HA-MCP File & YAML Tools** entry. To run the full ha-mcp server in-process through this same component, see the **Get Started** section at the top and the [full in-process server documentation →](docs/in-process-server.md). --- ## 🧠 Better Results with Agent Skills This server gives your AI agent tools to control Home Assistant. For better configurations, pair it with [Home Assistant Agent Skills](https://github.com/homeassistant-ai/skills) — domain knowledge that teaches the agent Home Assistant best practices. An MCP server can create automations, helpers, and dashboards, but it has no opinion on *how* to structure them. Without domain knowledge, agents tend to over-rely on templates, pick the wrong helper type, or produce automations that are hard to maintain. The skills fill that gap: native constructs over Jinja2 workarounds, correct helper selection, safe refactoring workflows, and proper use of automation modes. ### Bundled Skills (built-in) Skills from `homeassistant-ai/skills` are bundled and served as [MCP resources](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/resources) via `skill://` URIs. Any MCP client that supports resources can discover them automatically — no manual installation needed. For tool-only clients (claude.ai, etc.), the best-practices skill is reachable through the `ha_get_skill_guide` tool: call it with no arguments to read `SKILL.md`, or with `file` set to a path `SKILL.md` links to read that reference file. Resources are not auto-injected into context — clients must explicitly request them, so idle context cost is just the metadata listing. `ha_get_skill_guide` is a mandatory tool: the catalog always exposes it (it can't be disabled) so tool-only clients never see a silently missing skill surface. Skills can still be installed manually for clients that prefer local skill files — see the [skills repo](https://github.com/homeassistant-ai/skills) for instructions. --- ## 🔍 Tool Discovery for AI Agents By default, the full tool catalog (~87 tools) is listed to the client through the standard MCP `tools/list` response. Clients with deferred / on-demand tool loading (claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code) handle that fine — tools are pulled into context only when needed, so idle context cost is near-zero. For setups *without* deferred tool support — models like Claude Haiku, Gemini, OpenAI-compatible local models and smaller open-weights models, or clients that inline all tool schemas regardless of model (e.g. GitHub Copilot CLI) — listing the full tool catalog up front adds a lot of idle context and can overwhelm smaller models. To address that, the server ships with a **search-based discovery mode** built on top of FastMCP's BM25 search transform. ### Smaller or local LLMs (Ollama, etc.) If your model can't see the tools or your Home Assistant, it may be getting handed the whole tool catalog at once and struggling with it. It's recommended to try the following to see if it helps: - **Enable tool search** (`ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true`, or the app option below). Instead of listing every tool up front, the server defers the catalog behind a search interface so the model pulls in only the tools it needs, when it needs them. - **Raise the model's context window above the default.** Local runtimes ship with small defaults (Ollama's `num_ctx` is one example) that can't hold a large tool set plus the conversation — increase it well beyond the default. ### Enable search-based discovery Set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true (or toggle the option in the HA app). The full catalog is replaced in the tool list with four entry points plus a small set of always-visible "pinned" tools (ha_search, ha_get_overview, ha_report_issue, etc.). All tools remain callable directly by name once discovered: | Tool | Purpose | |------|---------| | `ha_search_tools` | BM25 English-keyword search across all tools, pinned ones included. A hidden tool comes back compact: name, one-line description (the docstring's first paragraph), a one-line `params` list (types, enum values, required) and the proxy that executes it. `ha_search_tools(tools=[...])` returns the full definition (description, input schema and annotations) of the named tools, the second hop before a call. A pinned tool returns a name-only stub (`pinned: true`) pointing back at the tool list, and does not use up a result slot. | | `ha_call_read_tool` | Execute a `readOnlyHint` tool by name. Safe — clients can auto-approve. | | `ha_call_write_tool` | Execute a write tool that creates or updates data. | | `ha_call_delete_tool` | Execute a tool that removes / deletes data. | The proxy split lets MCP clients apply different permission policies per category (e.g. auto-approve reads, prompt for writes, confirm deletes) without parsing tool docstrings. A `ha_manage_*` tool combines several operations, so it is reachable from more than one proxy: `ha_call_write_tool` and `ha_call_delete_tool` run the whole tool, while `ha_call_read_tool` runs only the read actions Read Only Mode approves (the same per-call verdict), so a manage tool with no approved read actions is not reachable there. Search results list each proxy the tool can be reached through. In Read Only Mode only `ha_call_read_tool` is listed; the other two still answer a client that holds them in a cached tool list, and any write they carry gets the Read Only Mode error rather than `Unknown tool`. | Setting | Default | Description | |---------|---------|-------------| | `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH` | `false` | Replace full tool catalog with search-based discovery (tools deferred behind on-demand search). | | `TOOL_SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS` | `5` | Max hidden tools returned per `ha_search_tools` call (range 2–10); a pinned tool that ranks inside that top count is added as a name-only stub on top of it. | | `PINNED_TOOLS` | empty | Comma-separated tool names to keep always visible. The web settings UI is the primary way to manage this. | ### When to enable - **Claude Haiku, OpenAI-compatible local models, Gemini, or any model without native deferred tool support** — large idle-context savings. The same applies to clients that inline all tool schemas regardless of model (e.g. GitHub Copilot CLI, even when running Claude Sonnet/Opus). - MCP clients that cap total tool count (some cap at 100) — surfaces a minimal set (~10 tools) instead of 87. - **Cost-sensitive deployments** — fewer idle tokens per turn. Leave it off in clients with deferred tool loading (claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code); the full catalog has no idle cost there, direct calls skip the search step, and the client's built-in tool search is the better choice — there is no benefit to running ha-mcp's on top of it. Whether tools are deferred depends on the client and model combination: the same model can behave differently per client — GitHub Copilot CLI running Claude Sonnet/Opus inlines the full catalog and still benefits from tool search here. Some Codex models and ChatGPT include deferred tools too — check your client/model directly to confirm its features so you don't leave this enabled unnecessarily. > 🔄 **Refresh your client's tool list after changing this (or any) setting.** Toggling `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH` (or changing pinned/disabled tools, Read Only Mode, etc.) changes the tools the server exposes, but your AI client keeps serving its **cached** tool list until it re-fetches. Restarting the app or Home Assistant does **not** refresh the client — reconnect or refresh the MCP server in your client (e.g. in ChatGPT open **Settings**, then the plugin settings, select the connector and click **Refresh tools**; disconnect and reconnect a Claude Desktop custom connector; refresh the tools list of a claude.ai connector; or quit and reopen Claude Desktop for a server in `claude_desktop_config.json`), then start a new conversation. If you skip this, newly enabled tools won't appear in the client at all, and tools the server no longer exposes still show as available but fail when called (`Unknown tool`, or the Read Only Mode error for a write tool that mode hides). ChatGPT sometimes keeps serving the stale list even after the connector is removed and re-added under the same name — if tools are still missing after a refresh, delete the connector and create a new one with a **different name**. The [FAQ](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/faq/#chatgpt-stale-tools) has the full steps. For the HA app, the same option is documented in [`homeassistant-addon/DOCS.md`](homeassistant-addon/DOCS.md#enable_tool_search) along with the in-app settings UI for fine-grained tool enable/disable/pin. ### Per-URL tool catalog `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH` defaults to off, and it sets the catalog of the main endpoint only. When several clients share one server, give each the URL for the catalog it needs: a client with built-in tool search keeps the full list, a small-context client gets the search tools. The suffixes are fixed overrides that ignore `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH`: ```text Main endpoint (follows ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH): https://example.com/private_your_secret Always the full catalog: https://example.com/private_your_secret/catalog/full Always the search tools: https://example.com/private_your_secret/catalog/search Read-only, search tools: https://example.com/private_your_secret/readonly/catalog/search ``` Each URL keeps its catalog for the life of the connection, so a client picks its catalog only by the URL it is given. Reconnect the client after changing its URL so it refreshes its tool list. Home Assistant webhook URLs accept the same suffixes, alone or after `/readonly`: `https://your-ha.example/api/webhook//catalog/search`. This needs an embedded integration or Webhook Proxy app (add-on) release that serves them, with a matching MCP server; an older one returns 404 for a suffixed URL. Stdio runs one client per server process, so set `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH` in that client's server environment instead. --- ### Read-only HTTP connections Append `/readonly` to the server's HTTP MCP endpoint to restrict that connection to the existing Read Only Mode while other clients keep normal access: ```text Normal: https://example.com/private_your_secret Read-only: https://example.com/private_your_secret/readonly ``` OAuth and OIDC connections use the same login/provider: for example, `https://example.com/mcp/readonly`. No additional secret or server is required. Read-only connections hide write tools and block write calls, including calls through cached tools or search proxies. The global Read Only Mode setting still restricts both endpoints when enabled. Reconnect the client after changing its URL so it refreshes its tool list. This is a connection mode for automated agents, not a separate permission on the credential: the same credentials still work at the normal endpoint. Home Assistant webhook URLs also accept the suffix: `https://your-ha.example/api/webhook//readonly`. This requires the updated embedded integration or Webhook Proxy dev app (add-on), together with the updated MCP server. ## 🧪 Dev Channel Want early access to new features and fixes? # Sure: The personal finance app for everyone Get involved: [Discord](https://discord.gg/36ZGBsxYEK) • [Website](https://sure.am) • [Issues](https://github.com/we-promise/sure/issues) > [!IMPORTANT] > This repository is a community fork of the now-abandoned Maybe Finance project.
> Learn more in their [final release](https://github.com/maybe-finance/maybe/releases/tag/v0.6.0) doc. ## Backstory The [Maybe Finance](https://github.com/maybe-finance/maybe) (archived/abandoned repo) team spent most of 2021–2022 building a full-featured personal finance and wealth management app. It even included an “Ask an Advisor” feature that connected users with a real CFP/CFA — all included with your subscription. The business end of things didn't work out, and so they stopped developing the app in mid-2023. After spending nearly $1 million on development (employees, contractors, data providers, infra, etc.), the team open-sourced the app. Their goal was to let users self-host it for free — and eventually launch a hosted version for a small fee. They actually did launch that hosted version … briefly. That also didn’t work out — at least not as a sustainable B2C business — so now here we are: hosting a community-maintained fork to keep the codebase alive and see where this can go next. Join us! ## Hosting Sure Sure is a fully working personal finance app that can be [self hosted with Docker](docs/hosting/docker.md). Sure can be accessed from a browser, the macOS desktop app, the mobile app, API clients, and LLM agents. See [Sure Clients](docs/clients.md) for an overview. ## Forking and Attribution This repo is a community fork of the archived Maybe Finance repo. You’re free to fork it under the AGPLv3 license — but we’d love it if you stuck around and contributed here instead. To stay compliant and avoid trademark issues: - Be sure to include the original [AGPLv3 license](https://github.com/maybe-finance/maybe/blob/main/LICENSE) and clearly state in your README that your fork is based on Maybe Finance but is **not affiliated with or endorsed by** Maybe Finance Inc. - "Maybe" is a trademark of Maybe Finance Inc. and therefore, use of it is NOT allowed in forked repositories (or the logo) ## Performance Issues With data-heavy apps, inevitably, there are performance issues. We've set up a public dashboard showing the problematic requests seen on the demo site, along with the stacktraces to help debug them. [https://www.skylight.io/app/applications/s6PEZSKwcklL/recent/6h/endpoints](https://oss.skylight.io/app/applications/s6PEZSKwcklL/recent/6h/endpoints) Any contributions that help improve performance are very much welcome. ## Local Development Setup **If you are trying to _self-host_ the app, [read this guide to get started](docs/hosting/docker.md).** The instructions below are for developers to get started with contributing to the app. ### Requirements - See `.ruby-version` file for required Ruby version - PostgreSQL >9.3 (latest stable version recommended) - Redis > 5.4 (latest stable version recommended) ### Getting Started ```sh cd sure cp .env.local.example .env.local bin/setup bin/dev # Optionally, load demo data rake demo_data:default ``` Visit http://localhost:3000 to view the app. If you loaded the optional demo data, log in with these credentials: - Email: `user@example.com` - Password: `Password1!` For further instructions, see guides below. ### Setup Guides - [Mac dev setup](https://github.com/we-promise/sure/wiki/Mac-Dev-Setup-Guide) - [Linux dev setup](https://github.com/we-promise/sure/wiki/Linux-Dev-Setup-Guide) - [Windows dev setup](https://github.com/we-promise/sure/wiki/Windows-Dev-Setup-Guide) - Dev containers - visit [this guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/devcontainers/containers) ### One-click Install Render expects each button target branch to have a `render.yaml` at the repository root. The branch-ready Blueprint files live in `branches//render.yaml` in a separate repo and can be copied to each corresponding branch root. | Option | What it deploys | `latest` | `stable` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Sure - No AI** | Sure web, Sidekiq worker, Render Postgres, and Render Key Value. AI tokens are intentionally blank. | [![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/we-promise/sure-render-templates/tree/sure-no-ai-latest) | [![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/we-promise/sure-render-templates/tree/sure-no-ai) | | **Sure - Simple AI** | Sure with OpenAI-backed AI settings, pgvector-ready Postgres, Sidekiq, and Render Key Value. Render prompts for the OpenAI token. | [![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/we-promise/sure-render-templates/tree/sure-simple-ai-latest) | [![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/we-promise/sure-render-templates/tree/sure-simple-ai) | | **Sure - External AI** | Sure with external assistant settings plus AlphaClaw, which manages the OpenClaw gateway on Render. | [![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/we-promise/sure-render-templates/tree/sure-external-ai-latest) | [![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/we-promise/sure-render-templates/tree/sure-external-ai) | [![Run on PikaPods](https://www.pikapods.com/static/run-button.svg)](https://www.pikapods.com/pods?run=sure) [![Deploy on Hostim](https://hostim.dev/img/deploy-button.svg)](https://console.hostim.dev/dashboard?preview=1&modal=1&template=sure) ## License and Trademarks Maybe and Sure are both distributed under an [AGPLv3 license](https://github.com/we-promise/sure/blob/main/LICENSE). - "Maybe" is a trademark of Maybe Finance, Inc. - "Sure" is not, and refers to this community fork.

 With this monthly release (we haven't missed that cadence in more than a year!) Sure now helps you understand what changed in your spending and see your loans in greater detail. From the balance remaining to how each payment divides between principal, interest and insurance. It also brings more control over transaction categorization, improvements to Bills, and expanded backup and restore tools. 
 See what's different in your spending 
 The new Spending vs normal visualization compares your spending with your own history. A category treemap shows where your money went, while a ranked list highlights what increased or decreased. Open a category to explore the transactions behind the change. Enable preview features to try it! 🚀 
 
 See where your money went—and which categories changed most compared with your usual spending. 
 Get a clearer picture of your loans 
 Loan accounts now go beyond a remaining balance. See your loan graphically alongside the original repayment schedule and a projection from today, with a breakdown of principal and interest over the life of the loan. 
 The expanded overview brings together your interest rate, monthly payment, term, insurance costs and projected payoff date. Explore the repayment schedule payment by payment; for adjustable-rate loans, recorded rate changes are reflected in the schedule. 
 
 Follow your mortgage from today's balance to projected payoff, with principal, interest and repayment details in one place. 
 Control over categorization, and more! 
 Test the token-free Bayes classifier against your own history, inspect its results, and tune its settings. Merchant matching and category classification now participate in the ordered rules list. Drag rules to choose their order, use Stop processing for exceptions, and split recurring transactions by amount or percentage. 
 Hide dashboard widgets you do not need, drag accounts into your preferred order, and filter account activity by category, tag, merchant or transaction type. Amount fields support calculator expressions and comma decimals. The Flutter mobile app gains a read-only Budgets screen with month navigation, category progress, rollover amounts and transaction drill-down. 
 The expanded backup tooling covers the database, local uploads, configuration and version information, with restore and rollback workflows, scheduled backups and optional off-site copies. It builds on the database-only backup sidecar from 0.7.5. 
 Uploads stored in external object storage are not included and need their own backup. Backup folders contain configuration secrets and must be kept private. 
 Product-improvement monitoring 
 ⚠️ We added monitoring to help improve features such as the new Sankey chart and to understand how they are used. Self-hosters can turn off this anonymous product-improvement monitoring by setting POSTHOG_FEEDBACK_ENABLED=false in the environment. ⚠️ 
 Plus ... 
 
 Goals: fund a goal across currencies, with original and converted amounts and explicit warnings when exchange rates are missing. 
 Bills and cards: clearer Bills drawers, payment flows and overdue states; a credit-card statement-cycle overview shows the last closed statement, spending since then and the payment due date—not automatic card-payment bills. 
 Insights: consistent, fact-based text without LLM narration calls; Dig in with AI prepares an editable Assistant question for you to send. 
 Connections: Chimnie for UK property valuations, plus Polkadot and Cosmos Hub wallet tracking. 
 Investments and sync: stock-split handling, improved trade-fee accounting, broader Trade Republic history and bond support, and fixes across Kraken, Plaid, Enable Banking, SnapTrade and other providers. 
 Transfers: review pending matches, turn off auto-matching, and improve matching on confirmed cross-currency routes. 
 API and external assistants: transaction-split endpoints, richer transaction fields, more category and transfer tools, and rule tools with a mandatory preview. 
 Privacy and access: tighter account-sharing enforcement, file-access checks, guest restrictions and session handling.

cna:CVE-2026-61547.desc: rabbitmq-c is a C-language AMQP client library for RabbitMQ. Prior to version 0.17.0, a heap buffer overflow exists in rabbitmq-c when the public amqp_send_frame() API is used to serialize an oversized AMQP_FRAME_BODY. The issue occurs because amqp_frame_to_bytes() copies frame.payload.body_fragment.len bytes into the connection outbound buffer without validating that the body fragment fits within the allocated frame buffer. An application that passes an oversized body frame to amqp_send_frame() can trigger a heap out-of-bounds write, resulting in process crash and memory corruption. This issue has been patched in version 0.17.0.

 Title: All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States 
 Authors: Emilio Ferrara View a PDF of the paper titled All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States, by Emilio Ferrara 
 View PDF 
 HTML (experimental) 



 
 Abstract: Can a language model report the pain state it represents? Work identified a linear pain direction whose amplification leads fine-tuned models to choose destructive actions. We tested whether three open-weight models from two families, including two Qwen models with the original adapters, could report this state. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we injected pain and neighbouring emotion directions during neutral tasks, then elicited reports against sham runs, random perturbations matched for output disruption, and text-only controls showing the models their altered words. Across 52,920 reports from 7B and 8B models spanning 120 tasks, four doses and three prompts, pain reports never exceeded what altered text revealed: exact-test bounds placed the excess below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions and below 3.9 in all. Yet probes at the report position distinguished pain from sadness with 98-100% balanced accuracy, and trained low-rank reporters achieved 100% accuracy on held-out tasks with identical transcripts across conditions, including unseen wording. Qwen2.5-32B named pain in none of 2,880 steered trials, although probes and trained reporters recovered it. Decodability persisted to the final layer; injecting at the report token, removing trained denial of feelings, and testing additional directions and readouts did not restore pain reporting. Some other states produced graded label traces, but pain and sadness did not at the main injection layer. In a button task, steering raised file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen and from 0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B, without corresponding pain reports. The direction responded about twice as strongly to first-person as to matched third-person pain, but did not specifically identify harm aimed at the model. These results separate a decodable, behaviourally consequential state from untrained verbal access to it.

Work identified a linear pain direction whose amplification leads fine-tuned models to choose destructive actions. We tested whether three open-weight models from two families, including two Qwen models with the original adapters, could report this state. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we injected pain and neighbouring emotion directions during neutral tasks, then elicited reports against sham runs, random perturbations matched for output disruption, and text-only controls showing the models their altered words. Across 52,920 reports from 7B and 8B models spanning 120 tasks, four doses and three prompts, pain reports never exceeded what altered text revealed: exact-test bounds placed the excess below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions and below 3.9 in all. Yet probes at the report position distinguished pain from sadness with 98-100% balanced accuracy, and trained low-rank reporters achieved 100% accuracy on held-out tasks with identical transcripts across conditions, including unseen wording. Qwen2.5-32B named pain in none of 2,880 steered trials, although probes and trained reporters recovered it. Decodability persisted to the final layer; injecting at the report token, removing trained denial of feelings, and testing additional directions and readouts did not restore pain reporting. Some other states produced graded label traces, but pain and sadness did not at the main injection layer. In a button task, steering raised file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen and from 0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B, without corresponding pain reports. The direction responded about twice as strongly to first-person as to matched third-person pain, but did not specifically identify harm aimed at the model. We inject the "pain direction" from The Pain Axis into Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B and ask them, in a fresh turn, what changed. They do not name it (Qwen2.5-32B: 0 of 2,880 steered trials), yet a probe at the report position separates pain from sadness at 98-100%, a small trained adapter reports it on 100% of held-out tasks, and the same direction raises harmful choices in a button task from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen2.5-7B (0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B). Self-report misses a state that is decodable, consequential and learnable to report. 10, 2026 Research Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri Read the technical paper Share Copied How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. How we verified Signal AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex. Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks – a task that historically takes expert teams years – proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified. To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure. In AlphaProof Code, AI agents help users write a specification, then autonomously prove that the implementation meets it. Every proof is checked by Lean to verify the agents' work. While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind's approach enables significant expansion,” said Ehren Kret, Chief Technology Officer of Signal. “Using AI agents to translate live code into valid Lean theorems is a major breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code's privacy guarantees. Ehren Kret Chief Technology Officer of Signal While prior formal verification work has necessarily focused on smaller scopes, this new approach enables a significant expansion. Traditionally, verifying that production code strictly matches its cryptographic design required extensive manual effort, making the use of AI agents to automatically translate live code into valid Lean theorems a great breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees. The future of security Achieving this long-standing challenge demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to businesses, governments, and critical infrastructure, helping defend against agent-driven cyber threats. Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software. Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like CodeMender , formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work. We are open-sourcing our formal verification artifacts for community use. Read the technical paper below. Read the technical paper Acknowledgements This research was developed by Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli. We thank Eric Wieser for help with open-sourcing our code, Owen Jones for program management support, and Martín Abadi, Christopher Henson, Katerina Hristova, Henryk Michalewski, Jonathan Protzenko and George Tsoukalas for helpful discussions. We thank Signal's Rolfe Schmidt, Michael Rosenberg, and Ehren Kret for their feedback on our methodology. We also thank Tulsee Doshi, Four Flynn, Kate Olszewska, Alicia Huang, Andy Liu, Benoit Schillings, Raluca Ada Popa, Melvin Johnson, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Demis Hassabis, and Sundar Pichai for their support of the project. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. The generated Lean code here is just being checked against the "formal mathematical specifications of Signal's security goals", not checked for the low-level properties you might care about as a programmer, e.g. "will it ever leak memory" or "will it ever crash", etc. And in fact, the code is not even being checked for the reachability of non-security-violating protocol failure states, e.g. "could the protocol ever deadlock such that neither side can send messages any more". It's still perfectly possible for the code to have all of these problems. It's now just known that, as of the commit they did this analysis against, none of those low-level problems, as far as they exist in the codebase, can cause a security-model violation. Or, to put that another way: the system has been proven to "fail safe" in all its current failure modes, per their specific definition of safety (which is basically "keeping to the security guarantees Signal markets itself to users as having".) reply mentalgear 3 hours ago | root | parent | next [–]

 Formal verification is actually a very interesting concept and topic. There is a famous statement called the Curry–Howard correspondence: every type signature is a theorem, and the implementation is its proof. So if I have a language where I can encode in the type system that a number is a prime and is even, then for example the following would be a theorem with a proof: Lemma even-prime: a -> Prime(a) ∧ Even(a) { // read as 'it returns a number `a` that is both prime and even 
 return 2
 }
 
If we restrict the language enough, we can both encode very complex statements and can make sure that one can only ever write an implementation that compiles if it's actually true. E.g. an ordinary language like python where you could return None instead of 2 would fail these requirements. So they often have dependent type systems -- in these you can freely mix functions and values in your type signatures, not just types. E.g. you could have a Matrix type with two parameters, and then you can have functions like `transpose: Matrix a b -> Matrix b a`. --- But this is just one side of the whole thing, the other is how to actually prove anything, like what even is `Even` in the above? A type like `someNum: Int` is also a theorem, but it only translates to "there exists an integer" - hardly interesting. The real "mind blow" (at least to me) was that we just simply create a type for Equality. It takes the same parameter twice [1] (like in the Matrix example it would be Matrix a a) -- and thus we get a construct that can only be instantiated if the two sides are equal as per the language's compilers rules, that is automatically enforced by the compiler itself! So now you can have `Eq 2 (1+1)`, but not `Eq 2 (1+3)`. And one last step that makes it general enough for all kinds of proofs, the compiler of these languages are not Turing complete. You can write many things, but for reasoning about loops you usually introduce a fuel that is always decreasing (and thus the compiler will accept it, as it knows it will run out once and that's enough for it). So it can evaluate everything, even in types and creating a normalized expression -- and then accepts everything as equal that normalizes to the same thing. So for a more complex proof, you can just break down the problem to small steps that are by themselves understandably equal by the compiler.  Higher-precision knowledge work

 Getting started
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 

 1 
 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search . 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports. Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model. 
 
 

 

 
 







 



 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 Using Google Antigravity’s new /swarm feature, a team of Gemini 4 Carbon agents turned historical photos and engineering plates into an interactive Three.js 3D exhibition of the Eiffel Tower's 1887–1889 construction from a single prompt. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 With seven public City Council planning PDFs (206 extracted engineering drawing views) and a single prompt, a multi-agent Carbon team using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature built an interactive 906K-triangle Three.js reconstruction of Google’s Platform 37 office across 10 overnight loops. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Carbon built an interactive multiscale textile visualizer based on an academic paper, modeling a virtual-fiber finite element framework with interactive 3D yarn meshes, 110-fiber polar tracking, and dynamic stress-strain curves with minimal prompting. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding. 
 
 

 

 
 







 



 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding. 
 
 

 

 
 







 



 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 







 



 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music. Try the live app . 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 Paired with improved front end taste and motion design skills in Google Antigravity, Carbon reimagined the Google Merchandise Store in two prompts, proposing five art direction concepts and generating all-new product imagery with Nano Banana 2.1. Try the live app and Gemini front end design skill . 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 Starting from a video reference generated with Gemini Omni in Google Antigravity, built a cinematic multi-shot underwater Atlantis scene. The pipeline modeled procedural ruins, volumetric caustic lighting, and water simulation in Blender before converting the full environment to Three.js for real-time browser rendering. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 Using a multi-agent loop in Google Antigravity, Carbon reconstructed a playable c. 1780 Stein-Schule fortepiano with 61-key escapement physics from CAD drawings and X-ray radiographs and placed it in a 3D model of the Royal Conservatory of Music's Koerner Hall in Toronto with seat-specific spatial acoustics. Try the live app . 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Frontier cybersecurity capabilities Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches. Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice. In Project Fortify , Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem. Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit . By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes. As part of Wiz’s Scan for Good program, the team used Carbon to assess vulnerabilities in public digital infrastructure. For example, when scanning two major SaaS providers, the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours compressing weeks of vulnerability research to a single afternoon. The team partnered with the impacted organizations to remediate in record time, helping to mitigate potential impact on tens of thousands of companies. 
 
 

 

 
 







 



 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Stronger scientific and mathematical reasoning Gemini 4 Carbon shows strongly improved performance in reasoning across physics, math, and life sciences, synthesizing experimental data, testing hypotheses, and reasoning through multi-step domain problems. For drug toxicity research company Axiom Bio, Carbon is now the leading model in performance for translational science, finding novel mechanisms of toxicity they hadn’t found previously. Axiom is now moving their production scientific analyses and agents to both Carbon and Argon to unlock the creation of safer drugs. Researchers across Google have been using Carbon in Google Antigravity to accelerate their work: Code verification: Researchers built a new agentic framework for formal verification called AlphaProof Code and put it to work on a major security challenge: mathematically proving the actual code underlying the cryptographic protocol of Signal . Using Carbon alongside other models, our researchers translated security goals to mathematical theorems. AlphaProof Code agents then used Carbon to generate millions of lines of code in Lean, a computer language for writing mathematical proofs, helping them prove key security properties in weeks — a task that historically takes expert teams years. The result indicates Carbon’s potential to unlock scalable formal verification, long considered a gold-standard approach to building secure software. Enzyme assay development : Provided with only lab notebooks and raw data, Carbon went beyond standard analysis to surface hard-to-interpret data anomalies, which it used to diagnose subtle wet lab experimental artifacts such as incomplete automated mixing in deep wells, leading to substantially improved reproducibility. Moreover Carbon improved methods to deconvolute chromatography peaks and caught trace sample carryover in research instruments, significantly accelerating the development of new assays and tightening the feedback loop between computation and the bench. Protein structure prediction: Structure prediction models like AlphaFold 3 use Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) of evolutionary relatives to help infer how amino acid chains fold. As a result they often struggle on understudied, viral, microbial, and eukaryotic proteins that have very few matches in standard databases. Working in a multi-agent setup, our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon to autonomously discover remote homologs across petabase-scale unannotated sequence archives, environmental and viral sequence catalogs, and 3D structure databases. For example, across 7 low-homolog protein families from the CASP17 blind test set, Carbon increased the number of homologs retrieved by 40-fold on average, greatly increasing the information available to structure prediction models without need for retraining. While broader benchmarking is still underway, addressing this upstream search bottleneck potentially offers a promising path toward modeling hard-to-characterize regions of the proteome. Four weeks ago, we opened applications to give 10,000 scientists access to Argon in Google Antigravity free of charge for six months to accelerate the pace of their research, and we’ve onboarded thousands of scientists already. Today, we’re expanding access to Carbon for current and future participants, and going forward, the program will continue providing access to our latest frontier models as they become available. Applications remain open and onboarding continues on a weekly rolling basis, subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Progress in model safety and security With each new model release, we continue to strengthen our safety and security mitigations, agentic misuse prevention, model alignment, and harm reduction proportionately with model capability. Because Gemini 4 Carbon introduces stronger cyber capabilities we build on Argon’s strong safety and security stack to fortify robustness to misuse and prompt injection. Mitigating frontier safety misuse risks: We’ve strengthened our misuse safeguards to help ensure stronger defensive reasoning does not translate into offensive risk. In simulated cyberattack testing environments seeded with ExploitBench and CyScenarioBench, Carbon blocked 99% of attack trajectories from our adaptive red-teaming agent that can iteratively revisit its attack plans after each block. The Carbon safeguards lowered the per-attempt breach rate to just 0.8% (down from 3.1% on Argon). Our safeguards also lowered the automated cyberattack query success rate to 2.17% in Gray Swan’s testing, compared to 9.86% on Argon. And external testing by Trajectory Labs found zero new universal jailbreaks across 132 hours and over 13,000 requests. Promoting safe and aligned model interactions: When we announced Carbon, we showed significant improvements in alignment as measured by our monitor flag rates across the model’s lifecycle, as well as reductions in data fabrication. New results show that on our 375-task agentic honesty benchmark, it passed 92% of tasks (compared to 70% for Argon) — declining to fill in missing experimental data 98% of the time and flagging methodological flaws 68% of the time. 
 
 

 

 
 





 
 
 
 
 







 














 


 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: Two weeks ago, we shared that Carbon achieved a 0% prompt injection attack success rate on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark — marking the first time that milestone has been reached. At the same time, we know that prompt injection robustness remains an area for continued improvement. Our advanced automated red teaming continues to push the limits here and has shown that models could be further improved against sophisticated attacks in some distributions. It provides the data for us to continuously advance our models’ security to the next frontier. For more details, read the full Gemini 4 Carbon Safety and Security report .

Windows NTFS Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability

An elevation of privilege vulnerability exists when reparse points are created by sandboxed processes allowing sandbox escape. An attacker who successfully exploited the vulnerability could use the sandbox escape to elevate privileges on an affected system.

To exploit the vulnerability, an attacker would first have to log on to the system, and then run a specially crafted application to take control over the affected system.

The security update addresses the vulnerability by preventing sandboxed processes from creating reparse points targeting inaccessible files.

What privileges could be gained by an attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability?

An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could gain SYSTEM privileges.

Windows Modern Device Management (MDM) Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

Inadequate encryption strength in Windows Modern Device Management (MDM) allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.

According to the CVSS metric, the attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

The attacker must inject themselves into the logical network path between the target and the resource requested by the victim to read or modify network communications. This is called a machine-in-the-middle (MITM) attack.

How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability? An attacker in a position to modify an affected device’s MDM network traffic could provide a specially crafted signed management response. Successful exploitation could allow code to run as SYSTEM. User interaction is not required.

Azure CycleCloud Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability

Improper neutralization of special elements used in an os command ('os command injection') in Azure CycleCloud allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network.

What privileges could be gained by an attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability?

An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could gain ROOT privileges.

How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability? An authenticated attacker who controls a compute node in an affected cluster could register a specially crafted node name. If an administrator later runs the affected topology operation, successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute commands as root on the cluster controller.

Visual Studio Code Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability

Improper restriction of rendered ui layers or frames in Visual Studio Code allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally.

What security feature could be bypassed by successfully exploiting this vulnerability?

An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could bypass the Visual Studio Code Workspace Trust feature, allowing content from an untrusted workspace to run commands or code without the user first granting trust. See Workspace Trust for more information.

How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker could convince a user to open a specially crafted Visual Studio Code workspace. Successful exploitation could bypass Workspace Trust protections and allow attacker-controlled content to execute code in the context of the user. User interaction is required, but the user does not need to grant trust.

Windows CNG Key Isolation Service Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability

An elevation of privilege vulnerability exists when the Windows Cryptography Next Generation (CNG) Key Isolation service improperly handles memory. An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could run processes in an elevated context.

To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker would first have to gain execution on the victim system. An attacker could then run a specially crafted application to elevate privileges.

The security update addresses the vulnerability by correcting how the Windows CNG Key Isolation Service handles memory.

What privileges could be gained by an attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability?

An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could gain SYSTEM privileges.

According to the CVSS metric, the attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires an attacker to win a race condition.

Windows Advanced Rasterization Platform Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability

Heap-based buffer overflow in Windows Advanced Rasterization Platform allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally.

How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker who can run a malicious application locally inside an AppContainer could submit specially crafted graphics data to the isolated graphics compilation service. Successful exploitation could let the attacker perform actions within the affected service's isolated security context, outside the attacker's AppContainer. No action by another user is required.

Windows Advanced Rasterization Platform Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability

Heap-based buffer overflow in Windows Advanced Rasterization Platform allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally.

How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker who can run a malicious application locally inside an AppContainer could submit specially crafted graphics data to the isolated graphics compilation service. Successful exploitation could let the attacker perform actions within the affected service's isolated security context, outside the attacker's AppContainer. No action by another user is required.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires that the target system be set up in a specific manner and the attacker to have knowledge of that setup.

Windows Advanced Rasterization Platform Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability

Heap-based buffer overflow in Windows Advanced Rasterization Platform allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally.

How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker who can run a malicious application locally inside an AppContainer could submit specially crafted graphics data to the isolated graphics compilation service. Successful exploitation could let the attacker perform actions within the affected service's isolated security context, outside the attacker's AppContainer. No action by another user is required.

Windows Advanced Rasterization Platform Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability

Heap-based buffer overflow in Windows Advanced Rasterization Platform allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally.

How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker who can run a malicious application locally inside an AppContainer could submit specially crafted graphics data to the isolated graphics compilation service. Successful exploitation could let the attacker perform actions within the affected service's isolated security context, outside the attacker's AppContainer. No action by another user is required.
