 Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers 
 [LWN subscriber-only content] 
 
 
 
 By Joe Brockmeier November 10, 2026 
 
 Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset
that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He
decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one
problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that
Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by
Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the
driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement
claims, a demand 
that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats
of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the
company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other
platforms. 

 Synaptics and Displaylink 

 The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to
a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other
devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink
Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for
Ubuntu. 

 The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based
platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an
open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the
 Extensible Virtual Display
Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and
allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for 
display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's
utilities. 

 
 
The LWN kernel-source database is the definitive source of information about kernel releases. Try a one-month free trial subscription for immediate access to LWN's kernel content and KSDB as well.
 
 
 A short
article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the
software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream
of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a
communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output
to the user's devices. 

 Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I
spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that
the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude
subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software. 

 Vino 

 He posted the first
patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's
dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an
incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that
he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. " If you have
knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for
isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see,
help would be very welcome. " He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance 
from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings , but no advice
specific to the problem he was trying to solve. 

 Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI 
GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the
approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to
his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few
issues. There was no reply to his issue. 

 He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his
correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is
available in this PDF compiled
by Lothian . He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went
unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On
July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of
Synaptics: 

 
 The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The
protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are
proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents
in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK. 

 From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing
beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe
is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on
avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently
written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent
infringement if it implements patented inventions. 
 

 Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the
" intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink ", so he wanted
to make him aware now rather than " have the situation become more formal
later ". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which
explains why the email made reference to the UK. 

 Cease and desist 

 On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of
intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice . The letter stated that Lothian had not
" substantially responded " to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued
with " public statements and further development activities ". It included
an appendix with a list of 125 patents that " cover fundamental aspects of
DisplayLink's architecture and operation ", but did not specify which patents
might be infringed by the work. 

 Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance
with, including ceasing development of " any software or other
implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent ", withdrawing submissions of
materials " made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing
lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or
organization ", and to identify in writing every location " in which the
relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or
distributed ". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed
confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands. 

 Lothian, instead, posted version
three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on
August 26. He said that the previous two versions had " never lit a
panel ", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks
without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set
posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko. 

 On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate
on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. " A claim chart
mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for
me to understand and properly respond to your concerns. " 

 He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was
being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which
was created to help open-source
developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It
holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection
to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that
he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to
" reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source
software ". 

 He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims " interact with our
respective OIN commitments ", and expressed a desire to sort things out with
Synaptics constructively. " I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics
and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either
of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities ".

 Lothian did not think he could " reasonably provide the signed undertaking "
Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent
claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no
response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on
September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his 
last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He
had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to
move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work. 

 Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned: 

 
As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent
infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink
patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next
two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary
compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation
of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your
infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now
we are escalating as we deem appropriate.
 

 The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be " single-handedly
eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by
educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our
proprietary technology ". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN,
and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other
organization. 

 Bateman sent a follow-up
letter , dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010
and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous
letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply
would result in the company seeking " monetary
compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to
create the attached documentation of your infringing acts ". That amount
would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were
complied with. 

 Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on
vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension
of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts " ideally with
someone qualified to help me read them ". Bateman replied 
that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no
further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that " DisplayLink is not a
member of OIN " and none of its technology was licensable through OIN. 

 OIN to the rescue? 

 Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community
directory . In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the
organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of
the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he
had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian
hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion. 

 OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System
Definition , but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a
Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs (" a
component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still
image or audio data stream or signal ") are not covered unless specifically
mentioned in this
list of components. 

 I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after
OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that
OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's
Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted
kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in
the UK, and provided a recommendation. 

 Status 

 Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up
entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's
demands. For now, he may continue working on some of components that are not
affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted
to the kernel. " Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I
just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics. " 

 Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally
replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not
intend to follow up on the comments: " You can't threaten to sue me and then
say 'can you update your pull request?' " 

 For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to
improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder
that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are
concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for
free-software developers and users.

# Auto Ontology Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own. It enables developers to: - Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs. - Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems. - Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer. - Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question. ## Benchmarks To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the [ontology SQL evaluation repository](https://github.com/NVIDIA/ontology-sql-eval/). > **Licensing & contributions.** Auto Ontology is distributed under the > [Apache License 2.0](./LICENSE). Third-party open-source components > bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in > [`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](./THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). **This project > is currently not accepting external contributions.**

## Key Features - **Natural-language querying** of structured data — questions are translated to SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM. - **Semantic catalog / ontology layer** over relational sources, stored in Postgres alongside the catalog it describes. - **Authentication & RBAC** —using [Better Auth](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth). - **Web UI** for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings. - **Flexible deployment** — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a local stack. ## Software Components | Component | Technology | Role | Default port | | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------ | | Frontend | Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma | Web UI, authentication, API gateway | 3000 | | Backend | FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain | Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs | 3001 | | Ingestion worker | FastAPI (Python 3.12+) | Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings | 3002 | | Postgres + pgvector | Relational Database | App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store | 5432 | | HashiCorp Vault | Optional | Secure storage of connection credentials | — | ### NVIDIA NIM Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted [NVIDIA API catalog](https://build.nvidia.com) (`integrate.api.nvidia.com`) or self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in `.env.example` are: - **LLM:** `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b` - **Embeddings:** `nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b` - **Reranking:** `nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2` The endpoints and models are configured via the `DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT`, `DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL`, `EMBED_ENDPOINT`, and `EMBED_MODEL` environment variables and require a `DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`. #### Model triplets Each model role is configured by a **triplet** of environment variables — `_ENDPOINT` (URL), `_API_KEY`, and `_MODEL`: | Prefix | Role | | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | | `DEFAULT_MODELS` | Shared default; every field below falls back to it. | | `REASONING` | Main chat / NL-to-SQL model. | | `NON_REASONING` | Lighter model used for entity extraction. | | `EMBED` | Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query). | | `RERANK` | Reranker used by the retrieval flow. | You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field left unset falls back to the matching `DEFAULT_MODELS_`. So the simplest setup is to fill in `DEFAULT_MODELS_*` and override per-triplet fields only where they differ (e.g. `EMBED_MODEL`, `NON_REASONING_MODEL`). `*_API_KEY` also falls back to the legacy `NVIDIA_API_KEY` for backward compatibility. ## Quickstart This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers, Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), and an NVIDIA API key (`nvapi-...`) from [build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com). 1. Clone the repository and create `.env`: ```bash git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology cp .env.example .env ``` Then set these values in `.env`: ```dotenv DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY=nvapi-... AUTH_SECRET= APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 POSTGRES_PASSWORD= CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD= PGADMIN_PASSWORD= ``` Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace each default password before you start it. `.env.example` also sets an API key per model role: replace each `nvapi-your-api-key-here` with your key, or delete those lines so they fall back to `DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`. 2. Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set: ```bash docker compose up -d --wait postgres git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \ POSTGRES_PASSWORD='' \ uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop) ``` 3. Build and start the rest of the stack: ```bash docker compose up -d --build ``` 4. Open and sign in with `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL` and `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` from `.env`. Go to **Settings → Semantic Compilation** and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts immediately and reports **Semantic compilation is ready** when it finishes. 5. Ask a question in **Chat**: > What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania > in June 2015? The agent resolves *revenue*, *product*, and *state* to terms in the ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it, so you can check the result against the source: ```text Answer: Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines. SQL: SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines FROM sales.invoicelines il JOIN sales.invoices i ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid JOIN warehouse.stockitems si ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid JOIN sales.customers c ON i.customerid = c.customerid JOIN application.cities ct ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll' AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania' AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01' Steps: Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province Validated the filter values against the data, then executed ``` 6. Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve against. An agent connected through [MCP](#mcp-server) checks answerability first and asks you to clarify: ```text You: What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015? Agent: check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend" Agent: I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another source I should connect? ``` If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for `localhost:3000` and sign in again. For other setup failures, see the [setup skill's troubleshooting guide](./skills/nvidia-ontology-setup/references/troubleshooting.md). ## How it works

Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify it, and the agent answers questions from it. The ontology holds three kinds of definition: - **Terms.** Business concepts such as *Customer* or *Invoice Line*, each with a description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them. - **SQL attributes.** Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the same way. - **Relationships.** How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from keys and from the data. **Generate.** The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source databases: 1. Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the catalog. 2. Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns. 3. Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and suggest SQL attributes from query history. 4. Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval. The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting **Order** shows its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes:

**Certify.** People make the draft trustworthy: 1. Test with real questions in Chat, or with `check_answerable` and `ask_question` over MCP. 2. Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API. 3. Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct. **Answer.** For each question, the agent: 1. Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names. 2. Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search. 3. Writes SQL from those candidates. 4. Checks the filter values and the query against the database, repairing the SQL when a check fails. 5. Runs the query and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took. When the candidates can't support a query, the agent reports that the question can't be answered from this data. Predictive questions go to KumoRFM when it's configured (see [Predictions](#predictions)). In Chat, each answer shows its SQL, and you can view the rows, download them as CSV, or read them as a chart:

Auto-Ontology is compatible with [Apache Ossie](https://ossie.apache.org/), the open standard for exchanging semantic models. Ossie includes a [converter for Auto-Ontology](https://github.com/apache/ossie-converters/tree/main/nvidia), which Auto-Ontology uses to import and export model definitions as Ossie YAML. Use **Settings → Import / Export**, or `POST /api/model/import` and `POST /api/model/export`. | Component | Technology | Role | Port | | ------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---- | | Frontend | Next.js, Better Auth, Prisma | Web UI, authentication, public API gateway | 3000 | | Backend | FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain | Text-to-SQL agent, catalog, ontology APIs | 3001 | | Ingestion service | FastAPI (Python 3.12+) | Ingestion and semantic compilation | 3002 | | MCP server | FastMCP | Read-only agent tools over the public API | 3003 | | Postgres + pgvector | PostgreSQL 17 | Catalog, ontology, app data, vector store | 5432 | | HashiCorp Vault | Optional | Connection credential storage | n/a | Keep ports 3001 and 3002 on a private network. FastAPI trusts the user identity the frontend forwards in the `x-auto-ontology-user-id` header, and the ingestion service's endpoints (ingest, delete, reset, compile) have no authentication of their own. Clients go through the web app on port 3000. ## Use it from your agent ### MCP server The [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server gives any MCP client read-only tools over the ontology. Each user signs in through Auto-Ontology, and every call runs with that user's permissions. | Job | Tools | | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | Readiness | `check_readiness`: can this deployment answer anything at all | | Terms | `search_terms`, `get_term`, `get_term_columns`, `get_term_sql_attributes`, `get_sql_attribute`, `describe_table` | | Answerability | `check_answerable`: does the ontology cover this question | | Questions | `ask_question`: the answer, the SQL, and the rows | Run the server against your deployment: ```bash AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 \ uvx --from "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git#subdirectory=mcp" auto-ontology-mcp ``` Cursor (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`): ```json { "mcpServers": { "auto-ontology": { "url": "http://localhost:3003/mcp" } } } ``` Claude Desktop (`claude_desktop_config.json`), bridged with [`mcp-remote`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-remote): ```json { "mcpServers": { "auto-ontology": { "command": "npx", "args": ["mcp-remote", "http://localhost:3003/mcp"] } } } ``` Restart the client after editing its config, then sign in when it prompts. Sign-in, configuration, and troubleshooting are in [docs/mcp.md](./docs/mcp.md). ### Agent skills Three skills teach a coding agent to work with Auto-Ontology. Start at [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md). | Skill | Covers | | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | | [`nvidia-ontology-setup`](./skills/nvidia-ontology-setup/) | Install, connect sources, compile, prove readiness | | [`nvidia-ontology-management`](./skills/nvidia-ontology-management/) | Inspect, model, certify, import/export, and publish | | [`nvidia-ontology-query`](./skills/nvidia-ontology-query/) | Ask questions and validate the SQL, rows, and answer | ### REST API Ask a question with `POST /api/chat/completions` on the web app's origin. Mint an API token under the user menu → **API Tokens**. The response is a server-sent event stream: a `result` event carries the answer, and `data: [DONE]` ends the stream. ```bash curl -N http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions \ -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"}' ``` ```python import json import os import requests response = requests.post( "http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions", headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]}, json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"}, stream=True, timeout=900, ) response.raise_for_status() for line in response.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True): if not line or not line.startswith("data:"): continue payload = line.removeprefix("data:").strip() if payload == "[DONE]": break event = json.loads(payload) if event["type"] == "result": print(event["answer"]["response"]) print(event["answer"]["sql_code"]) elif event["type"] == "error": raise RuntimeError(event["message"]) ``` Event types, multi-turn conversations, and the gateway trust boundary are in [docs/conversation-api.md](./docs/conversation-api.md). Every other operation is in the [OpenAPI spec](./docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json). ## Connectors, models, and predictions ### Sources Auto-Ontology connects to ten engines: - PostgreSQL - MySQL - Databricks - Snowflake - ClickHouse - Trino - Apache Kyuubi - HeavyDB - DuckDB - SQLite Add connections under **Settings → Connections**, or list them in `CONNECTION_STRINGS`. DuckDB and SQLite are connection-string only. See [docs/connections.md](./docs/connections.md) for URL schemes, scoping, and credential storage. ### Models Auto-Ontology uses four model roles. With an `nvapi-` key, each defaults to an NVIDIA NIM on [build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com): | Role | Default model | What it does | | --------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `REASONING` | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b` | Builds the ontology (terms, relationships, SQL attributes), writes each answer's SQL and explanation, and grades answerability | | `NON_REASONING` | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b` | Runs the agent's faster steps: question intent, entity extraction, candidate selection, and SQL checks and repair | | `EMBED` | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-embed-1b` | Indexes tables, columns, terms, and SQL attributes in pgvector, and matches each question to them | | `RERANK` | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-rerank-8b` | Ranks candidate tables when compilation builds bridge-table SQL attributes | To use self-hosted NIM or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set `_ENDPOINT`, `_API_KEY`, and `_MODEL`. Any field you leave unset falls back to `DEFAULT_MODELS_`, so the simplest setup fills in `DEFAULT_MODELS_*` and overrides only what differs. Use models that support structured output, and keep the embedding model the same for ingestion and queries. [`.env.example`](./.env.example) documents every variable. ### Predictions Set `KUMO_RFM_API_KEY` and the agent routes predictive questions to KumoRFM. KumoRFM is a hosted service: to answer, the agent uploads the connected tables to it, capped by `KUMO_MAX_TABLES` (20 by default) and `KUMO_MAX_ROWS_PER_TABLE` (unlimited unless set). Review what that sends, and complete your organization's data review, before you enable it. ## Integrate with us To integrate an agent platform, application, or storage provider with Auto-Ontology, [open an integration request](https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology/issues/new?template=integration.yml). The Auto-Ontology team maintains the code and doesn't accept external pull requests. Integration requests and bug reports are welcome as issues. Report security vulnerabilities through [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md). Maintainer workflow is in [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Reference | Topic | Doc | | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | | Kubernetes deployment with Helm | [DEPLOYMENT.md](./DEPLOYMENT.md) | | Connections, scoping, and Vault | [docs/connections.md](./docs/connections.md) | | Authentication, SSO, and API tokens | [docs/authentication.md](./docs/authentication.md) | | Conversation API | [docs/conversation-api.md](./docs/conversation-api.md) | | MCP server | [docs/mcp.md](./docs/mcp.md) | | REST API | [docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json](./docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json) | ## License Auto-Ontology is licensed under the [Apache License, Version 2.0](./LICENSE). SPDX identifier: `Apache-2.0`. Each NVIDIA-authored source file in this repository carries an SPDX header of the form: ```text SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2024-2026, NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. All rights reserved. SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 ``` Third-party open-source components used by Auto-Ontology are enumerated, with their upstream licenses and project URLs, in [`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](./THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Components added by the container images are listed separately in [`CONTAINER_THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](./CONTAINER_THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). ## Notice and Disclaimer NOTICE AND DISCLAIMER: This software automatically retrieves, accesses or interacts with external materials. Those retrieved materials are not distributed with this software and are governed solely by separate terms, conditions and licenses.  NVIDIA Agent Toolkit Expands, Grounding Enterprise Agents in Company Data 
 
 October 21, 2026 by Erik Pounds

 Agents are only as useful as what they know, and only as trustworthy as the boundaries they run within.  
 Leading enterprises are using the open source NVIDIA Agent Toolkit — now expanded with new tools — to customize and control agents, use company data to inform their answers and actions, monitor what they do and govern how they operate.  
 NVIDIA Agent Toolkit comprises: 
 
 The new NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation with NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries 
 NVIDIA open models including Nemotron Retriever and the new Kumo family 
 NVIDIA OpenShell secure agent runtime 
 NVIDIA NemoClaw secure agent blueprints 
 Tools and skills, like NeMo Relay and NeMo Compass  
 
 Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements 
 
 To develop agents that accomplish real work and are trustworthy from development to deployment, builders need an open agent stack that brings together the models, harness, runtime, data and tools. 
 NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation helps enterprises turn data into company intelligence agents can use. Agents can find relevant information, understand what it means for the business and use it to make predictions and help people decide what to do next. Companies can use Agent Knowledge Foundation without moving data, rebuilding existing workflows or changing governance controls.  
 The foundation features NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries , including cuDF, cuGraph, cuML, cuOpt and cuVS, and the new Auto-Ontology library, which translates raw company data into familiar business concepts — like customers, products and orders — and maps how they relate.  
 It also includes NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever and Kumo Structured open models — Kumo Tabular, Kumo Relational, Kumo Time Series and Kumo Forecast — which help agents find relevant company information to answer questions and make predictions.  
 OpenShell provides the secure runtime boundary, giving enterprises control over what agents can access and do. NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints provide reference designs for building secure, specialized agents. Effortless Web Scraping for the Modern Web





Selection methods · Fetchers · Spiders · Proxy Rotation · CLI · MCP

Scrapling is a Python Web Scraping framework that brings fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, powerful parsing, and concurrent crawling into one library. Scrape static pages, render JavaScript, interact with websites, and extract data from the API calls behind them. Build crawlers with reusable sessions, proxy rotation, automatic retries, pause/resume, and built-in data exports. Use it from Python, the terminal, or your AI agent through its MCP server and Agent Skill. From extracting a few fields to collecting a whole website as clean Markdown, Scrapling covers the full scraping workflow. ## What you can do with Scrapling - **[Fetch & interact](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/fetching/choosing.html)**: Fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, JavaScript rendering, Cloudflare Turnstile/Interstitial handling, persistent sessions, and background API capture. - **[Parse & extract](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/parsing/selection.html)**: CSS, XPath, text and regex search, adaptive element tracking, similar-element matching, and clean Markdown output. - **[Crawl & export](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/spiders/getting-started.html)**: Concurrent spiders, proxy rotation, retries, AutoThrottle, pause/resume, streaming, ready-made templates, and JSON/JSONL/CSV/XML exports. - **[Scrape with AI or from your terminal](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ai/mcp-server.html)**: An MCP server for AI agents to browse and extract data, an Agent Skill, CLI commands, and an interactive shell. Start with a single page: ```python from scrapling.fetchers import Fetcher page = Fetcher.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/') quotes = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall() print(quotes) ``` Or scale up with a spider: ```python from scrapling.spiders import Spider, Response class QuotesSpider(Spider): name = "quotes" start_urls = ["https://quotes.toscrape.com/"] async def parse(self, response: Response): for quote in response.css('.quote'): yield { "text": quote.css('.text::text').get(), "author": quote.css('.author::text').get(), } result = QuotesSpider().start() print(len(result.items)) result.items.to_json("quotes.json") ``` This prints `10` and saves the quotes and authors to `quotes.json`.

Click [here](https://github.com/sponsors/D4Vinci) and choose the tier that suits you! --- ## Key Features ### Spiders - A Full Crawling Framework - 🕷️ **Scrapy-like Spider API**: Define spiders with `start_urls`, async `parse` callbacks, and `Request`/`Response` objects. - ⚡ **Concurrent Crawling**: Configurable concurrency limits, per-domain throttling, and download delays. - 🔄 **Multi-Session Support**: Unified interface for HTTP requests, and stealthy headless browsers in a single spider - route requests to different sessions by ID. - 💾 **Pause & Resume**: Save pending requests and seen URLs with `crawldir`. Press Ctrl+C to stop gracefully and restart with the same directory. - 📡 **Streaming Mode**: Stream scraped items as they arrive via `async for item in spider.stream()` with real-time stats - ideal for UI, pipelines, and long-running crawls. - 🛡️ **Blocked Request Detection**: Automatic detection and retry of blocked requests with customizable logic. - 🚦 **AutoThrottle**: Stop guessing delays. The spider tunes the delay of each domain on its own from how fast the website responds, then doubles it (or waits what `Retry-After` asks) whenever the website starts blocking or rate-limiting you, and speeds back up once it stops. - 🤖 **Robots.txt Compliance**: Optional `robots_txt_obey` flag that respects `Disallow`, `Crawl-delay`, and `Request-rate` directives with per-domain caching. - 🧪 **Development Mode**: Cache responses to disk on the first run and replay them on subsequent runs - iterate on your `parse()` logic without re-hitting the target servers. - 🧩 **Ready-made Spider Templates**: Skip the boilerplate with `CrawlSpider` for rule-based link following, `SitemapSpider` for sitemap/robots.txt-driven crawls, `XMLFeedSpider`/`CSVFeedSpider` for iterating XML/RSS and CSV feeds, and `ShopifySpider` to collect products from public Shopify stores, one item per variant. - 🔗 **Link Extraction**: A standalone `LinkExtractor` primitive with allow/deny patterns, domain filters, CSS/XPath scoping, extension filtering, and canonicalization - use it inside the templates or on its own. - 📦 **Built-in Export**: Export results through hooks and your own pipeline or the built-in JSON/JSONL/CSV/XML exporters with `result.items.to_json()`, `to_jsonl()`, `to_csv()`, and `to_xml()`. ### Advanced Websites Fetching with Session Support - **HTTP Requests**: Fast and stealthy HTTP requests with the `Fetcher` class. Can impersonate browsers' TLS fingerprint, headers, and use HTTP/3. - **Dynamic Loading**: Fetch dynamic websites with full browser automation through the `StealthyFetcher` class supporting Playwright's Chromium and Google's Chrome. - **Anti-bot Bypass**: Advanced stealth capabilities with `StealthyFetcher` and fingerprint spoofing. Can easily bypass all types of Cloudflare's Turnstile/Interstitial with automation. - **Session Management**: Persistent session support with `FetcherSession` and `StealthySession` classes for cookie and state management across requests. - **Proxy Rotation**: Built-in `ProxyRotator` with cyclic or custom rotation strategies across all session types, plus per-request proxy overrides. - **Domain & Ad Blocking**: Block requests to specific domains (and their subdomains) or enable built-in ad blocking (~3,500 known ad/tracker domains) in browser-based fetchers. - **DNS Leak Prevention**: Optional DNS-over-HTTPS support to route DNS queries through Cloudflare's DoH, preventing DNS leaks when using proxies. - **Remote Browsers**: Instead of launching a browser locally, connect to one that's already running through CDP with `cdp_url`, whether it's on the same machine, another host, or a managed browser provider. You can also point any browser fetcher at your own Chromium build with `executable_path`. - **Background API Capture**: Enable `record_requests=True` on a browser session, then search its saved responses with `session.network.search(limit=None)`. Read API data and HTTP errors across page loads without sending requests again. History is bounded and saves text response bodies. - **Async Support**: Complete async support across all fetchers and dedicated async session classes. ### Parsing and Data Extraction - 🔄 **Smart Element Tracking**: Relocate elements after website changes using intelligent similarity algorithms. - 🎯 **Smart Flexible Selection**: CSS selectors, XPath selectors, filter-based search, text search, regex search, and more. - 🔍 **Find Similar Elements**: Automatically locate elements similar to found elements. ### AI Features - 🤖 **MCP Server**: Let AI chatbots and agents (Claude/Cursor/etc) scrape through Scrapling with HTTP requests, browser actions, screenshots, saved login state, and background API responses. Uses our stealthy browser with the right tools to enable suitable AI models to bypass any CAPTCHA is faces while working (not to mention our Cloudflare solver). It uses a lot of methods to reduce the content sent to the model, block ads, and protect it against Prompt-Injection. Remote browsers over CDP and HTTP transport with authentication options are included. ([demo video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qyFk3ZNwOxE)) - 🧠 **Agent Skill**: A ready-to-install [Agent Skill](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ai/agent-skill.html) that teaches coding agents the whole library, so the code they write with Scrapling matches the current API instead of guessing. - 📚 **RAG-ready Markdown**: Turn any page into clean, sanitized, LLM-ready Markdown with one line (`page.markdown()`), or crawl a whole website into a Markdown corpus with the `ContentSpider` template, all without an LLM in the loop. ([docs](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ai/building-rag-systems.html)) ### High-Performance & battle-tested Architecture - 🚀 **Lightning Fast**: Optimized performance outperforming most Python scraping libraries. - 🔋 **Memory Efficient**: Optimized data structures and lazy loading for a minimal memory footprint. - ⚡ **Fast JSON Serialization**: 10x faster than the standard library. - 🏗️ **Battle tested**: Not only does Scrapling have 92% test coverage and full type hints coverage, but it has been used daily by hundreds of Web Scrapers over the past year. ### Developer/Web Scraper Friendly Experience - 🎯 **Interactive Web Scraping Shell**: Optional built-in IPython shell with Scrapling integration, shortcuts, and new tools to speed up Web Scraping scripts development, like converting curl requests to Scrapling requests and viewing requests results in your browser. - 🚀 **Use it directly from the Terminal**: Optionally, you can use Scrapling to scrape a URL without writing a single line of code! - 🛠️ **Rich Navigation API**: Advanced DOM traversal with parent, sibling, and child navigation methods. - 🧬 **Enhanced Text Processing**: Built-in regex, cleaning methods, and optimized string operations. - 📝 **Auto Selector Generation**: Generate robust CSS/XPath selectors for any element. - 🔌 **Familiar API**: Similar to Scrapy/BeautifulSoup with the same pseudo-elements used in Scrapy/Parsel. - 🤝 **Drop-in Scrapy Integration**: Already invested in Scrapy? Decorate any callback with `scrapling_response` to parse the responses you already fetch with Scrapling's parser, no rewrite needed. - 📘 **Complete Type Coverage**: Full type hints for excellent IDE support and code completion. The entire codebase is automatically scanned with **PyRight** and **MyPy** with each change. - 🔋 **Ready Docker image**: With each release, a Docker image containing all browsers is automatically built and pushed. ## Getting Started Let's give you a quick glimpse of what Scrapling can do without deep diving. ### Basic Usage HTTP requests with session support ```python from scrapling.fetchers import Fetcher, FetcherSession with FetcherSession(impersonate='chrome') as session: # Use latest version of Chrome's TLS fingerprint page = session.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/', stealthy_headers=True) quotes = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall() # Or use one-off requests page = Fetcher.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/') quotes = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall() ``` Advanced stealth mode ```python from scrapling.fetchers import StealthyFetcher, StealthySession with StealthySession(headless=True, solve_cloudflare=True) as session: # Keep the browser open until you finish page = session.fetch('https://nopecha.com/demo/cloudflare', google_search=False) data = page.css('#padded_content a').getall() # Or use one-off request style, it opens the browser for this request, then closes it after finishing page = StealthyFetcher.fetch('https://nopecha.com/demo/cloudflare', solve_cloudflare=True) data = page.css('#padded_content a').getall() ``` Full browser automation ```python from scrapling.fetchers import StealthyFetcher, StealthySession with StealthySession(headless=True, disable_resources=False, network_idle=True) as session: # Keep the browser open until you finish page = session.fetch('https://quotes.toscrape.com/', load_dom=False) data = page.xpath('//span[@class="text"]/text()').getall() # XPath selector if you prefer it # Or use one-off request style, it opens the browser for this request, then closes it after finishing page = StealthyFetcher.fetch('https://quotes.toscrape.com/') data = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall() ``` ### Spiders Build full crawlers with concurrent requests, multiple session types, and pause/resume: ```python from scrapling.spiders import Spider, Response class QuotesSpider(Spider): name = "quotes" start_urls = ["https://quotes.toscrape.com/"] concurrent_requests = 10 async def parse(self, response: Response): for quote in response.css('.quote'): yield { "text": quote.css('.text::text').get(), "author": quote.css('.author::text').get(), } next_page = response.css('.next a') if next_page: yield response.follow(next_page[0].attrib['href']) result = QuotesSpider().start() print(f"Scraped {len(result.items)} quotes") result.items.to_json("quotes.json") ``` Use multiple session types in a single spider: ```python from scrapling.spiders import Spider, Request, Response from scrapling.fetchers import FetcherSession, AsyncStealthySession class MultiSessionSpider(Spider): name = "multi" start_urls = ["https://example.com/"] def configure_sessions(self, manager): manager.add("fast", FetcherSession(impersonate="chrome")) manager.add("stealth", AsyncStealthySession(headless=True), lazy=True) async def parse(self, response: Response): for link in response.css('a::attr(href)').getall(): # Route protected pages through the stealth session if "protected" in link: yield Request(link, sid="stealth") else: yield Request(link, sid="fast", callback=self.parse) # explicit callback ``` Pause and resume long crawls with checkpoints by running the spider like this: ```python QuotesSpider(crawldir="./crawl_data").start() ``` With `crawldir` set, press Ctrl+C to save pending requests and seen URLs. Restart with the same `crawldir` to resume. Save scraped items separately. Or skip writing the crawling logic altogether with the ready-made templates, like pulling an entire Shopify store's catalog: ```python from scrapling.spiders import ShopifySpider class MyStore(ShopifySpider): target_website = "example.com" result = MyStore().start() # Every product in the store, one item per variant ``` The template reads products exposed through public collection endpoints, one item per variant. ### Advanced Parsing & Navigation ```python from scrapling.fetchers import Fetcher # Rich element selection and navigation page = Fetcher.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/') # Get quotes with multiple selection methods quotes = page.css('.quote') # CSS selector quotes = page.xpath('//div[@class="quote"]') # XPath quotes = page.find_all('div', {'class': 'quote'}) # BeautifulSoup-style # Same as quotes = page.find_all('div', class_='quote') quotes = page.find_all(['div'], class_='quote') quotes = page.find_all(class_='quote') # and so on... # Find element by text content quotes = page.find_by_text('Albert Einstein', first_match=False) # Advanced navigation quote_text = page.css('.quote')[0].css('.text::text').get() quote_texts = page.css('.quote').css('.text::text').getall() # Chained selectors first_quote = page.css('.quote')[0] author = first_quote.css('.author::text').get() next_quote = first_quote.next parent_container = first_quote.parent # Element relationships and similarity similar_elements = first_quote.find_similar() below_elements = first_quote.below_elements ``` You can use the parser right away if you don't want to fetch websites like below: ```python from scrapling.parser import Selector page = Selector("...") ``` And it works precisely the same way! ### Async Session Management Examples ```python import asyncio from scrapling.fetchers import FetcherSession, AsyncStealthySession async def main(): async with FetcherSession(http3=True) as http_session: # `FetcherSession` is context-aware and can work in both sync/async patterns page1 = await http_session.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/') page2 = await http_session.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/page/2/', impersonate='chrome') print(len(page1.css('.quote')), len(page2.css('.quote'))) async with AsyncStealthySession(max_pages=2) as browser_session: urls = ['https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/', 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/page/2/'] pages = await asyncio.gather(*(browser_session.fetch(url, wait_selector='.quote') for url in urls)) print([len(page.css('.quote')) for page in pages]) asyncio.run(main()) ``` ## CLI & Interactive Shell Scrapling includes a powerful command-line interface: [![asciicast](https://asciinema.org/a/736339.svg)](https://asciinema.org/a/736339) Launch the interactive Web Scraping shell ```bash pip install "scrapling[shell]" scrapling shell ``` Extract pages to a file directly without programming. Use `--css-selector` to pick the content, or `--ai-targeted` to select and sanitize the `body` content. Use `.txt` for text, `.md` for Markdown, or `.html` for HTML. ```bash scrapling extract get 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/' quotes.md scrapling extract get 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/' quotes.txt --css-selector '.quote' --impersonate 'chrome' scrapling extract fetch 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/' quotes.md --css-selector '.quote' --wait-selector '.quote' --no-headless scrapling extract fetch 'https://nopecha.com/demo/cloudflare' captchas.html --css-selector '#padded_content a' --solve-cloudflare ``` > [!NOTE] > There are many additional features, but we want to keep this page concise, including the MCP server and the interactive Web Scraping Shell. Check out the full documentation [here](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) ## Performance Benchmarks Scrapling isn't just powerful-it's also blazing fast. The following benchmarks compare Scrapling's parser with the latest versions of other popular libraries. ### Text Extraction Speed Test (5000 nested elements) | # | Library | Time (ms) | vs Scrapling | |---|:-----------------:|:---------:|:------------:| | 1 | Scrapling | 1.99 | 1.0x | | 2 | Parsel/Scrapy | 2.06 | 1.035 | | 3 | Raw Lxml | 2.56 | 1.286 | | 4 | PyQuery | 23.98 | ~12x | | 5 | Selectolax | 197.02 | ~99x | | 6 | MechanicalSoup | 1545.15 | ~776.5x | | 7 | BS4 with Lxml | 1562.1 | ~785.0x | | 8 | BS4 with html5lib | 3412.73 | ~1714.9x | ### Element Similarity & Text Search Performance Scrapling's adaptive element finding capabilities significantly outperform alternatives: | Library | Time (ms) | vs Scrapling | |-------------|:---------:|:------------:| | Scrapling | 2.3 | 1.0x | | AutoScraper | 12.58 | 5.47x | > All benchmarks represent averages of 100+ runs. See [benchmarks.py](https://github.com/D4Vinci/Scrapling/blob/main/benchmarks.py) for methodology. ## Installation Scrapling requires Python 3.10 or higher: ```bash pip install scrapling ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > This installation only includes the parser engine and its dependencies, without any fetchers or commandline dependencies. So importing anything from `scrapling.fetchers` or `scrapling.spiders`, like in the examples above, will raise `ModuleNotFoundError` with this installation alone. If you are going to use any of the fetchers or spiders, install the fetchers' dependencies first as shown below. ### Optional Dependencies 1. If you are going to use any of the extra features below, the fetchers, or their classes, you will need to install fetchers' dependencies and their browser dependencies as follows: ```bash pip install "scrapling[fetchers]" scrapling install # normal install scrapling install --force # force reinstall ``` This downloads all browsers, along with their system dependencies and fingerprint manipulation dependencies. Or you can install them from the code instead of running a command like this: ```python from scrapling.cli import install install([], standalone_mode=False) # normal install install(["--force"], standalone_mode=False) # force reinstall ``` 2. Extra features: - Install the MCP server feature: ```bash pip install "scrapling[ai]" ``` - Install dependencies for ([building RAG systems](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ai/building-rag-systems.html)): ```bash pip install "scrapling[rag]" ``` - Install shell features (Web Scraping shell and the `extract` command): ```bash pip install "scrapling[shell]" ``` - Install everything: ```bash pip install "scrapling[all]" ``` Run `scrapling install` when you need browser fetchers. HTTP requests do not need a browser installation. ### Docker You can also install a Docker image with all extras and browsers with the following command from DockerHub: ```bash docker pull pyd4vinci/scrapling ``` Or download it from the GitHub registry: ```bash docker pull ghcr.io/d4vinci/scrapling:latest ``` This image is automatically built and pushed using GitHub Actions and the repository's main branch. ## Contributing We welcome contributions! Please read our [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/D4Vinci/Scrapling/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) before getting started. ## Disclaimer > [!CAUTION] > This library is provided for educational and research purposes only. By using this library, you agree to comply with local and international data scraping and privacy laws. The authors and contributors are not responsible for any misuse of this software. Always respect the terms of service of websites and robots.txt files. ## 🎓 Citations If you have used our library for research purposes please quote us with the following reference: ```text @misc{scrapling, author = {Karim Shoair}, title = {Scrapling}, year = {2024}, url = {https://github.com/D4Vinci/Scrapling}, note = {A Python Web Scraping framework for everything from a single request to a full-scale crawl!} } ``` ## License This work is licensed under the BSD-3-Clause License. ## Acknowledgments This project includes code adapted from: - Parsel (BSD License)-Used for [translator](https://github.com/D4Vinci/Scrapling/blob/main/scrapling/core/translator.py) submodule ---

 Watch the page in motion : record a short video and share it as a sequence of frames with timestamps to help the agent understand animations, moving controls, and changes that a single screenshot can miss. Pair this with the existing ability to chain actions! 
 Drag, inspect, adjust, and drop : hold a mouse button, move an item or slider, inspect the page while still holding it, then adjust and release. Supports left, right, and middle buttons. 
 Reuse a logged-in remote browser or start with a separate browser context, so the agent can choose the right session for the job. 
 Spend fewer tokens on tool descriptions with shorter text and less repeated guidance. 
 
 
 
 Dedicated remote browser sessions with control over login reuse . RemoteSession and AsyncRemoteSession connect to an existing Chromium browser through an HTTP or WebSocket CDP endpoint. They support the usual stealth session features, including Cloudflare solving. Both classes are also available in the interactive shell. (Check the docs ) 
 from scrapling . fetchers import RemoteSession 

 with RemoteSession ( cdp_url = "http://localhost:9222" , new_context = False ) as session :
 page = session . fetch ( "https://example.com" ) 
 
 new_context=False reuses the browser's existing default context and login state. Its context settings stay in use, and its existing tabs remain open when Scrapling disconnects. 
 The default, new_context=True , creates a separate context and closes it when the session ends. Scrapling uses its own tabs in either mode. 
 
 
 
 Choose your spider's log file encoding with log_file_encoding="utf-8" or another encoding. The default, None , keeps Python's default encoding. (Check the docs )

 Scrapling is a Python Web Scraping framework that brings fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, powerful parsing, and concurrent crawling into one library. 
 Scrape static pages, render JavaScript, interact with websites, and extract data from the API calls behind them. Build crawlers with reusable sessions, proxy rotation, automatic retries, pause/resume, and built-in data exports. 
 Use it from Python, the terminal, or your AI agent through its MCP server and Agent Skill. From extracting a few fields to collecting a whole website as clean Markdown, Scrapling covers the full scraping workflow. 
 What you can do with Scrapling 
 
 Fetch & interact : Fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, JavaScript rendering, Cloudflare Turnstile/Interstitial handling, persistent sessions, and background API capture. 
 Parse & extract : CSS, XPath, text and regex search, adaptive element tracking, similar-element matching, and clean Markdown output. 
 Crawl & export : Concurrent spiders, proxy rotation, retries, AutoThrottle, pause/resume, streaming, ready-made templates, and JSON/JSONL/CSV/XML exports. 
 Scrape with AI or from your terminal : An MCP server for AI agents to browse and extract data, an Agent Skill, CLI commands, and an interactive shell. 
 
 Start with a single page: 
 from scrapling . fetchers import Fetcher 

 page = Fetcher . get ( 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/' )
 quotes = page . css ( '.quote .text::text' ). getall ()
 print ( quotes ) 
 Or scale up with a spider: 
 from scrapling . spiders import Spider , Response 

 class QuotesSpider ( Spider ):
 name = "quotes" 
 start_urls = [ "https://quotes.toscrape.com/" ]

 async def parse ( self , response : Response ):
 for quote in response . css ( '.quote' ):
 yield {
 "text" : quote . css ( '.text::text' ). get (),
 "author" : quote . css ( '.author::text' ). get (),
 }

 result = QuotesSpider (). start ()
 print ( len ( result . items ))
 result . items . to_json ( "quotes.json" ) 
 This prints 10 and saves the quotes and authors to quotes.json .

 Key Features 
 Spiders - A Full Crawling Framework 
 
 🕷️ Scrapy-like Spider API : Define spiders with start_urls , async parse callbacks, and Request / Response objects. 
 ⚡ Concurrent Crawling : Configurable concurrency limits, per-domain throttling, and download delays. 
 🔄 Multi-Session Support : Unified interface for HTTP requests, and stealthy headless browsers in a single spider - route requests to different sessions by ID. 
 💾 Pause & Resume : Save pending requests and seen URLs with crawldir . Press Ctrl+C to stop gracefully and restart with the same directory. 
 📡 Streaming Mode : Stream scraped items as they arrive via async for item in spider.stream() with real-time stats - ideal for UI, pipelines, and long-running crawls. 
 🛡️ Blocked Request Detection : Automatic detection and retry of blocked requests with customizable logic. 
 🚦 AutoThrottle : Stop guessing delays. The spider tunes the delay of each domain on its own from how fast the website responds, then doubles it (or waits what Retry-After asks) whenever the website starts blocking or rate-limiting you, and speeds back up once it stops. 
 🤖 Robots.txt Compliance : Optional robots_txt_obey flag that respects Disallow , Crawl-delay , and Request-rate directives with per-domain caching. 
 🧪 Development Mode : Cache responses to disk on the first run and replay them on subsequent runs - iterate on your parse() logic without re-hitting the target servers. 
 🧩 Ready-made Spider Templates : Skip the boilerplate with CrawlSpider for rule-based link following, SitemapSpider for sitemap/robots.txt-driven crawls, XMLFeedSpider / CSVFeedSpider for iterating XML/RSS and CSV feeds, and ShopifySpider to collect products from public Shopify stores, one item per variant. 
 🔗 Link Extraction : A standalone LinkExtractor primitive with allow/deny patterns, domain filters, CSS/XPath scoping, extension filtering, and canonicalization - use it inside the templates or on its own. 
 📦 Built-in Export : Export results through hooks and your own pipeline or the built-in JSON/JSONL/CSV/XML exporters with result.items.to_json() , to_jsonl() , to_csv() , and to_xml() . 
 
 Advanced Websites Fetching with Session Support 
 
 HTTP Requests : Fast and stealthy HTTP requests with the Fetcher class. Can impersonate browsers' TLS fingerprint, headers, and use HTTP/3. 
 Dynamic Loading : Fetch dynamic websites with full browser automation through the StealthyFetcher class supporting Playwright's Chromium and Google's Chrome. 
 Anti-bot Bypass : Advanced stealth capabilities with StealthyFetcher and fingerprint spoofing. Can easily bypass all types of Cloudflare's Turnstile/Interstitial with automation. 
 Session Management : Persistent session support with FetcherSession and StealthySession classes for cookie and state management across requests. 
 Proxy Rotation : Built-in ProxyRotator with cyclic or custom rotation strategies across all session types, plus per-request proxy overrides. 
 Domain & Ad Blocking : Block requests to specific domains (and their subdomains) or enable built-in ad blocking (~3,500 known ad/tracker domains) in browser-based fetchers. 
 DNS Leak Prevention : Optional DNS-over-HTTPS support to route DNS queries through Cloudflare's DoH, preventing DNS leaks when using proxies. 
 Remote Browsers : Instead of launching a browser locally, connect to one that's already running through CDP with cdp_url , whether it's on the same machine, another host, or a managed browser provider. You can also point any browser fetcher at your own Chromium build with executable_path . 
 Background API Capture : Enable record_requests=True on a browser session, then search its saved responses with session.network.search(limit=None) . Read API data and HTTP errors across page loads without sending requests again. History is bounded and saves text response bodies. 
 Async Support : Complete async support across all fetchers and dedicated async session classes. 
 
 Parsing and Data Extraction 
 
 🔄 Smart Element Tracking : Relocate elements after website changes using intelligent similarity algorithms. 
 🎯 Smart Flexible Selection : CSS selectors, XPath selectors, filter-based search, text search, regex search, and more. 
 🔍 Find Similar Elements : Automatically locate elements similar to found elements. 
 
 AI Features 
 
 🤖 MCP Server : Let AI chatbots and agents (Claude/Cursor/etc) scrape through Scrapling with HTTP requests, browser actions, screenshots, saved login state, and background API responses. Uses our stealthy browser with the right tools to enable suitable AI models to bypass any CAPTCHA is faces while working (not to mention our Cloudflare solver). It uses a lot of methods to reduce the content sent to the model, block ads, and protect it against Prompt-Injection. Remote browsers over CDP and HTTP transport with authentication options are included. ( demo video ) 
 🧠 Agent Skill : A ready-to-install Agent Skill that teaches coding agents the whole library, so the code they write with Scrapling matches the current API instead of guessing. 
 📚 RAG-ready Markdown : Turn any page into clean, sanitized, LLM-ready Markdown with one line ( page.markdown() ), or crawl a whole website into a Markdown corpus with the ContentSpider template, all without an LLM in the loop. ( docs ) 
 
 High-Performance & battle-tested Architecture 
 
 🚀 Lightning Fast : Optimized performance outperforming most Python scraping libraries. 
 🔋 Memory Efficient : Optimized data structures and lazy loading for a minimal memory footprint. 
 ⚡ Fast JSON Serialization : 10x faster than the standard library. 
 🏗️ Battle tested : Not only does Scrapling have 92% test coverage and full type hints coverage, but it has been used daily by hundreds of Web Scrapers over the past year. 
 
 Developer/Web Scraper Friendly Experience 
 
 🎯 Interactive Web Scraping Shell : Optional built-in IPython shell with Scrapling integration, shortcuts, and new tools to speed up Web Scraping scripts development, like converting curl requests to Scrapling requests and viewing requests results in your browser. 
 🚀 Use it directly from the Terminal : Optionally, you can use Scrapling to scrape a URL without writing a single line of code!

 Getting Started 
 Let's give you a quick glimpse of what Scrapling can do without deep diving. 
 Basic Usage 
 HTTP requests with session support 
 from scrapling . fetchers import Fetcher , FetcherSession 

 with FetcherSession ( impersonate = 'chrome' ) as session : # Use latest version of Chrome's TLS fingerprint 
 page = session . get ( 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/' , stealthy_headers = True )
 quotes = page . css ( '.quote .text::text' ). getall ()

 # Or use one-off requests 
 page = Fetcher . get ( 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/' )
 quotes = page . css ( '.quote .text::text' ). getall () 
 Advanced stealth mode 
 from scrapling . fetchers import StealthyFetcher , StealthySession 

 with StealthySession ( headless = True , solve_cloudflare = True ) as session : # Keep the browser open until you finish 
 page = session . fetch ( 'https://nopecha.com/demo/cloudflare' , google_search = False )
 data = page . css ( '#padded_content a' ). getall ()

 # Or use one-off request style, it opens the browser for this request, then closes it after finishing 
 page = StealthyFetcher . fetch ( 'https://nopecha.com/demo/cloudflare' , solve_cloudflare = True )
 data = page . css ( '#padded_content a' ). getall () 
 Full browser automation 
 from scrapling . fetchers import StealthyFetcher , StealthySession 

 with StealthySession ( headless = True , disable_resources = False , network_idle = True ) as session : # Keep the browser open until you finish 
 page = session . fetch ( 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/' , load_dom = False )

 # Or use one-off request style, it opens the browser for this request, then closes it after finishing 
 page = StealthyFetcher . fetch ( 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/' )

 Spiders 
 Build full crawlers with concurrent requests, multiple session types, and pause/resume: 
 from scrapling . spiders import Spider , Response 

 class QuotesSpider ( Spider ):
 name = "quotes" 
 start_urls = [ "https://quotes.toscrape.com/" ]
 concurrent_requests = 10 
 
 async def parse ( self , response : Response ):
 for quote in response . css ( '.quote' ):
 yield {
 "text" : quote . css ( '.text::text' ). get (),
 "author" : quote . css ( '.author::text' ). get (),
 }
 
 next_page = response . css ( '.next a' )
 if next_page :
 yield response . follow ( next_page [ 0 ]. attrib [ 'href' ])

 result = QuotesSpider (). start ()
 print ( f"Scraped { len ( result . items ) } quotes" )
 result . items . to_json ( "quotes.json" ) 
 Use multiple session types in a single spider: 
 from scrapling . spiders import Spider , Request , Response 
 from scrapling . fetchers import FetcherSession , AsyncStealthySession 

 class MultiSessionSpider ( Spider ):
 name = "multi" 
 start_urls = [ "https://example.com/" ]
 
 def configure_sessions ( self , manager ):
 manager . add ( "fast" , FetcherSession ( impersonate = "chrome" ))
 manager . add ( "stealth" , AsyncStealthySession ( headless = True ), lazy = True )
 
 async def parse ( self , response : Response ):
 for link in response . css ( 'a::attr(href)' ). getall ():
 # Route protected pages through the stealth session 
 if "protected" in link :
 yield Request ( link , sid = "stealth" )
 else :
 yield Request ( link , sid = "fast" , callback = self . parse ) # explicit callback 
 Pause and resume long crawls with checkpoints by running the spider like this: 
 QuotesSpider ( crawldir = "./crawl_data" ). start () 
 With crawldir set, press Ctrl+C to save pending requests and seen URLs. Restart with the same crawldir to resume. Save scraped items separately. 
 Or skip writing the crawling logic altogether with the ready-made templates, like pulling an entire Shopify store's catalog: 
 from scrapling . spiders import ShopifySpider 

 class MyStore ( ShopifySpider ):
 target_website = "example.com" 

 result = MyStore (). start () # Every product in the store, one item per variant 
 The template reads products exposed through public collection endpoints, one item per variant. 
 Advanced Parsing & Navigation 
 from scrapling . fetchers import Fetcher 

 # Rich element selection and navigation 
 page = Fetcher . get ( 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/' )

 # Get quotes with multiple selection methods 
 quotes = page . css ( '.quote' ) # CSS selector 
 quotes = page . xpath ( '//div[@class="quote"]' ) # XPath 
 quotes = page . find_all ( 'div' , { 'class' : 'quote' }) # BeautifulSoup-style 
 # Same as 
 quotes = page . find_all ( 'div' , class_ = 'quote' )
 quotes = page . find_all ([ 'div' ], class_ = 'quote' )
 quotes = page . find_all ( class_ = 'quote' ) # and so on... 
 # Find element by text content 
 quotes = page . find_by_text ( 'Albert Einstein' , first_match = False )

 # Advanced navigation 
 quote_text = page . css ( '.quote' )[ 0 ]. css ( '.text::text' ). get ()
 quote_texts = page . css ( '.quote' ). css ( '.text::text' ). getall () # Chained selectors 
 first_quote = page . css ( '.quote' )[ 0 ]
 author = first_quote . css ( '.author::text' ). get ()
 next_quote = first_quote . next 
 parent_container = first_quote . parent 

 # Element relationships and similarity 
 similar_elements = first_quote . find_similar ()
 below_elements = first_quote . below_elements 
 You can use the parser right away if you don't want to fetch websites like below: 
 from scrapling . parser import Selector 

 page = Selector ( "<html>...</html>" ) 
 And it works precisely the same way! 
 Async Session Management Examples 
 import asyncio 
 from scrapling . fetchers import FetcherSession , AsyncStealthySession 

 async def main ():
 async with FetcherSession ( http3 = True ) as http_session : # `FetcherSession` is context-aware and can work in both sync/async patterns 
 page1 = await http_session . get ( 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/' )
 page2 = await http_session . get ( 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/page/2/' , impersonate = 'chrome' )
 print ( len ( page1 . css ( '.quote' )), len ( page2 . css ( '.quote' )))

 async with AsyncStealthySession ( max_pages = 2 ) as browser_session :
 urls = [ 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/' , 'https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/page/2/' ]
 pages = await asyncio . gather ( * ( browser_session . fetch ( url , wait_selector = '.quote' ) for url in urls ))
 print ([ len ( page . css ( '.quote' )) for page in pages ])

 asyncio . run ( main ())

 Scrapling requires Python 3.10 or higher: 
 pip install scrapling 
 Important This installation only includes the parser engine and its dependencies, without any fetchers or commandline dependencies. So importing anything from scrapling.fetchers or scrapling.spiders , like in the examples above, will raise ModuleNotFoundError with this installation alone. If you are going to use any of the fetchers or spiders, install the fetchers' dependencies first as shown below. 
 
 Optional Dependencies 
 
 
 If you are going to use any of the extra features below, the fetchers, or their classes, you will need to install fetchers' dependencies and their browser dependencies as follows: 
 pip install " scrapling[fetchers] " 

scrapling install # normal install 
scrapling install --force # force reinstall 
 This downloads all browsers, along with their system dependencies and fingerprint manipulation dependencies. 
 Or you can install them from the code instead of running a command like this: 
 from scrapling . cli import install 

 install ([], standalone_mode = False ) # normal install 
 install ([ "--force" ], standalone_mode = False ) # force reinstall 
 
 
 Extra features: 
 
 Install the MCP server feature:
 pip install " scrapling[ai] " 
 
 Install dependencies for ( building RAG systems ):
 pip install " scrapling[rag] " 
 
 Install shell features (Web Scraping shell and the extract command):
 pip install " scrapling[shell] " 
 
 Install everything:
 pip install " scrapling[all] " 
 
 
 Run scrapling install when you need browser fetchers. HTTP requests do not need a browser installation. 
 
 
 Docker 
 You can also install a Docker image with all extras and browsers with the following command from DockerHub: 
 docker pull pyd4vinci/scrapling 
 Or download it from the GitHub registry: 
 docker pull ghcr.io/d4vinci/scrapling:latest 
 This image is automatically built and pushed using GitHub Actions and the repository's main branch.

# Modern Web Guidance [Modern Web Guidance](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. *Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.* [Documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) · [Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/) · [Source Code](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src) · [Report an Issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues) ## Quickstart ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install ``` This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See [Alternative Installation Methods](#-alternative-installation-methods) below. #### Try it out (without installing) ```shell # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop" # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer" # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . ``` ## Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. **Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap.** Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: * **Modern Browser APIs**: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. * **Performance & Accessibility**: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. ## What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are **designed to be token-efficient**; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. ### Core Disciplines

🎨 User Experience

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color).

📐 CSS Layout

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid, modern color spaces like oklch, text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

⚡ Performance

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield).

📝 Forms & UI

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

♿ Accessibility

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

🤖 Built-in AI

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).
_View an example:_ [the `navigation-drawer` guide](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-components/navigation-drawer.md). #### The full list
